News.title: Families of two cyclists who died when car crashed into them pay tribute to dad-of-2 and ‘amazing’ mum – as man charged
News.content:
'LOVED FOREVER' Families of two cyclists who died when car crashed into them pay tribute to dad-of-2 and ‘amazing’ mum – as man charged

TRIBUTES have been paid to a dad-of-two and an “amazing” mum who sadly died while cycling when a car crashed into them.

The incident in Cobham, Kent, unfolded on Sunday as Steven Anscomb and Natasha Lewis cycled through the village.



Tragically, both Natasha and Steven were pronounced dead at the scene, despite the best efforts of medics.

The grieving family of Mr Anscomb, his wife Fiona and daughters Liberty and Imogen have shared the following tribute: “Steven was an amazing, kind, caring, hardworking dad, friend, and the most amazing husband.



“On Sunday he went out for his last ride before his big bike ride to Amsterdam. But sadly, he never came home.

“He will be so very deeply missed by so many and has been robbed of the special times of life.



“We love you forever Steve.”

While, Ms Lewis’s devastated daughter, Hermione, said: “No words can describe what an amazing, thoughtful, and strong woman she was.

“I am truly so grateful to have her as my mum. She was so healthy and exercise was one of her true loves. She had so many more years to experience this life.

“My heart goes out to everyone that has ever felt this pain. My mum was one of a kind.



“Mum, I love you so much.”

A 22-year-old man has been charged with causing death by dangerous driving in connection with the tragic collision.

Three riders were struck by a white Ford Focus during the smash with one rushed to hospital with minor injuries.

Two men and a woman were arrested at the scene as an investigation was launched.

Aaron Turner, 22, was subsequently charged with two counts of causing death by dangerous driving.



Turner, from nearby Higham, is also charged with failing to stop at the scene of a road traffic collision and possession of a class C drug.

He was remanded into custody and will appear at Medway Magistrates’ Court today.

A 21-year-old man and 19-year-old woman who were arrested have since been released on bail.

The force’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit (SCIU) has appealed for any witnesses or anyone with dashcam footage to get in touch.

News.title: EasyJet flight evacuated after power bank bursts into flames as passenger flee
News.content:
TERRIFIED passengers were evacuated after a power bank exploded into flames on an easyJet plane.

A power bank caught fire in the overhead locker as smoke began to fill the cabin just before it was set to take off from Italy to Prague, the Czech capital.



Cabin crew noticed smoke snaking out from the overhead locker and the captain immediately halted the aircraft towards the runway on September 10.

Pilots then declared a mayday and ordered everyone to get disembark for safety.



All 146 passengers on the taxiing Airbus A320 slid down inflated chutes onto the tarmac at the Milan Malpensa Airport in Italy.

Firefighters at the airport reached the troubled plane within minutes, followed by ambulances soon after.

The aircraft was taken to the airport fire station soon after leaving the gate.

Passengers on nearby taxiing aircraft were also evacuated as a precaution.



Airport operator SEA brought the airport to a stand-still where take-offs and landings were prohibited while the emergency team dealt with the fire.

But SEA confirmed the airport returned to full swing by 7:30pm.

Two people suffered bruises jumping down the inflatable slides but no serious injuries have been reported.

Italy’s air accident agency, ANSV, has launched a safety inquiry after the incident.

Early investigations found a lithium power bank overheating in the overhead locker, which led to it catching fire.



The Civil Aviation Authority said that the average passenger takes four different lithium power devices onto a plane.

Most airlines ban power banks from being stored in overhead hold luggage.

In 2024, there were 316 incidents where lithium ion batteries in hold bags were detected by UK authorities.

This doubled in 2025 to 643 reported incidents.

EasyJet‘s website reminds passengers that “power banks are prohibited from use on easyJet aircraft and must not be used to charge other devices”.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The low-fare airline also reminds that “power banks must be carried in carry-on baggage only and it is recommended that power banks are carried whey they can be monitored i.e. on your person.”

The Sun has contacted easyJet for comment.

News.title: Man, 46, charged with murder of ‘inseparable’ couple, 80 & 78, found stabbed to death at home by their carer
News.content:
DOUBLE STABBING Man, 46, charged with murder of ‘inseparable’ couple, 80 & 78, found stabbed to death at home by their carer

A MAN has been charged with murder after an “inseparable couple” were found dead by their carer last week.

Cops were called to the address in Blackburn at 8.22am on Monday after reports two people had been found with stab injuries.



Ismail Ahmed Leli, 80, and Fatima Leli, 78, were tragically pronounced dead at the scene despite the best efforts of emergency services.

Yasin Leli has now been charged with two offences of murder following the deaths.



The 46-year-old was arrested the same day the bodies were found.

Heartbroken family members described the pair as an “inseparable couple” who were “devoted to one another”.



They said in a statement: “On behalf of our entire family, we are heartbroken to share that we have lost our parents, the oldest and most cherished members of our family.

“Married and inseparable for over sixty years, they were the very heart of who we are — devoted to one another and loved by everyone who knew them.

“Their loss has left a void that words cannot describe, and we are still coming to terms with what has happened.”

Lancashire Constabulary has asked anyone with any information to come forward.



Leli has been remanded in custody to appear at Blackburn Magistrates Court today.

News.title: Plans to legalise assisted dying are REJECTED by MPs after knife-edge vote
News.content:
DEATH BILL Plans to legalise assisted dying are REJECTED by MPs after knife-edge vote

PLANS to legalise assisted dying were rejected by MPs today after a knife-edge Commons vote.

The controversial Bill was defeated by just 16 votes, with 286 MPs voting against and 270 in favour.



It would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to seek help to end their lives, subject to approval by two doctors and an expert panel.

Some MPs cheered and pumped their fists as the result was announced after an emotional four-and-a-half-hour debate, while others hugged in the chamber.



The defeat is a major blow to campaigners who wanted terminally ill adults in England and Wales to be given the right to seek help to end their lives.

MPs had previously backed assisted dying but the original Bill ran out of time in the House of Lords earlier this year.



Labour MP Lauren Edwards then brought back near-identical legislation in an attempt to get the plans over the line.

She urged MPs to “grasp” the opportunity to deliver “choice and dignity” for people at the end of their lives.

But opponents warned safeguards were not strong enough to protect vulnerable people and argued the NHS and social care system were not ready.

Former health minister Dr Zubir Ahmed, a cancer surgeon, warned he was “as often wrong as I am right” when asked to predict whether a patient had six months left to live.



He also described the Bill as being “less about relieving suffering and more about bypassing its possibility”.

Labour former minister Janet Daby also revealed she had switched sides after backing assisted dying previously, saying her “conscience was not at peace” after her earlier vote.

She also said: She also said: “I cannot shake from my mind a conversation I had with someone some time ago about assisted dying.

“They’d been diagnosed with HIV and Aids, and this was before the time of advanced medication for this illness. Their body was breaking down, and they had been informed that their prognosis was bleak.

“They said had assisted dying been an option for them then, they would have taken it. However, it wasn’t an option, and after some time, they have since been stabilised on medication.



“They’re in full-time work, and although they do have side effects and they do feel tired, they are living a meaningful life, and they are no longer, as you can imagine, an advocate for assisted dying.”

Supporters including former Cabinet ministers Liz Kendall and Hilary Benn argued the law was needed to give dying people greater choice and control over their final days.

Mr Benn told MPs terminally ill Brits were already travelling to Switzerland for assisted deaths, while Ms Kendall said people should have “as much control, say and choice over their lives” as possible.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham did not vote after saying he did not want to “unduly influence the debate” while the Government remained neutral and MPs were given a free vote.

Mr Burnham has previously said Britain’s palliative care system needs to be fixed before assisted dying is legalised.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The issue has deeply divided Parliament, with the majority in favour narrowing from 55 at the Bill’s first Commons vote to just 23 at its next hurdle last year.

Ms Edwards had warned ahead of today’s crunch vote that it could be another decade before Parliament gets another chance to legalise assisted dying.

News.title: Why do the clocks go back earlier this year and when do they change?
News.content:
SUMMER is coming to a close as the UK begins the transition from the bright, sunny months to the much cooler autumn and winter seasons.

And with that, comes a change to the clocks as in just a matter of weeks we will swap British Summer Time (BST) for Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). But why do clocks go back earlier this year?



Why do the clocks go back earlier this year?

If you pay attention to when clocks go back in the UK, you’d know that the change usually takes place in the last few days of October.

This year however, we will gain an hour on Sunday, October 25, with the clocks changing to Greenwich Mean Time at exactly 2am.



And although that may seem at least a couple of days early, it’s because the change always occurs on the last Sunday of the month.

So because the 25th is the fourth and final Sunday of October, that is exactly when we will gain an hour of sleep in 2026.

This won’t be the case in the next couple of years, with the final day of British Summer Time falling on October 31 in 2027, and then October 29 in 2028.

When do the clocks go forward in 2027?

Looking ahead to next year, you might want to go to sleep slightly earlier than usual on Saturday, March 27.

That’s because overnight we will see the return of British Summer Time, with clocks going forward at 1am on Sunday, March 28, 2027, and resulting in us losing a full hour of sleep.



Similarly to the October clock change, the schedule is fixed and we will always change time zone on the last Sunday in March.

And as previously mentioned, next year we will move back into Greenwich Mean Time on Sunday, October 31 at 2am.

Why do the clocks change?

The introduction of moving the clocks forward and backward dates back to 1907 when campaigns were started in Britain by builder William Willett.

He argued that moving the clocks forward in summer meant people could make better use of the daylight.



The original proposal was a complicated system, and attempts to introduce daylight saving legislation were blocked several times by the government between 1908 and 1916.

The change was finally introduced during World War I, when The Summer Time Act received Royal Assent on May 17, 1916.

The clocks went forward for the first time on May 21 of that year.

News.title: Three teen boys among four stabbed at KFC on busy high street – as eight held over ‘attempted murder’ & cops give update
News.content:
KNIFE RAMPAGE Three teen boys among four stabbed at KFC on busy high street – as eight held over ‘attempted murder’ & cops give update

THREE teenage boys are among four people who were stabbed in an alleged broad daylight knife attack at a KFC, as police hold eight over attempted murder.

The brawl on Bromley High Street, in South East London, unfolded shortly after 2pm yesterday and left a 21-year-old man in critical condition.



Four people were taken to hospital in the aftermath of the terrifying incident, the London Ambulance Service said.

An Air Ambulance helicopter was dispatched to the scene and three boys, aged between 14 and 17, and a 21-year-old man were rushed for treatment.



The teenagers received treatment for non-life-threatening injuries while the man was left in a critical condition.

However, following medical assessment, his injuries have since been deemed non-life-threatening.



All four of those taken to hospital, along with four other boys aged between 14 and 17, are among the eight who were arrested.

All eight remain in police custody as an investigation into the harrowing incident continues.



Witnesses described loud bangs and screams of horror as the altercation — feared to be between two rival local gangs — spilled into an alleyway in The Mall shopping centre.

Police set up a cordon around part of Bromley High Street and a side road the attackers are thought to have used in a bid to flee the scene.

Forensic police were last night seen examining evidence, including a rucksack, inside the fast food restaurant.

A Met Police spokesperson said: “At around 14:15hrs on Thursday, 10 September, officers were called to reports of an altercation on Bromley High Street.

“Officers attended the scene alongside the London Ambulance Service and London’s Air Ambulance and found three boys, aged between 14 and 17, and a 21-year-old man suffering from stab wounds.



“The boys were taken to hospital where they received treatment for non-life-threatening injuries.

“The man was also taken to hospital in a critical condition, however, following medical assessment, his injuries have since been deemed non-life-threatening.

“All four of those injured, along with four other boys aged between 14 and 17, have since been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and remain in police custody.

“Chief Inspector David Cooper, who leads policing in the local area, said:

“We recognise the impact this incident will have on the local community, and officers are working quickly to establish the full circumstances.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“There will be an increased police presence in the area, and we encourage anyone with information or concerns to speak to officers.”

“This incident is being treated as an isolated incident.”

News.title: King Harald’s older sister Princess Astrid dies aged 94 just two days after attending late Norway monarch’s funeral
News.content:
ROYAL FAREWELL King Harald’s older sister Princess Astrid dies aged 94 just two days after attending late Norway monarch’s funeral

KING HARALD’S older sister Princess Astrid has died aged 94, just two days after attending the late Norway King’s funeral.

In a statement the palace said: “His Majesty the King has received with great sadness the news that Princess Astrid has passed away.”



Flags will be thrown at half mast from the palace balcony to commemorate the late princess, King Haakon announced.

The news comes just two days after Princess Astrid attended her late brother’s funeral.



Sitting in a packed Oslo Cathedral, she said goodbye to her little brother and thanked him for “everything we’ve had together”.

She was pictured sat by the window at the Palace, looking out at a sea of flowers and grieving Norwegians.

King Harald was Europe’s oldest living monarch and had been on the throne since 1991 but was put on royal “sick leave” in August after falling ill with a blood disorder.

He passed away on August 28, at the age of 2026.



The palace confirmed his son as King Haakon VIII after he served as regent while Harald was on sick leave.

In a tribute to his late aunt, King Haakon described the Princess as “committed” with an “infectious spirit”.

A statement read: “Already at the age of 22, she had to step into the role of first lady when my grandmother, Crown Princess Märtha, passed away.

“In her work, Princess Astrid was always particularly concerned with care and inclusion for the most vulnerable in society.”

King Haakon also described the princesses endless support for King Harald and the family.



“We learned a lot from her, and she was not afraid to speak up. Her passing is a great loss for us. We will miss her”, he said.

In her last official assignment for the royal house, Princess Astrid visited Dyslexia Norway as the charity celebrated its 50th anniversary in Oslo in May.

Princess Astrid served four kings throughout her life.



First her grandfather King Haakon, then her father King Olav, her younger brother King Harald and her nephew King Haakon VIII.

King Harald previously described his sister as “boundlessly loyal”.

Before his death, King Harald was still technically in the line of succession to the British Royal Family.

He was the great-grandson of Edward VII and his godparents included Queen Mary and her son George VI – who were the late Queen Elizabeth’s grandmother and father.

Following the news of his cousin’s death, King Charles paid an emotional tribute.



In a statement released by Buckingham Palace, the King said: “It is with the most profound sadness that my wife and I have learned of the death of my dear cousin, King Harald V of Norway.

“For 35 years, King Harald served his people with unwavering dedication, guiding Norway through times of great change with warmth and humility.

“As Norway mourns the loss of so towering a figure, my whole family join in remembering a much-loved kinsman and friend whose kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty echoed from across the sea and across the decades.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

King Harald had been married to Queen Sonja for almost 60 years with the royal couple making it their mission to connect more with both the public and the media.

The couple shared two children, Princess Märtha Louise and new King Haakon.

News.title: Heathrow passengers left ‘vomiting blood’ after mask-clad gang sprayed tear gas at women & fled with their suitcases
News.content:
AIRPORT PANIC Heathrow passengers left ‘vomiting blood’ after mask-clad gang sprayed tear gas at women & fled with their suitcases

DOZENS of Heathrow Airport passengers were left “vomiting blood” after mask-clad gang sprayed tear gas and stole suitcases.

The busy airport’s Terminal 3 was closed for hours after the horrifying incident on December 7 last year which saw over twenty people treated by paramedics.



Armed cops stormed the Terminal 3 multi storey car park after a group of masked men doused multiple victims with the substance at around 8.11am.

Tyrone Richards, 31, Anton Clarke-Butcher, 25, Omoneke Whyte, 31, and Denzel Eduardo, 29, have now pleaded guilty to affray at Isleworth Crown Court in June.



At the time of the attack, the car park area was busy with passengers arriving and meeting people from flights.

Five people were rushed to hospital following the “intense” attack, which was sparked after a woman was robbed of her suitcase at around 8.10am.

Today, a sentencing hearing at Isleworth Crown Court heard that three of the defendants, wearing face coverings and dark clothing, sprayed a substance “believed to be CS spray” into a lift at an airport car park just after 8am.

The lift contained two women who had arrived on a flight from Johannesburg in South Africa that morning and two men who had met the women at the airport.



The court heard that the defendants were prevented from entering the lift by the group as “innocent parties ran away from the lift in some distress”.

Gas was emitted once the lift arrived at the ground floor, causing “difficulties for people, particularly at a Caffè Nero nearby” with some people being taken to hospital, the court heard.

A barista at Caffè Nero, who started to cough and vomit blood, told the court she was “scared” as she “felt fine one minute and then almost instantly unwell”.

The women who had arrived from Johannesburg then went to an airport taxi forecourt where the defendants followed them and took their suitcases – which were never recovered.

CS gas, which is used by police forces worldwide as tear gas to temporarily incapacitate people, was sprayed in the face of one of the women at close range at 8.03am “causing her to start coughing and choking”, the court heard.



It sparked severe travel delays for passengers including problems with shuttle buses and trains, after Terminal 3 was locked down following the incident.

A customer service agent at Terminal 3 said the incident was “terrifying”, adding she “felt dizzy and like I was going to pass out”.

The staff member also claimed that a woman in a wheelchair she was assisting “was struggling to breathe and using an inhaler”.



A mother who arrived from a flight from South Africa with her 14-month-old son said her child started to cough, telling the court: “I was immediately afraid for my baby’s safety and my own safety.”

A man who was ordering a taxi from the airport’s car park said “20 to 30 people were all coughing” after the incident and he was “struggling to breathe”.

Prosecutor Gary Rutter said he “could not say exactly what led to this incident”, but “one may suspect what was going on”.



He added that the incident left “members of the public, coughing, vomiting, and some vomited blood”.

Richards was arrested while still at the airport and the other three defendants were later identified and arrested separately.

Genevieve Moss, representing Eduardo, said the CS gas “was discharged by the rival group”, adding that he has asthma and this would have had a “dangerous impact on him”.

The lawyer said Eduardo, who has 12 previous convictions for 18 offences, would have “not agreed to take part in any activity involving such a substance” and expressed “deep remorse”.

Rushnay Sikander, representing Whyte, said he was “very remorseful”, adding he had a “traumatic childhood” including his father being murdered when he was five years old and that he had been the victim of three separate stabbings.



Shanda McAteer, representing Clarke-Butcher, who has 14 convictions for 31 offences, said he denied releasing the gas and “genuinely expresses remorse”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Patrick Harte, representing Richards, who has three previous convictions, said he was “not present when the first spray was released” and was “sorry to innocent bystanders suffering anguish”.

The sentencing hearing continues.

News.title: AI boom helps drive surprise UK growth in July
News.content:
Rob Arnold, co-founder of Ascendea, an AI firm which employs nine people, believes the UK hasn't seen the real economic growth potential from the technology yet.

He says his company is able to develop apps for other businesses "100 times quicker at a 50th of the cost" because of AI, but that the UK government needs to do more to invest in the sector as there are currently better opportunities in the US.

He knows a few small UK-based AI firms that have either moved to the US or are thinking of doing so due to a lack of UK government support.

Alongside grants and funding, he says the government also needs to invest in training companies on how to use AI as it can be dangerous if not understood properly. "It's like playing with a weapon," he says.

Paul Dales, the chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said July's data showed "the resilience of the economy in the first half of the year continued into the second half".

However, he added that higher energy prices and borrowing costs would soon start to hit growth, especially if the rises seen this week are sustained.

The Iran war has led to a sharp jump in oil prices, which has fed through to higher energy and fuel prices - affecting households and businesses.

This rise in energy costs has led to fears that inflation will remain high, and increase the chance that central banks will hike interest rates to keep price rises under control.

The Bank of England is meeting next week to discuss interest rates. Economists widely expect rates to be held, but some have predicted an increase before the end of the year.

Chancellor John Healey said the economy, was "demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty".

"Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year," he added.

"But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home - from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing."

Healey is to present his first Budget in October. He told BBC News this week that he wants people to confident about the economy, despite acknowledging the challenge of "historic high" borrowing costs.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said nobody in the government "should be high-fiving themselves" over the latest figures.

"Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we've got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years."

News.title: New hurricane season record as 'historic' El Niño leaves Atlantic eerily quiet
News.content:
A new hurricane season record will be set this week as a historic and still strengthening El NiÃ±o stifles tropical development in the Atlantic.

To date, no hurricanes have formed in the basin, despite this week marking the peak of the season on average - and there's no sign of development in the near future.

It means a new record will be be set for the latest date in the satellite era (1960s onward) without an Atlantic hurricane forming.

Currently, the record is 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.

In an average season, there would have been eight named tropical storms and three hurricanes by this point.

This year, however, there have only been five tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly and Edouard.

With few indications that there will be any development in the next week, this will mean the longest stretch into in a season where no hurricane has formed in the modern satellite era.

News.title: Kate visits patients at cancer hospital she raised funds for
News.content:
The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical.

"I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said.

"But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important.

"It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.

Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour.

"When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."

He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".

The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through.

"There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.

News.title: Polanski selected as Green Party candidate for Starmer's former seat
News.content:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski has been selected as the party's candidate in the by-election for Sir Keir Starmer's former seat in Parliament.

Polanski, who is a London Assembly member, will stand in Holborn and St Pancras on 8 October as he seeks to become an MP.

He was voted to be the party's candidate by members of the Camden Green Party ahead of local councillor Hamza Chowdhury.

Polanski said the Greens "might be the underdog in this election but we have the momentum and we can win".

He also spoke of how he made Camden "my home" when he first moved to London 20 years ago, adding he has "lived and worked across Holborn and St Pancras for many of the years since".

Polanski said: "I love this place but I also know times are tough here in Holborn and St Pancras. My story of constantly moving around flats is such a common story for Londoners and I know so many people are struggling right now."

He argued that voting Green "sends a clear signal" to the council and government that "we demand better for our communities".

Polanski added he is "confident but not complacent" about his chances.

He also said the election is about "putting pressure" on Prime Minister Andy Burnham, noting a Green MP would "work with him constructively to challenge him on the gaps in his plans".

Announcing the result, Green MP Hannah Spencer said members had "overwhelmingly" chosen Polanski.

The Greens finished second to Labour at the elections for Camden Council earlier this year.

The by-election is an early test of Burnham's popularity with the public and whether Labour under his leadership is able to fend off the challenge from the Greens in inner-city constituencies.

For Polanski, it will be a test on whether he can provide evidence that he can deliver on his ambition for the Greens to "replace" Labour.

Labour has held the inner London seat since it was created in 1983 and the party's candidate for the by-election is Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali.

The seat became vacant after former Prime Minister Sir Keir announced he was standing down as an MP to focus on a role in international affairs.

News.title: As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes next
News.content:
Republicans descended on Dallas this week to turn their midterm prospects around, hoping an unprecedented convention dominated by President Donald Trump would energise voters ahead of the November election.

Many left the gathering - billed ahead of time by supporters as a "Trump-a-palooza" political fest - just as worried about the party's chances in 2026, and wondering what the Republicans' future will look like after the president leaves office.

Vice-President JD Vance, who is widely viewed as a top contender to succeed Trump, offered his a party a glimpse of its potential future during his keynote address on Thursday night.

"We've got to take care of business this November," Vance told the crowds.

"Then we'll worry about what comes next."

His speech was interrupted at one point by chants of "48" - a nod to Trump's successor, who will become the 48th US president if they win in 2028. Vance let the chant linger briefly before waving it away.

News.title: Hull City footballer in crash near training ground
News.content:
Premier League winger Sorba Thomas has been involved in a car crash close to Hull City's training ground, the club has confirmed.

The 27-year-old walked away from the crash, which happened on Millhouse Woods Lane in Cottingham on Friday morning. His vehicle, a grey Land Rover Defender, was pictured on its roof, with broken windows.

Humberside Police said emergency services remained at the scene and asked people to avoid the area.

In a statement, the club said it was "relieved" to hear its player, who joined the Tigers from Championship side Stoke City earlier this month, was unharmed.

The club added: "The club is aware of images of Sorba's car circulating on social media and can reassure supporters that he has sustained no injuries and emerged from his vehicle completely unscathed."

A woman who lives at the scene said the crash, which happened at about 08:30 BST, woke her up.

"I was laid in bed [and] heard a noise â crash, bang," she said.

"I got up, come down and the car is in my hedge."

An NHS worker who lives on the road said the incident had left him unable to go to work as the road was blocked.

"There will be patients who will miss appointments because of this," he said.

"It's one road in and one road out. It was an accident waiting to happen."

News.title: Spies, strategies and missed opportunities: How the lessons of 9/11 are still being learnt
News.content:
No one can question that 9/11 was a colossal intelligence failure, or to be more specific, a failure of imagination in the US intelligence community. At the time both the CIA and the FBI were in possession of information which, if shared properly, could have prevented what happened.

The 9/11 Commission Report that followed blamed "failures of imagination, policy, capabilities and management" on the US government. The CIA and FBI, the report concluded, failed to properly assess intelligence and share information with each other and take sufficient steps to disrupt the plot.

This most basic of lessons has since been largely â although not completely â learnt, and sharing between Western intelligence agencies is infinitely better than it was in 2001.

The old rivalries between say, MI5 and Police Counter Terrorism have dissolved, first with regional 'fusion centres' dotted around the UK and now, most recently, with the establishment of the high-security Counter Terrorism Operations Centre in London. Here MI5 intelligence officers might find themselves sitting literally right next to police officers whose job it is to take the executive action to stop a terrorist plot. Equally, they might find themselves sitting next to a US federal agent from the FBI or a language specialist seconded from GCHQ.

Since 9/11, there has also been a root-and-branch reorganisation of US intelligence with the establishment of a National Counter Terrorism Center just outside Washington DC and a Director of National Intelligence to ensure that information is shared where it needs to be between the 18 separate US intelligence agencies. The relationship between the CIA and its UK counterpart, the Secret Intelligence Service (better known as MI6) is perhaps the closest one in the world. This is supplemented by the Five Eyes alliance that pools intelligence between the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

Yet disastrous failures of intelligence, assessment and strategic planning have still occurred since the planes hit the Twin Towers. In the run-up to the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, MI6 unwisely allowed its intelligence to be politicised, leading to the organisation suffering its worst reputational setback since the days of betrayal by the double agent Kim Philby and other Soviet moles in the 1950s and 60s.

News.title: I was in the epicentre - I'm so lucky to have lived
News.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic details of the aftermath from the 9/11 attacks.

On 11 September 2001, photographer and documentary filmmaker Paul Berriff was living and working in New York City.

He was caught up in the 9/11 attacks and still remembers the day in vivid detail.

More recently, he has become one of thousands of survivors to be diagnosed with terminal illnesses connected with the long-term effects of that day.

Now aged 80 and living near Northallerton in North Yorkshire, Berriff has recalled the events.

"Somebody came into the office and said a plane had hit the twin towers," he said.

First thinking it was likely to be a light aircraft or helicopter, often seen flying around the landmark, he phoned his wife who was at their home in Lower Manhattan.

She told him about "fire engines and people running around" and his "news instinct kicked in" and he travelled to the scene to document the events on camera.

As Berriff, a sound recordist and assistant producer approached, they could see "both towers were on fire".

"We could see these black dots coming down from the side of each building and we wondered what it was," he said.

"As we got nearer, we could see it was people jumping, so we knew it was pretty serious."

They headed to the base of the towers, where assistant fire commissioner Steve Gregory was sending firefighters in.

News.title: Families of British victims mark 25th anniversary of 9/11
News.content:
Families of British victims of 9/11 were among those who gathered in London's Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park on Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks in the US.

The event, hosted by UK charity Since 9/11, was held near a memorial sculpture made from steel recovered from the ruins of the World Trade Center.

In a video address played to attendees, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "On this anniversary, we must remember that hatred and fear did not have the last word on 9/11."

There were 67 British citizens among the 2,977 people murdered on 9/11.

The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester, with the US ambassador to the UK, have separately attended a special Changing of the Guard ceremony while a number of vigils are taking place in the US.

A memorial has been held at the site of the World Trade Center in New York, with relatives of the victims reading out their names.

At a ceremony at the Pentagon, in Virginia, President Donald Trump said the US would "never, ever forget", adding "on days like 9/11, we learn what a country is truly made of".

News.title: Rayner defends pause to local council overhaul
News.content:
Angela Rayner has defended her decision to pause plans to redraw local council boundaries, saying she wanted to ensure they would survive legal challenge.

The local government secretary also told the BBC she wanted to be "clear-eyed" about what the planned shake-up in 16 areas of England was likely to achieve.

It comes after earlier this week she abandoned proposals in four other areas, in the face of legal threats from Reform and Conservative-led authorities.

The surprise announcement on Monday has thrown the reorganisation plans into doubt, and drawn criticism from local leaders preparing for the changes.

Councils in affected areas have been drawing up proposals and consulting with residents since the reorganisation was announced in late 2024, in a process that is already thought to have cost millions of pounds.

Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Rayner conceded the decision to press pause had been "difficult" and she understood local authorities had put a "lot of time and effort" into their plans.

But she added she wanted to have "all the information" about the proposals before going ahead with them, after her reappointment to her cabinet role under Andy Burnham, ten months after her resignation last year.

"I got the legal advice and I hadn't had the time to review and to go through all of that, and court cases were looming," she told the podcast.

"If I'm making a decision that is highly likely to be in legal challenge, I want to make sure I've dotted my i's and crossed my t's," she added.

Rayner also said she wanted was "really clear-eyed on where we were going" with the plans, after Burnham had asked her to look again at the blueprints, which were announced by her predecessor Steve Reed.

News.title: Man admits murder of woman missing for 28 years
News.content:
A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of a woman who went missing 28 years ago, after telling police he disposed of her decomposed body months after he killed her.

Patricia Lashley, who was 33 at the time, was last seen near her home on Hall Street, Dudley, in September 1998.

Trevor Dunkley, 66, pleaded guilty to her murder and a separate count of preventing her lawful burial at a hearing at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday.

Dunkley's barrister Balbir Singh told Judge Michael Chambers KC that Lashley's body had never been found, and had decomposed after initially being put in the cellar.

"When he was moving about nine months to a year later, the skeleton was disposed of into the bins," Singh added.

Dunkley, of Himley Road, Dudley, showed no emotion in the dock as his barrister told the court that the charges had been brought based on a police interview.

He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced at the same court on 6 November.

News.title: First arrest over anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth
News.content:
The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible.

"Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.

This comes after RNLI volunteers were targeted on social media.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said.

"This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."

The disorder in Portsmouth followed a separate anti-migrant protest at the Port of Dover the day before.

News.title: Eight held over Bromley KFC multiple stabbing
News.content:
Eight people have been questioned on suspicion of attempted murder after a multiple stabbing at a KFC restaurant in south-east London.

The Met Police, ambulance service and air ambulance were called out to reports of an altercation involving several people on Bromley High Street at about 14.15 BST on Thursday.

A 21-year-old man and three boys aged between 14 and 17 were taken to hospital with stab wounds. The man's condition was previously critical but is now not thought to be life-threatening.

The Met said those four, plus four other boys aged between 14 and 17 have since been arrested and remain in custody.

News.title: Man loses appeal against murder conviction of British soldier
News.content:
A man who was jailed for the murder of a British soldier in Londonderry more than 40 years ago has had his appeal against his conviction dismissed.

John McDevitt, 61, claimed he was coerced by police officers using oppressive interview techniques into making a false confession to the killing of Private Neil Clarke on Easter Monday in 1984.

Pte Clarke was killed after he exited a military Land Rover that had been attacked with petrol bombs in the Bishop Street area of Derry.

The appeal, which was heard by Chief Justice Siobhan Keegan, Justice Adrian Colton and Justice Stephen Fowler, was rejected after the Court of Appeal in Belfast found that it "must fail on its facts."

McDevitt spent more than 10 years in prison after he was found guilty of Pte Clarke's murder.

In October 2024 the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) referred McDevitt's murder conviction to Northern Ireland's Court of Appeal following concerns about the credibility of police witnesses.

In April 2024, a further four convictions were then later referred to the Court of Appeal.

News.title: Man who let mum die on bathroom floor jailed
News.content:
A man who failed to help his 74-year-old mother as she lay for two weeks slowly dying on their bathroom floor has been sentenced to six-and-a-half years in prison.

Stewart Irwin, from Carlisle, finally dialled 999 in the early afternoon of 28 July 2023, and told the call handler his mother's skin had "started to turn blue".

Carlisle Crown Court heard paramedics who attended the two-bed Rydal Street flat found the pensioner unconscious, semi-naked and malnourished.

Mr Justice Bright said Irwin "made a conscious decision" to leave his mother without help and "must have realised that she was approaching death".

Warning: This story contains descriptions of injuries some readers may find distressing.

"Initially, paramedics thought Veronica Irwin had already died," prosecutor Phil Barnes KC told Carlisle Crown Court.

Even from outside the front door, medics detected the strong and distinct smell of a decomposing human body.

The court heard she was dangerously cold and some wounds extended, in places, through the full thickness of her skin.

Mrs Irwin, who was 4ft 10in tall and weighed just over seven stones, was transported to hospital but died later that evening from hypothermia and neglected pressure ulcers which covered more than a third of her body surface.

"No attention appeared to have been given to her basic hygiene needs," said Barnes.

News.title: Fraud-accused Southern Water boss appears in court
News.content:
The former chief executive of Southern Water has appeared in court charged with conspiracy to defraud, over allegations water quality tests were manipulated to avoid penalties.

Matthew Wright, 60, who denies any wrongdoing, appeared at Bromley Magistrates' Court on Friday alongside three other former employees.

Wright, along with Philip Barker, 57, Clive Massey, 64, and Mark Gregory, 63, are accused of conspiracy to defraud the Environment Agency and water regulator Ofwat.

It is alleged that between January 2012 and December 2017, the group manipulated a self-monitoring regime by carrying out artificial "no-flow events" at wastewater treatment works, to avoid failing environmental checks.

The alleged conduct could have avoided fines of Â£45m or higher, according to the charges.

Barker, Massey and Gregory were officers or senior operations managers at Southern Water at the time of the alleged offences, a previous High Court ruling states.

Southern Water has separately been charged with dozens of offences of failing to comply with environmental permit conditions.

Three further defendants - Mark Butler, 45, David James, 58, and Terry Stephens, 67 - also appeared in court on Friday accused of the same offence.

District Judge Stephen Leake said he was satisfied the charges were "related" and sent the case to Maidstone Crown Court, where the defendants will appear on 9 October.

Wright, Gregory and Butler appeared in person, while the others attended via video link. All seven were granted unconditional bail.

News.title: ‘Just in case I die, IPP killed me’: The harrowing warning of prisoner trapped on indefinite jail term
News.content:
For free real time breaking news alerts sent straight to your inbox sign up to our breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Sign up to our free breaking news emails Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Inside a cell on a wing for vulnerable inmates in Lancashire, Wayne Gregory left a message smeared in blood on the wall for the prison officers who found him: “Just in case I die, IPP killed me.”

He had also hidden a note written in biro on his upper thigh for those who examined him at the morgue, begging the coroner to investigate his detention on an Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentence.

Although he survived, the disturbing incident was just one of a series of horrifying acts of self-harm which have marked the latter half of his 19 years trapped on an indefinite jail term with no release date in sight.

His face and body, now irrevocably scarred by serious injuries which he regularly reopens, are evidence of the devastating toll the uncertain punishment has taken on him.

He is one of almost 2,300 IPP prisoners still languishing on the open-ended jail terms, which were scrapped in 2012 and have been described as “psychological torture” by the United Nations.

Hundreds like Gregory have unravelled during the punishment, including Carl Lamb, who cut off his own ear, and Thomas White, who set himself alight in desperation. At least 96 prisoners have taken their own lives in despair.

open image in gallery Wayne Gregory, who was sentenced to less than three years but has served almost 20, has repeatedly injured his own face in prison ( Supplied )

Last month, the prime minister announced he would finally end the injustice of the IPP sentence before the end of this parliament, bringing hope to thousands of such prisoners for the first time in two decades.

However, details of how the scandal will be addressed, including how complex inmates will be supported towards release, have not yet been decided.

Gregory, currently held at medium security HMP Garth, said he was “happy” at the news and the “end is in sight”, but revealed he was still struggling after years of self-harming.

When he was jailed in 2007, Gregory was told he must serve a minimum of two years and 275 days for a violent and serious attack he carried out with his brother, who was also handed an IPP sentence with the same tariff.

But while his brother was freed eight years ago and has rebuilt his life in the community, Gregory – whose anxiety means he struggles to complete the rehabilitative prison courses needed to secure his release by the parole board – has been left to languish.

His feelings of despair and frustration have spiralled into a devastating cycle of self-harm and destructive behaviour, which has prevented him from passing the parole board’s release test.

Now aged 42, he is battling to earn a place at a secure hospital where he hopes to start recovering, but, shockingly, he has been told he cannot be transferred to the medium secure unit until he stops self-harming.

“My brother has been released… and fitted back into society with no issues and started a family, whereas I’m covered in scars, frustrated, angry, institutionalised and suffering from crippling anxiety of groups of people developed over this sentence,” he told The Independent.

He said he turned to increasingly extreme self-harm as a “direct result” of the jail term.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has pledged to end the injustice of IPP sentences ( PA )

Gregory grew up in multiple care homes and foster placements before getting into trouble with the law as a teenager, receiving his first conviction at 15, before he was eventually handed an IPP sentence for wounding with intent in a joint attack on an extended family member when he was 23.

Both he and his brother were refused parole at their first hearing in 2011, but two years later his brother progressed to a Category D open prison while he was told to do more courses.

“I couldn’t understand why I couldn’t progress when my brother had, even though I was trying my hardest to complete anything asked of me,” he explained.

He first mutilated his own face in 2015, in what he describes as a “major cry for help”, which saw him inflict a serious wound to the right side of his mouth and cheek.

He warned staff at the prison he was going to start “chopping myself to bits” before he inflicted the wound, telling them: “It feels like I’m never ever gonna get out of this. So why do I give a s*** what I look like now? Nobody's gonna see me anyway.”

“I honestly felt at this point that I was in an endless pit of despair, and I was telling everyone this,” he added.

Around a year later, he caused a similar injury to the left side of his face, having failed to complete a three-year course due to his struggles with group therapy.

open image in gallery Almost 2,300 IPP prisoners are in jail without a release date, long after the sentence was abolished ( PA )

He believes his anxiety during group courses has seriously hampered his ability to progress in prison, adding that although officials know he needs one-to-one support, he has been told there are no resources to provide this.

Although he was briefly transferred to an open prison at HMP Leyhill in 2023, he was returned to a closed prison within a matter of weeks after he self-harmed again.

In 2024, he was considered for a placement in a 15-bed registered care home for men with complex needs, including substance misuse issues and mental health challenges.

However, this offer was withdrawn shortly before his parole hearing after Gregory started speaking out about his IPP sentence and first made contact with The Independent. According to documents in his parole dossier, the option of placement at the site operated by the Langley Trust was withdrawn because of the risk of negative publicity.

A spokesperson for the Langley Trust said: “We are unable to confirm or deny any connection with any named individuals, as we are required by law to protect our clients' information.”

Gregory is now hoping to join a major habeas corpus legal challenge brought against the government after the United Nations found a number of over-tariff IPP prisoners are being arbitrarily detained under international human rights law.

Gregory pleaded “when will it end”, adding: “I just cannot live like this.”

open image in gallery Carl Lamb, pictured as a child, has never been released from his IPP jail term ( Supplied )

Other prisoners have resorted to extremes, including Carl Lamb, who cut off his own ear with a razor blade in front of a prison officer in protest at his IPP sentence.

He was jailed with a tariff of one year, seven months and 25 days in 2006 for grievous bodily harm with intent following a road rage incident when he was 26. Now 46, he has never been released.

His brother Danny Eggar, 38, said he had watched his mental health severely deteriorate over the last decade, including some shocking acts of self-harm and inflicting the injury to his ear in 2020.

“For me, it’s not the physical scars, it’s what it’s done to him mentally,” he told The Independent. “My brother is not the same person that I knew 10 years ago. He had his life taken away from him.”

He described the uncertainty of not having a release date as “mental torture”, adding: “It’s an absolutely inhumane prison sentence.”

Lamb, currently held at HMP Woodhill in Milton Keynes, said he feels hopeful for the first time in “many years” after hearing the prime minister’s pledge to finally end the injustice.

He told The Independent: “A lot of people suffered deeply because of this sentence. I've been around and seen many prisoners in dark places – the suffering really can’t go on. What a joy it would be if the sentence was ended for people.”

open image in gallery IPP prisoner Thomas White with his son Kayden, aged just ten months ( Margaret White )

The Independent previously revealed how Thomas White, who has served more than 14 years for stealing a mobile phone, set himself alight and later smashed his face on the floor in desperation.

His family spent six years campaigning for his transfer to a hospital after his mental health deteriorated during the jail term. However, he has now been returned to Category B HMP Gartree, without a release date, after just ten months of care.

His devastated sister, pastor Clara White, called for a clear timeline for how the government will end the injustice for IPP prisoners.

“My brother has served more than seven times the punishment that the court originally considered appropriate,” she said. “He is a severely unwell man who needs treatment, stability and hope. Instead, he is being sent back to prison with no release date and no certainty about what his future holds.

“Andy Burnham’s pledge to resolve the IPP injustice is a welcome first step, but we now need a clear timeline and plan from the government.”

Justice secretary Alex Norris said the government will table legislation to end the IPP sentence “once and for all” by the end of this parliament.

“These are complex cases, and some of these offenders have committed serious crimes,” he told the Commons last week.

“Public safety will always be my top priority, and we must balance that with fairness. It will take time to get this right, but work will begin immediately, and on a cross-party basis.”

A cross-party oversight group will help to guide this, including the architect of the flawed sentence, Lord David Blunkett, and former justice secretary Robert Buckland, who have both called for IPP reform.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI), email jo@samaritans.org, or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week. If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

News.title: I shortlisted 45 of the best beauty advent calendars for 2026 – here’s my ranking
News.content:
When do beauty advent calendars usually launch?

In previous years, Liberty has kicked off the advent proceedings at the end of July, with most retailers and brands following suit into August and September. In 2026, however, a glut of beauty advent calendars dropped in July, including Harrods, Lush, Tatcha and Fortnum and Mason. The majority of other advents were subsequently revealed – in one way or another, with some brands still holding exact product rosters close to their chests – through the first week of August. We’re now in the throes of September and autumn, with just M&S keeping most details hidden, though I’m expecting all brands to have shown their hands by the end of the month.

Are beauty advent calendars worth it?

In short, yes, beauty advent calendars are always worth more than what you’ll pay; however, you have to consider whether they’ll be worth it for you personally. I’ve been diving into the best beauty advent calendars since 2015 (my first was from M&S) and I can say with confidence that some brands undoubtedly offer a better haul than others. Key things to consider are:

Do you travel a lot – Minis are part and parcel of a beauty advent calendar, so having a place to use them will be key.

Are you unsure where to start in your skincare, haircare or make-up routine – Minis can also be a great way to introduce yourself to premium brands without forking out so much initially

Do you have the time – With everything from face masks to hair bonding treatments within, these products will seriously level up your beauty regimen, but you’ll need to set aside an extra five or ten minutes to use them

What’s your budget – If you’re looking to spend less than £100, you’ll definitely have less big-name brands to choose from your haul. I recommend tallying up the cost of the products you like the look of to ensure you’re getting more than £100 of value from those formulas specifically. Extra products aren’t valuable if you won’t use them.

What is the price range of beauty advent calendars?

Beauty advent calendars can range in price from £40 to £650, with brands such as Revolution (£37.50, Boots.com) sitting at the lower end, and luxury perfumers like Byredo in the premium price category. More typically, the core beauty advent calendars (from Boots to Harrods) cost between £100 and £285 – though I’d argue you don’t need to spend more than £250 to take home a seriously spectacular haul.

What is the cheapest beauty advent calendar?

While there are calendars from make-up brands such as W7 (approximately £24) that offer beauty advent calendars below £30, I’d recommend looking to the likes of Revolution (£37.50, Boots.com), Soap and Glory (£43.20, Boots.com) and Boots x Macmillan (£44, Boots.com) for more exciting yet affordable products.

For instance, W7 mimics packaging from Charlotte Tilbury and Estee Lauder products – to name a few – but doesn’t *actually* replicate the formula. However the Boots x Macmillan calendar boasts best-selling brands including Liz Earle and No7. After all, if your calendar costs less but you never use the products within, have you really saved money?

What was the most popular beauty advent calendar last year?

In 2025 the Space NK beauty advent calendar was arguably the most popular and sold out within a few weeks of its September launch. In fact, in previous years it was reported that two Space NK advent calendars sold every minute after its release. Following closely behind the Cult Beauty advent calendar is always a best-seller and, this year, the Harrods fragrance advent calendar has already sold out, so I’m expecting the retailer’s main beauty offering to run out of stock in the coming weeks, too.

Why you can trust IndyBest reviews

As a senior shopping writer, this will be Lucy Smith’s third year reviewing the best beauty advent calendars for IndyBest. Prior to her professional coverage, Lucy has been purchasing beauty advents from M&S, The White Company and more since 2015, putting her experience in the category at more than 10 years. Elsewhere, Lucy covers all the latest beauty launches – such as the Dyson supersonic travel dryer – year round, so she knows what the must-have products of 2026 are for this year’s advent offering. Plus, having reviewed everything from the best foundations to the best hyaluronic acid, she’s well versed in the brands that pop (and the ones that flop), so you can trust that her round-up of the best beauty advent calendars for 2026 isn’t full of hot air.

Everton boss David Moyes has confirmed that Jack Grealish is in line to start in Saturday's fixture against Tottenham.

The England winger has returned to Hill Dickinson Stadium on loan for a second campaign, and delivered an impressive performance from the bench against Manchester United last weekend.

"I think Jack is ready to play," Moyes told a press conference. "He’s probably a boy who needs a football more than he needs the training sometimes.

"Game time helps Jack. But that’s still him building up to get to his best. He’s had a good week’s training and beginning to look ready to start."

Grealish quickly became a popular figure among Toffees supporters before a foot injury in January prematurely ended his initial loan spell.

open image in gallery Moyes is excited by Grealish's progress ( Reuters )

When asked about expectations for the 31-year-old's return, Moyes said: "Incredibly exciting if he gives us what he gave us at the start of last season. If we get that level from him then we’ll be thrilled."

Meanwhile, fellow summer arrival Christian Norgaard remains out with an injury and is not expected back until after the upcoming international break.

"I don’t think we expected it to be as long as this," Moyes stated. "He’s hugely important for us, someone who we’re looking forward to gaining his experience, his nous and getting to know him, and at the moment we’ve not had him on the grass, so that’s been the disappointing thing."

Everton are yet to taste defeat in the Premier League this season after following up a win over Crystal Palace with draws against Bournemouth and Manchester United.

Next up is a trip to Spurs, who are still looking for their first win of the season. Roberto De Zerbi’s men have not scored a goal yet this season, but did collect their first point following a goalless draw with Nottingham Forest last weekend after previous defeats by Brentford and Newcastle.

Spurs have also been boosted by the news that Lucas Bergvall has signed a new contract with the club. The Swedish midfielder was linked with a move away over the summer, but has now ended speculation over his immediate future.

A former minister who has stage 4 incurable breast cancer has made an impassioned plea against assisted dying, giving an emotional account of her experience of receiving a terminal diagnosis.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill has returned to Parliament, after running out of time earlier this year.

Ashley Dalton, the Labour MP for West Lancashire, who resigned from her post as a health minister earlier this year while she continues to undergo chemotherapy, urged colleagues to vote against the bill and expressed concern over a lack of safeguards.

"The last time this House considered this bill at second reading, I was keeping a secret”, Ms Dalton said. “Whilst honourable and right honourable members were debating the issue, I was grappling with my own terminal diagnosis.

open image in gallery The former minister has become a firm opponent to assisted dying legislation ( ParliamentTV )

“I was told I have stage four incurable metastatic breast cancer. I was overwhelmed with grief, fear, and anxiety. I was scared of what was to come, and I was fearful of how it would impact my family and my loved ones.

“I was scared that I was going to get really poorly, and thinking, how will I cope? How will my family cope? How will I be cared for? How will I afford it? How badly will it hurt? How long will it last?

"When you hear those words, depression, anxiety, grief, fear, shame, and guilt come in bounds. Suicide risk is highest immediately after diagnosis, and it usually falls quickly within three to six months.”

She argued that this bill "makes no provision to support this difficult transition or to create safeguards around it”, warning that an individual can "also be suicidal and have unmet mental health needs prior to developing a terminal illness, and then ask the state to kill them, without any assessment of their psychological health, just their mental capacity”.

"I would be lying if I said that when thinking about all that was to come, I didn't consider that it might just be fairer and easier on everyone if I just got the dying over with as soon as possible”, she said.

“Having treatable depression, however, will not exclude anyone from an assisted death within this bill, and depression is common among people with terminal illness. But it is often treatable.”

The Bill would allow adults in England and Wales, with fewer than six months to live, to apply for an assisted death subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But Ms Dalton argued that it is extremely difficult to assess how long someone has left to live.

"I don't know how long I will live. I will be on treatment for life, however long or short that may be. I, at the moment, live between scans in nine to 12 week blocks of time. The last scan may show the disease is stable, but the next scan might show that it is growing again. If the disease is stable, the drug's working, and we can carry on.

open image in gallery Assisted dying campaigners demonstrate in front of the Houses of Parliament as MPs debate whether to legalise assisted dying for terminally ill people ( Reuters )

"Eventually, the drug will stop working, the cancer will grow, and we'll have to try another drug and see if that works. At some point, we'll either run out of drugs to try, or I'll be too poorly to tolerate them. Then I die. It could be months. It could be years. No one really knows. Prognosis is notoriously difficult to predict.”

Ms Dalton also claimed that people with terminal diagnoses have been “scaremongered” into "believing our deaths will be horrific”.

“The idea that it is not possible to alleviate pain and discomfort is false. People have been terrorized with tales of people vomiting up their own feces as though this is commonplace during death. It is vanishingly rare, and you know, bowel obstructions are more common, but they are treatable. I know. I've had one.

"It's nothing short of irresponsible to scaremonger people like me into believing our deaths will be horrific, when all the evidence suggests that with access to good palliative care, deaths are on the whole gentle”, she said.

Closing out her emotional intervention, Ms Dalton told the Commons: "My days may be numbered, but that doesn't mean that I want this chamber to rush through bad law just so I might have a chance to see it or use it. It's of huge importance.

"If honourable and right honourable members have any doubt that the exact bill before us today is not the best it could be, is anything less than excellent, well thought out, and robustly drafted legislation that protects the vulnerable and recognises the expertise of our world-class clinicians, and a bill that I and other terminally ill people deserve, then I urge them to vote no or vote abstain.”

Lauren Edwards, the MP who has re-introduced the Bill to the Commons, taking over from its previous sponsor Kim Leadbeater, has urged her fellow MPs to send the near-identical Bill back to the Lords “so that they can finish what they started” in scrutinising the legislation.

The Bill’s fall in the Lords in April prompted claims of a “denial of democracy” from supporters who criticised some peers for tabling hundreds of amendments and effectively talking the legislation out.

Ms Edwards said MPs on Friday were being asked to consider “who ultimately decides the laws that govern our nations” – a reference to the fact the Lords is an unelected chamber.

Ahead of the debate around 70 MPs had put their names forward to speak on the Bill – with the chamber’s green benches almost full – and a vote is expected to take place by 2.30pm.

While the Bill passed two votes in the Commons in 2024 and 2025, the second vote saw the majority in favour of the Bill narrow to 23 from 55.

A 9/11 widow interrupted Friday's annual reading of victims' names at ground zero in New York City to accuse Saudi Arabia of complicity in the al Qaeda terror attacks that claimed thousands of innocent lives.

After announcing the name of her late husband, Tom Strada, Terry Strada said, “You are missed more with each year that passes.”

Strada, the national chair of 9/11 Families United, then sparked applause by saying it had been “25 years, and still we have no justice” for the alleged role Saudi Arabia played in the attacks on September 11, 2001.

She accused the kingdom of having “fomented a rancid culture of anti-American terrorism around the globe” and of having “sent its agents to support the radical Islamic hijackers” who flew passenger planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center. The attacks killed 2,753 people, including hundreds of heroic first responders.

Terry Strada, a 9/11 widow and national chair of 9/11 Families United, condemns Saudi Arabia during a 25th anniversary memorial ceremony in New York City on September 11, 2026 ( AP Photo/Pamela Smith )

Strada then turned her ire on unidentified U.S. government officials.

“But for 25 years, administration after administration — including leaders in front of us here today — chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families,” she said. “ It has been one betrayal after another.”

Strada said President Donald Trump — who reportedly skipped the ceremony in part because he wouldn’t be allowed to give a speech — “can still change that,” and she called on him to do so.

“Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through,” she said.

Strada also asked Vice President JD Vance, who was in the audience, to “carry that message back” to the White House.

“Stand with the families. Stand with the survivors. Stand with Americans,” she said. “As my husband Tom would have said, that is always the right thing to do.”

A civil lawsuit over Saudi Arabia’s alleged involvement in the 9/11 terrorist hijackings — which also killed hundreds of people at the Pentagon and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania — is heading toward a trial after a federal judge in New York City last denied a motion to dismiss the case, ABC News reported last week.

Newly revealed records include a video recording that allegedly shows a Saudi agent casing the U.S. Capitol in Washington, as well as a sketch that allegedly shows calculations for navigating a plane toward a ground target, according to ABC News.

Follow for more on this developing story
