World.title: Russian assets are not the focus now, Brussels says as calls for action grow louder
World.content:
The immobilised assets from the Russian Central Bank are not "the primary focus" at the moment, the European Commission said on Friday amid growing calls to channel the €210 billion into additional support for cash-strapped Ukraine.

 

Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, backed by the Baltics, have asked the executive to devise new legal options to tap the assets.

Ukraine has endorsed the initiative and pitched creating an EU-owned custodian to hold the assets kept at Euroclear, a depository in central Brussels.

And this week, a cross-party group of 122 members of the European Parliament sent a letter to the Commission, pleading to "reopen the political discussion" on the assets and advance the custodian pitch to "overcome" the Belgian objections.

But on Friday, the Commission sought to tamp down the momentum.

"That's not the primary focus," Paula Pinho, the Commission's chief spokesperson, said. "We had worked extensively on this, and now the focus is somewhere else."

The Commission's priority, Pinho explained, is twofold.

On the one hand, to continue the gradual disbursements of the €90 billion loan, which covers financial and military assistance for Ukraine.

On the other hand, to engage with the Ukrainian government and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to figure out the exact scope of the budget shortfall.

Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy caught allies off guard when he asked them to plug a $27 billion (€23 billion) deficit in the Ministry of Defence. Kyiv has also flagged €32.6 billion in uncovered budget needs for next year.

Since then, EU and IMF officials have been scrambling to understand the nature and the origin of the eye-popping number.

Zelenskyy's request laid bare the enormous task that Europe faces in helping a country under invasion without US contributions. It also helped revive the push to tap into the Russian assets, which supporters say would spare European taxpayers.

The Commission tried to use the assets last year through an inventive, multi-layered legal proposal that fell apart in December at a make-or-break summit. The executive, which invested a great deal of political capital defending the scheme, met furious resistance from Belgium and strong reservations from Euroclear.

"We left it in December at a very important discussion at the European Council. We never said that it was out of the table. It remains there as a tool," Pinho said.

The Commission, she added, needs to gauge Ukraine's additional financial needs "before we can speak of concrete possible tools to address them".

Separately, Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told Euronews that his services were ready to "re-engage" on the assets and "help find a way forward".

But he stopped short of committing to a new legal text, noting the Commission would wait for guarantees that an "agreement can be reached among member states".

Belgium has already said its objections had not "magically disappeared". Meanwhile, Euroclear is battling a legal challenge from the Russian Central Bank.

World.title: French ESA astronaut Thomas Pesquet: Europe must 'maximise scientific return' from ISS before closure
World.content:
French astronaut Thomas Pesquet told Euronews that Europe and France must "maximise the scientific return" from ESA's next private mission aboard PAM-6 to the International Space Station (ISS), which he will lead in summer 2027.

 

Speaking to Euronews at the International Space Summit held in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday, Pesquet said "we know the ISS is coming to an end soon and we don't know when Europe and specifically France's next turn, will come again, given that long-term missions to the ISS are assigned on a rotating basis."

The ISS is scheduled to retire and be deorbited in 2030 due to its ageing hardware and maintenance issues, as well as the space sector's shift towards commercial activities.

Russia and the US launched the first segments in late 1998, and astronauts moved in two years later. Europe and Japan added their own modules, and Canada provided robotic arms.

Pesquet is part of the European Space Agency's (ESA) Astronaut Corps, which selects, trains, and provides crew members for US and Russian space missions.

French ESA astronaut Thomas Pesquet speaks to Euronews, 9 September Euronews

The International Space Summit — co-hosted by France and Germany — gathered space industry leaders, heads of state and astronauts to call for greater European sovereignty and investment in the space sector.

At present, ESA does not have its own operational crewed spacecraft or crewed launcher.

For Pesquet, the move towards greater European space sovereignty is a step in the right direction, given that consistent partnerships on the world stage have become a "challenge".

"Given the upheavals in the geopolitical landscape, without getting into the details, it’s clear that it’s difficult to rely on long term partners, consistency has become a rare commodity on the international stage. We believe we must first do things ourselves first."

"That is something that will not change in coming years," he added.

Europe's push to build up its military space assets has been driven by Russia's war in Ukraine, as well as a decision to distance itself from its longstanding dependence on the US in the space domain.

Kyiv's reliance on Elon Musk's Starlink has shown the strategic importance of space services in war, given that satellite networks can provide connectivity even when infrastructure is damaged or destroyed.

"Going forward, maybe there will be more small stations rather than one large station — a European station. I’d really like to see American, Indian, and Chinese stations. We’re also preparing for that world, which is coming very quickly," said Pesquet.

Despite this, he assured that once astronauts lift off, geopolitics down on Earth usually get left behind. A single space crew can include astronauts and cosmonauts from several agencies — from Europe's ESA, Russia's Roscosmos and the United States' NASA.

"I remember the early days of my career, around 2011, when we already tended to focus on the things we had in common, on the very things that brought us together — rather than talking about the things that divided us."

"When you’re part of a crew — on a boat, in a plane, or in a submarine, it's part of collective intelligence, so we keep this attitude. Obviously, relations between organisations aren't always easy. But at least at our level we don’t want that to affect our work, we don’t want it to affect safety, so we maintain healthy relationships."

Europe 'needs' a new space strategy

ESA significantly increased its funding in November 2025, approving a record-breaking €22.3 billion budget for 2026–2028, with €35 billion for space for security and defence.

For Géraldine Naja, director of space transportation at ESA, Europe has "understood" that it needs a change of strategy after typically investing far less than the US and China in space.

"If you compare GNP and the number of people, we are spending six times less than the US," she said.

For Naja, the successful launch of the first commercial rocket — Spectrum — to orbit from mainland Europe by German startup Isar Aerospace on Saturday marked a significant step in the right direction.

"Spectrum is a rocket built and developed by Isar Aerospace, which was incubated in Bavaria, which benefited from several ESA programmes that aim to support new companies and help them commercialise their products."

"Space is very important to defence because the technologies are different and also we have now realised that space tools are absolutely necessary for any defence policy."

"When you look at what is going around us, unfortunately, most of the weapons require communication, navigational tools, which can only be provided by space. Space itself can become a theatre for war," she said.

World.title: Houthis seize key Yemeni island in Bab el-Mandeb, taking control of the strait
World.content:
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Friday, after capturing an island located in the middle of the crucial Red Sea waterway, a local government official and eyewitnesses said.

 

"Boats carrying armed Houthi fighters reached Mayyun Island after government forces withdrew from it yesterday," the official said, referring to a rocky volcanic island also known as Perim that divides the narrowest part of the strait into two shipping lanes.

"The Houthis have completed their takeover of the Bab el-Mandeb area and Mayyun Island, which is located in the middle of the strait," he added, speaking on condition of anonymity.

An eyewitness said gunmen were "deploying along the Bab el-Mandeb shore and are driving around in military vehicles."

Further reports emerged on Friday that the group also seized the town of Dhubab and the coastal village of Murad, meaning that all of Yemen's Red Sea coast was now under Houthi control in an 18-hour blitz.

Government military sources said that the Houthis have besieged government troops on the Hanish islands, following earlier reports that the Zuqar island — the largest of the three major islands in the Red Sea archipelago further north from Bab el-Mandeb — was already captured.

They said they were unsure about the status of their soldiers, who number more than 2,000, but believe the Houthis have ordered them to surrender.

A senior military official said that the besieged forces have appealed to authorities for "rescue, food and water, and the lifting of the siege, which would require air support".

On Thursday, Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from government forces in a blitz offensive that also saw them taking control of Zuqar Island in the southern Red Sea "after rocket attacks and a ground assault carried out using boats transporting fighters," according to military sources.

By Thursday evening, multiple videos appeared online of Houthi fighters' apparent celebrations in Mokha and their seizure of considerable weapons and equipment left behind by government forces. Euronews could not verify the authenticity of the footage.

The Houthis, who controlled about one-third of Yemen's territory prior to the offensive, have previously targeted shipping in the narrow waterway which links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal.

Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb account for more than one quarter of seaborne crude oil and petroleum trade. Nearly one-third of the world's container traffic passes through the Red Sea alone.

The Houthis have also reportedly consulted with Tehran on imposing a safe passage toll through the strait over the summer, in an apparent plot to further strain global economies.

Yemen's internationally recognised government has repeatedly warned of Houthi plans for taking control of the waterway, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears".

Yet a member of the Houthis' politburo on Friday sought to allay global fears for international shipping, stating the group posed "no danger" to Red Sea cargo routes.

"Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly," Hazem al-Assad told the Al-Araby al-Jadeed news outlet. "There is no cause for international concern, as they face no danger from the Yemeni side."

The Houthis corrected this statement to say Saudi Arabia remains an exception.

"Maritime navigation is safe for all companies except Saudi ships, which have already been banned," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Friday evening.

Houthis marching on

Formally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis came to power in late 2014 after storming Sana'a and seizing the presidential palace and key military sites, forcing Yemen's government into exile.

The group is part of Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

The group triggered a return to hostilities in Yemen's civil war in July, when they let an Iranian plane land in defiance of Saudi control of Yemeni airspace.

Riyadh retaliated by striking the airport, triggering the Houthis to declare a blockade on the kingdom targeting its oil trade in July.

The Houthis engaged in a large-scale offensive last week against government forces backed by Saudi Arabia, while also launching attacks on Saudi territory that left dozens wounded, leading Riyadh to respond with daily strikes on Houthi-held parts of Yemen.

Saudi Arabia, which earlier this week said it had always offered “opportunities for negotiation,” also said it has the right to defend itself.

Houthi attacks on oil infrastructure and Saudi tankers have further contributed to a spike in oil prices, which surpassed $100 a barrel on Thursday.

A friend in need

Last month, Saudi Arabia signed a NATO-style mutual defence agreement with Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan in Mecca, but it seems unlikely either of the two would get involved.

On Tuesday, Pakistani Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistan would "honour" the pact "in case there is a need".

Just one day later, the Pakistan foreign ministry said that the Mecca pact was a "defensive alliance focused on deterrence".

"There is no such thing under discussion right now. When the time comes, we will act under the agreement," spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told the press at the weekly media briefing.

In July, US President Donald Trump said Washington would respond against the Houthis if they attempted to block maritime traffic in the Red Sea, after weeks of US strikes from March 2025 — early in Trump's second term — hit a range of military and industrial targets.

However, Washington is reportedly reluctant to enter the fray at this time as it remains bogged down in its own war with Iran since February.

According to US outlets, Trump rejected a request from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for strikes on Houthi positions as they approached Mokha on Thursday. Riyadh and the White House are yet to comment on these reports.

Tehran salutes 'resounding victory'

Tehran chimed in on Friday, calling for an end to Saudi Arabia's blockade of Yemen and the immediate resumption of talks, in its first public statement since the Houthi Red Sea offensive.

In a statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency, Iran's foreign ministry said Yemen’s sovereignty must be respected, and its problems cannot be resolved through a blockade or military alliances.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their "resounding victory" on Friday.

Meanwhile, reports have claimed that Iran's elite paramilitary IRGC has deployed dozens of advisors to aid the Houthis in their operations. Euronews could not independently verify the claims at this time.

A potential disruption to Bab el-Mandeb would work in Iran's favour, as its blockade of Hormuz has put significant pressure on the world's energy markets, sparking a crisis that could worsen even further as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.

"The Houthi offensive to capture territory near the Bab al Mandeb advances Iranian objectives under the current regional campaign that Iran is waging against the United States and its allies," Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said in its latest analysis on Friday.

"Iran has recently pursued the following lines of effort under this regional campaign: targeting US naval forces, attacking US forces across the region, (and) disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," it added.

"The Houthis and Iran may currently share a common objective in Houthi control over the Red Sea coastline, but the nature of their relationship means that the Houthis will independently determine their level of involvement in supporting other Iranian objectives."

The leader of Yemen's internationally recognised governing council on Thursday urged Arab and other nations to help it defend the country's coasts.

"The protection of Yemen's coasts and the restoration of state control over its territory, ports and waters is a joint Yemeni, Egyptian, Arab and international interest," Rashad al-Alimi, who heads Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, said during a meeting with Egypt's ambassador.

The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and has displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

World.title: France cuts growth forecast as economy lags behind European neighbours
World.content:
France's government has cut its forecast for economic growth in 2026 from 0.7% to 0.5%, as weak activity in the first half of the year weighs on the outlook.

 

Economy Minister Roland Lescure announced the downgrade on Friday after the French economy contracted by 0.2% in the first quarter and stagnated in the second, putting the nation increasingly at odds with some of its main European neighbours.

Germany, Italy, Spain, and the UK all recorded growth during the first two quarters of the year. Germany posted growth of 0.4% and 0.3%, Italy 0.3% and 0.2%, Spain 0.6% and 0.7%, and the UK 0.6% and 0.4%.

The new forecasts come a day after even more pessimistic projections from INSEE, the French statistics office. It lowered its forecast for 2026 growth from 0.7% to 0.4%, warning that the French economy was "losing ground."

Lescure nevertheless forecast growth of 1% in 2027. He added that he expected inflation to reach 2.1% in 2026 and 1.8% next year.

The downward revision makes the government’s budget equation more complicated. Weaker growth is likely to weigh more heavily on public finances, even though the government had set itself the goal of bringing the deficit down to 5% of GDP in 2026, from 5.1% in 2025. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had already admitted he was not "very optimistic" about hitting that target.

French economy 'stalled'

According to INSEE, "all the engines of domestic demand" are "stalled."

Household consumption remains weak and investment is falling, hit by a slowdown in public projects linked to the municipal electoral cycle.

The institute also highlights the impact of heatwaves, which are particularly severe for agriculture. For its part, the government estimates that, if nothing is done, climate change could shave 3.6% off French GDP by 2050.

INSEE also reports that the labour market is "more degraded than elsewhere in Europe," with rising unemployment and sluggish wage growth.

Deteriorating public finances are also limiting budgetary support for the economy.

Activity is nonetheless expected to pick up slightly in the second half of the year. INSEE is forecasting growth of 0.1% in the third quarter and 0.2% in the fourth. For the year as a whole, however, the expansion of the French economy would remain roughly three times weaker than that of its neighbours in the eurozone and the UK.

Rising inflation, falling purchasing power

Another piece of bad news for households is that inflation is expected to keep rising, reaching 2.9% at the end of the year, compared with 2.4% in August.

In this context, purchasing power is set to fall by 0.4% over the year as a whole, due in particular to the decline in paid employment and rising prices.

"A large share of households" is likely to be affected, according to INSEE.

Household consumption, traditionally a key driver of the French economy, would therefore grow by only 0.3% in 2026. Households are also expected to dip further into their savings, with the savings rate falling from 17.8% of gross income in 2025 to 17.3% this year.

Business investment, for its part, would fall by 0.3%, while household investment would drop by 1.3%.

INSEE nevertheless stresses that "some uncertainties remain," notably regarding the impact of heatwaves on activity in the third quarter and developments in the situation in the Middle East.

World.title: EU pledges €6.1bn for Ukraine, including aid for Patriot interceptors
World.content:
The European Union is set to provide Ukraine with €6.1 billion in additional assistance to help the war-weary country purchase military equipment, notably the Patriot interceptors badly needed to shoot down Russia's devastating ballistic missiles.

 

The funding, announcedon Friday, will come from the bloc's €90 billion support loan, which reserves €28.3 billion for military aid and €16.7 billion for budget aid this year.

The loan's "Made In Europe" requirement will be lifted to procure Patriots, which are made in the United States, and drones, which depend on Chinese components.

The newly allocated €6.1 billion represents the final allocation under the €28.3 billion envelope. Payments are being made in gradual instalments after Brussels checks and verifies the contracts that Kyiv signs with private companies.

So far, €8.35 billion in defence funding has been wired.

"The Ukrainian military edge depends on the rapid availability of critical products in the required quantities and within very short time frames," Andrius Kubilius, the European Commissioner for Defence, said at a press conference.

"Accelerating EU deliveries through de-stocking, reprioritising orders and ramping up production remains crucial."

The news comes as allies race to supply Ukraine with air defence systems as Russia escalates its bombing campaign, including through jet-powered drones, ahead of a winter that EU officials expect to be the harshest yet of the war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy estimates his army will need about 300 Patriot interceptors to make it through the winter safely.

The scarcity of PAC-3 interceptors, made by US defence giant Lockheed Martin, has severely constrained Kyiv's ability to repel Russia's ballistic missiles effectively. Moscow has exploited the weakness to double down on lethal airstrikes.

The war in the Middle East has compounded the backlog in production chains, which was burdensome to begin with. A single PAC-3 interceptor has a 24-month manufacturing lead time and a price tag of roughly $4 million (€3.45 billion).

In a bid to speed things up, Brussels is seeking to convince member states that still have Patriot interceptors in their national stockpiles to donate them to Ukraine and replace them later on with the deliveries scheduled for 2027 – in other words, a swap.

"The Ukrainians, as we understand, will put all the efforts now to have those interceptors as much as possible before winter," Kubilius said.

"NATO is also very intensively working on that," he added, referring to the alliance's PURL programme, which mobilises US-made weaponry for Ukraine.

"I hope that that will be really realised in an effective way."

Kubilius spoke to the press after the first meeting of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance, which intends to combine the former's industrial scale with the latter's innovative prowess to foster joint production of unmanned aerial vehicles.

The meeting gathered 18 companies from the bloc and 9 from Ukraine, he said.

The alliance builds upon the EU-Ukraine Drone Deal signed in July.

World.title: EU needs to 'pin down' Ukraine's exact budget needs, Dombrovskis tells Euronews
World.content:
The European Union needs to "pin down" the precise scope of Ukraine's growing budget needs before deciding how to fill the gap, Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis, who oversees support for the war-weary country, told Euronews.

 

"We obviously need to do a proper, detailed assessment, but we understand that the war continues to rage at high intensity. If anything, Russia is intensifying its attacks," Dombrovskis said in an interview recorded in Riga, Latvia.

"Correspondingly, the economic situation in Ukraine is also very difficult. So we can understand that this may lead to higher financing needs for Ukraine," he added.

"There are still open questions."

Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy caught allies off guard when he asked them to plug a $27 billion (€23 billion) deficit in the Ministry of Defence.

Kyiv argues the shortfall is the result of bringing forward funds earmarked for the second half of the year to cover costs in the first six months.

The €23 billion is needed for personnel, social support and weapons purchases, including around €6 billion in advance payments for deliveries due at the beginning of 2027.

Brussels, though, is not yet convinced and wants a comprehensive breakdown to understand how big the gap is, where it comes from and how it can be filled. The International Monetary Fund is also involved in the technical talks.

As a possible solution, Zelenskyy has suggested that the EU accelerate disbursements under its €90 billion support loan. But this would upset the bloc's original timeline, which reserves €45 billion for 2026 and another €45 billion for 2027.

Frontloading payments risks running out of assistance next year and exacerbating the problem.

The Commission has not yet received a formal request from Kyiv to do so.

"First of all, we need to find out exactly what these additional financing needs are and then discuss with the Ukrainian authorities how we are financing them," Dombrovskis said, noting that the €90 billion loan allows for "some adjustments".

The unexpected shortfall has raised questions over accountability and transparency, issues that have dogged Ukraine since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. The country has faced multiple corruption scandals and reports of fraud, waste and misspending.

As a condition for the loan, Kyiv granted Brussels monitoring rights over its bank account. The Commission also checks contracts for weapons purchases.

"We attach very strong attention to questions of good governance, good financial management and anti-corruption in all those programmes, and those are also part of the conditionality of our macro-financial assistance programme," Dombrovskis said.

So far, €3.2 billion in budgetary aid and €8.35 billion in military aid have been paid out under the €45 billion tranche earmarked for 2026.

A 'way forward' on the assets

As an alternative to speeding up the loan, Ukraine has encouraged EU countries to reconsider tapping into the immobilised assets of the Russian Central Bank.

The EU holds €210 billion of these assets, most of them in Euroclear in Belgium.

Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, backed by the Baltic states, are leading a new push to revive the untested plan, which fell apart last year after fraught discussions.

Belgium has already warned that its objections have not "magically disappeared".

The Commission is willing to assist member states, Dombrovskis said, but has stopped short of committing to tabling a new legal text.

"Last year, we came forward with a concrete legislative proposal to use those assets. Unfortunately, member states were not able to agree on this, mainly because of resistance (from) Belgium," he said.

"But we certainly are ready to re-engage in those discussions, seek those additional reassurances which may be needed and help find a way forward."

Dombrovskis declined to say what changes in the political constellation would be required to prod the executive into taking the issue further. But he hinted that it would wait for guarantees that an "agreement can be reached among member states".

In the previous attempt, Belgian officials lambasted the Commission for failing to consult the country before pitching the audacious plan, which has no precedent.

Seeking to break the deadlock, Ukraine has proposed moving the Russian assets held in Euroclear to an EU-owned custodian.

A cross-party coalition of 122 Members of the European Parliament has also backed the transfer. As the debate rumbles on, Brussels is turning up the pressure on Western allies, who are expected to finance one-third of Kyiv's needs.

US President Donald Trump said last week that he would ask Europeans to repay the American aid provided to Ukraine under the previous administration.

In his interview with Euronews, Dombrovskis brushed off Trump's threat.

"The European Union and its member states are by far the largest supporter and financial contributor to Ukraine," he said.

"But it's important that other jurisdictions, including the US, are also playing their part. So that's, in a sense, how we are looking at this question."

World.title: US inflation holds at 3.4% as monthly price rises hit fastest pace since May
World.content:
The last major data point before the Fed meets has arrived, and it arrived while Americans were paying record prices at the pump.

 

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday afternoon that the annual rate held steady, with core inflation, which strips out food and energy, easing to 2.4% from 2.5%.

Every figure matched the consensus of economists and the monthly number is where the pressure shows.

Prices rose 0.4% in August against 0.1% in July, a fourfold acceleration and the fastest pace in three months. The annual rate stayed flat only because it is measured against the strong summer of 2025.

What it means for the Fed meeting

Markets had largely made up their minds before the figures landed.

CME's FedWatch tool put the probability of a quarter-point increase at the 16 September meeting at 67.4%, up sharply from around 40% before Chairman Warsh's Jackson Hole address in late August.

Following the inflation data release, those odds moved to 91.6%.

Warsh's first keynote as chair was the turning point as he argued the American economy had strengthened rather than weakened, that the labour market was consistent with full employment, and that he "would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive."

On inflation Warsh was blunt by stating that "we must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do."

By that test, Friday's numbers are ambiguous.

Core inflation has now fallen for a second month and sits within half a point of the 2% target, which is underlying inflation moving in the right direction. The monthly acceleration points the other way.

Warsh also refused to say what would trigger a move, rejecting forward guidance as a practice that "has overstayed its welcome". The Fed has held its benchmark rate at 3.50% to 3.75% since December, though three regional presidents dissented in July in favour of an increase, the most in one direction since 2016.

A fuel shock with no obvious end

The pressure is coming from energy, and it is intensifying.

US crude futures topped $100 a barrel this week as fighting between American and Iranian forces escalated around the Strait of Hormuz, with Washington striking five Iranian tankers after attempted missile attacks on a US Navy warship.

Diesel is where it bites hardest.

The US national average crossed $6 a gallon on Friday for the first time in the country's history, at least in nominal terms, according to the American Automobile Association, and leaving truckers and farmers paying around 63% more than a year ago.

In California the average is close to $8. As for petrol, it is averaging $4.22 nationwide, against $2.98 before the war began.

Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries prompted Moscow to ban diesel exports, removing roughly 800,000 barrels a day, while disruption around Hormuz has cost another 1.2 million.

Refineries representing about 5 million barrels a day of capacity have been shut by the two wars, and close to 8% of global diesel supply is currently disrupted.

Some retailers have already added delivery surcharges, and the effect on grocery prices tends to arrive with a lag, which means the energy shock in Friday's numbers may not yet be the whole of it.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
World.content:
New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform.

India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019.

The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult.

Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit.

India's difficult BRICS chairship To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains.

New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition

Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order.

Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy.

"These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW.

However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal.

India's geopolitical strategy is heavily impacted by its relationships with both the West and fellow BRICS powers Image: Manish Swarup/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier.

International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access.

The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment.

Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset.

"The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha.

"It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations.

BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow

India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11.

With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran.

Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead.

With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage.

"Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation.

"BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added.

Fears of Chinese dominance

The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China.

Tracking the tense relationship between India and China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. At the same time, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West.

India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency.

What is BRICS Pay? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'"

"Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements."

India's 'America Plus' strategy

Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China.

EU-India trade agreement: consequences for the economy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW.

"India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University.

But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns.

"A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said.

In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West.

The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
World.content:
Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling to make a living.

A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending over a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.

With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — namely Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail.

In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

Ride-hailing apps have gained in popularity across Africa over the past decade, but not all of them seem to be profitable Image: Afolabi Sotunde/REUTERS

A difficult market to crack

Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale. The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.

However, it's not only Uber that is having to deal with its frustration over the current situation:

Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility, especially in markets like Nigeria.

In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20 — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.

Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers

Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good," while firmly stressing that the high commission rates were adding greatly to his existing woes.

He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€ 20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."

"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty-handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick up another client]," he explained.

"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."

Uber makes UK drivers workers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in the megacity Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business model.

The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other drivers who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.

"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."

In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged several strikes and protests over soaring operating costs, low fares and working conditions, as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have also been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.

Their pleas and concerns, however, remainlargely unheard, as they find themselves having to prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.

Dollars versus naira

Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision; however, the decision comes against the backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded the purchasing power of millions of people while pushing them deeper and deeper into poverty.

This also makes such consumers less likely to use the transport company.

Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means that fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."

Rising fuel costs due to the war in Iran coupled with Nigeria's abolition of the state fuel subsidy have led petrol prices to skyrocket Image: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

Effiong added that while Uber's cost base is dollar-linked, the drivers' revenue is the shrinking naira, leading to the overall maths not working anymore, and forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins.

Thia is despite the fact that Nigeria's ride-hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.

"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.

Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."

The complex economics of ride-hailing

There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution.

But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit creates a loss of a service many users had considered safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.

Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives.

"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.

Spain restricts ride-hailing services To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber: Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing change to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?

In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, at times resorting to violence as part of local taxi wars.

Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?

As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.

In some markets, the competition between ride-hailing apps and traditional taxi services can have brutal consequences Image: Daniel Irungu/dpa/picture alliance

Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
World.content:
Skip next section Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'

09/11/2026 September 11, 2026 Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain'

Speaking to DW about the BRICS Summit, former UN diplomat Shashi Tharoor said that the expansion of the bloc has made it the voice of the Global South.

The BRICS coalition started out with four member countries; Brazil, Russia, India and China but now has 11 members and partner countries after the economic bloc decided to open up membership for more countries in 2023.

Tharoor noted that while Iran joined the coalition, US strategic partners Egypt and Ethiopia also joined

"The expansion that took place in Johannesburg turned out to be one in which both sets of geopolitical points of view were accommodated," Tharoor noted in an interview with DW.

He argued that, "in some ways the expansion has made it much more the voice of the global south."

However, he also said that while the majority of the world is represented in the new 11-member BRICS, the chances of having a consensus has also decreased.

"I would say that BRICS is functioning, but the contradictions remain, and some contradictions have become even more apparent," he said.

He said that when BRICS leaders met this year, they "could not agree on any particular language, and so the chair, India, issued a chair statement instead… it wasn't just Iran, it was also Ukraine that they couldn't agree on."

Tharoor noted that the bloc has a "built-in set of geopolitical divergences which will crop up whenever issues divide the members."

World.title: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
World.content:
The Houthi takeovers of Mokha, Dhubab and Perim in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait threaten to push Yemen deeper into the Middle East war. The Iran-backed group has made advances against Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia.

Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen's internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States.

The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces.

The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran's. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces.

"This is actually a full-scale war," Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "It hasn't been given that name yet but we are marching there full time," Al-Muslimi said.

Houthis 'much stronger'

The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen's government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split.

The Houthis control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and most of the country's north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east.

The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen's joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January.

Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. "The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger," Manea said, "while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented."

The Houthis targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and said Riyadh retaliated across four provinces in Yemen Image: Al Masirah/REUTERS

What's Pakistan's role?

Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen's ousted government. "Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it," Manea said.

The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position.

"At present, I consider the second scenario more likely," Manea said.

Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: "The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost."

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came.

Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. "But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out," Gower said. "Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran," she added, "and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation."

Thousands of civilians fled their homes this week, while nearly 200 were killed in the fighting, according to international bodies Image: AFP

Humanitarian toll rises

Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the "harsh reality" of a return to war.

The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen's conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence.

The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warned that around 18,500 people have been displaced. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's chief of mission, said in a statement. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before," he said. "Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild."

This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. "When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost," she said.

"Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life," she said. "The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war," she added.

World.title: Germany charges 7 suspected Hamas members over attack plot
World.content:
Prosecutors say the suspects had moved beyond general preparations and were already pursuing a concrete plan for a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets.

German federal prosecutors on Friday charged seven suspected members of the Islamist militant group Hamas.

The men allegedly plotted to carry out a deadly attack on Israeli or Jewish targets in Germany or Austria.

What are the charges?

The men are accused of helping procure weapons, membership in a foreign terrorist organization, and taking part in preparations for act of violence endangering the state, the Federal Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe said on Friday.

Investigators believe the suspects, who were arrested in Germany and abroad over recent months, were already pursuing a concrete attack plan.

The men are accused of helping obtain guns and ammunition for an attack targeting representatives of Israel, Jewish people or people regarded as pro-Israel.

The plot allegedly became concrete by July 2025 and was intended to take place on the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel.

Prosecutors say that one of the suspects recorded a video claiming responsibility in advance and announcing the planned attack in the name of Hamas.

How Europe, the US can better protect Jewish communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

All seven men also face weapons charges, while three are additionally accused of violating Germany's War Weapons Control Act.

What weapons had allegedly been obtained?

By the time three of the suspects were arrested in Berlin on October 1, 2025, prosecutors say the group had obtained:

one functioning fully automatic rifle

13 functioning handguns

more than 700 rounds of ammunition

Part of the arsenal was allegedly moved to Vienna and stored there by another suspect who is being prosecuted separately.

According to prosecutors, all seven belonged to Hamas and several were tasked by senior Hamas officials with securing the weapons.

The suspects were arrested between October 2025 and May 2026 and remain in pre-trial detention.

Another alleged participant, Mohammed A., was arrested in London on November 3, 2025, at the request of German authorities.

He has not yet been transferred to Germany and is being prosecuted separately.
