World.title: PCG: 30 cadavers recovered from fire-hit MV June Aster
World.content:
Philippine Coast Guard personnel begin retrieving remains from the fire-ravaged MV June Aster off Coron, Palawan, on Sept. 11, 2026. Authorities said an initial 30 cadavers had been recovered after the fire was declared out and the vessel was assessed for safety. (Photo from the PCG)

PUERTO PRINCESA CITY, Palawan — Authorities have recovered an initial 30 cadavers from the fire-ravaged MV June Aster, Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemie Cayabyab said Friday night, Sept. 11.

Cayabyab told reporters that the charred remains were recovered after the fire was declared out and the vessel underwent a safety assessment.

The retrieval and transfer of the remains began at around 5:16 p.m. Friday using the BRP Cape Engaño (MRRV-4411), she said.

Article continues after this 

READ: MV June Aster tragedy: Rescuers find suspected charred remains aboard

Cayabyab said the remains are scheduled to be transported to the Port of Coron and are expected to arrive at around 11 a.m. Saturday.

The June Aster caught fire around 6:45 p.m. Wednesday while sailing from Manila to Coron. The vessel was about 1.2 nautical miles northeast of Barangay Marcilla when the blaze broke out.

An initial investigation said the vessel, which left Manila on Tuesday night, had initially been reported to be carrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members.

The PCG, however, said two persons listed in the passenger manifest did not board the vessel.

Survivors earlier reported hearing an explosion before thick smoke and flames rapidly spread through the vessel. One survivor said the fire may have started in the cargo hold, where vehicles and other cargo were stored. The cause of the fire has yet to be determined. /mcm

World.title: Ilocos Sur town rolls out 40 vehicles using tobacco tax funds
World.content:
Forty newly procured Toyota Tamaraw FX units are lined up in Sta. Lucia, Ilocos Sur. Thirty-six will be distributed to the town’s barangays to support public services and help farmers transport agricultural products. — Photo courtesy of Sta. Lucia LGU

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — The municipal government has procured 40 brand-new Toyota Tamaraw FX units using its share from the tobacco excise tax under Republic Act No. 7171 to improve public services and transportation in the town’s 36 barangays.

Mayor Joseph Simon Valdez announced Friday, Sept. 11, that 36 of the vehicles would be distributed to each barangay, while the remaining four would be used by the municipal government.

The vehicles are expected to help barangays transport agricultural products, assist farmers in accessing essential services and bring government programs and assistance to residents.

Article continues after this 

READ: DOF proposes unified, higher tobacco excise tax starting 2027

The procurement was funded through the municipality’s tobacco excise tax share (under Republic Act 7171) for calendar year 2023.

World.title: Bacolod unveils MassKara 2026 with more activities, new venues
World.content:
MassKara dancers perform during the launch of the MassKara Festival 2026 in Bacolod City on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. — Photo by Ronnie Baldonado/Contributor

BACOLOD CITY — New venues and an expanded lineup of activities will mark this year’s MassKara Festival, which will run from Oct. 1 to 18, with major events scheduled from Oct. 16 to 18.

The festival was formally launched on Friday, Sept. 11, at Roy’s Hotel, where organizers also unveiled the “Share the Smile. Celebrate Gugma” campaign and introduced the contestants for Miss Bacolod MassKara 2026 and participants in the street dance competition.

Festival director Rodney Mitz Ascalon said the changes were aimed at giving more communities and sectors opportunities to take part in the city’s annual celebration.

Article continues after this 

READ: The enduring smile of MassKara: A festival of resilience and unity

“MassKara is more than a festival; it is a feeling, it is our identity, and it is our way of sharing who we are,” Ascalon said during the launch at Roy’s Hotel on Friday.

He said the festival would include drivers and transport groups, senior citizens, persons with disabilities, women, athletes, artists, youth, volunteers and animal advocates.

“MassKara should not only be watched; it should be experienced, it should be shared, and it should belong to everyone,” he said.

Ascalon said the Miss Bacolod MassKara 2026 pageant would be held at the STI Gymnasium.

Article continues after this 

The street dance competition will be staged along Araneta Street, while the arena competition will be held between the bridgeways of SM City Bacolod in the reclamation area.

The winners of the street dance and arena competitions will be awarded at the Bacolod Public Plaza.

Article continues after this 

The school and barangay street dance and arena competitions are scheduled for Oct. 17 and 18, respectively.

Eight barangays will compete in the barangay category: Barangays 6, 10, 13, Alangilan, Bata, Mandalagan, Handumanan and Taculing.

The school category will feature Montevista Elementary School, Sum-ag Elementary School, Vista Alegre-Granada Relocation Elementary School, Vista Alegre Elementary School, Mandalagan Elementary School, Handumanan Elementary School 1 and Education Training Center School II.

Ascalon said discussions were also underway for a high school category.

Seven barangays will participate in the Electric MassKara at The Upper East on Oct. 16. They are Barangays 12, 17, 19, 21, 14, Villamonte and Tangub.

The festival also introduced a twin-logo concept created by Bacolod artist Mark Lester Jarmin.

Organizers said the two logos represent different visual faces of MassKara and reflect the festival’s evolving identity while retaining its connection to Bacolod’s culture.

The launch also introduced the festival’s newest ambassadors, “To Max” and “’Day Kara,” who will represent the City of Smiles and the celebration’s message of joy and love.

The festival calendar includes competitions, community activities, sporting events, pageants, food events, concerts and other entertainment.

READ: Fil-Ams explore Philippine tribal groups’ rich cultural traditions

Among the activities are MassKareppin, MasskaRap Battle, Choreographers Showdown, PetsKara, Drum and Lyre Corps Competition, SingKara, Super KidsKara and MassKara Hataw Sayaw sa Plaza.

Concerts and other entertainment events are scheduled at the Bacolod City Government Center, Bacolod Public Plaza, SM City Bacolod, Ayala Malls Capitol Central, Megaworld and other venues.

Organizers said additional schedules, particularly for accredited sporting events, would be announced later.

Ascalon said his second year leading the festival was not simply about expanding it but making it more relevant to Bacolod residents.

“We don’t just make MassKara bigger; we make it matter,” he said.

Bacolod Rep. Alfredo Abelardo Benitez said the festival helps promote the city as a destination for visitors. He also said Bacolod is the third-fastest-growing city in the country.

Mayor Greg Gasataya thanked the sponsors for their support, saying their contributions would help ensure the success of this year’s celebration.

“Your support is a big part of the success of MassKara. We may not be able to repay your generosity, but we assure you that we will honor every commitment we have made and deliver what we have promised,” Gasataya said.

“We will give our best in this year’s MassKara Festival,” he added.

World.title: Manila Water maintains water quality amid ‘habagat’ challenges
World.content:
Manila Water conducts rigorous laboratory testing and analysis as part of its comprehensive water quality monitoring program, helping ensure that the water delivered to customers remains safe, potable and compliant with the stringent parameters of the Philippine National Standards for Drinking Water.

Despite the challenges brought by the southwest monsoon or habagat, Manila Water continued to provide safe and potable water to more than 7.9 million customers across the East Zone of Metro Manila and Rizal Province, maintaining high water quality standards even as heavy rains affected raw water sources.

Heavy rainfall during the Habagat season can significantly increase the turbidity, or cloudiness, of raw water sources as runoff carries silt, mud and other particles into rivers and reservoirs. These conditions require more intensive treatment and monitoring to ensure that water remains safe for public consumption.

To address these challenges, Manila Water’s treatment plants are designed to operate within a water quality envelope that enables facilities to effectively process highly turbid raw water while maintaining compliance with drinking water standards. The treatment process employs multiple barriers, including coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration and disinfection, supported by continuous monitoring and operational adjustments as needed.

Article continues after this 

READ: Manila Water, Manila Water Foundation aid Montalban flood recovery

For July 2026, Manila Water achieved 100% compliance with the Philippine National Standards for Drinking Water (PNSDW) at its treatment plant outlets, demonstrating the effectiveness and resilience of its treatment processes amid challenging weather conditions.

The company also recorded 99.75% compliance with PNSDW requirements across its distribution network, significantly exceeding the regulatory target of 95%.

Further reinforcing its commitment to public health and regulatory compliance, Manila Water attained 100% compliance with required water quality monitoring and sampling activities during the month. A total of 6,780 water quality samples were collected and analyzed across water treatment plants, service reservoirs, pumping stations, distribution lines and customer taps, fully meeting regulatory sampling requirements.

“Despite the challenges brought by heavy rains during the Habagat season, our treatment facilities and water quality teams work continuously to ensure that the water reaching customers remains safe, potable and compliant with national standards,” said Dittie Galang, Manila Water Communication Affairs Group Head.

Article continues after this 

Central to these efforts is Manila Water’s Water Safety Plan, a comprehensive risk management framework that identifies and manages potential hazards from source to tap. The program is implemented across the company’s water treatment and distribution systems to help ensure the continuous delivery of safe drinking water even under varying environmental conditions.

Manila Water continues to invest in advanced treatment technologies, laboratory capabilities and operational improvements to strengthen system resilience during extreme weather events. Through these efforts, the company remains committed to protecting public health and ensuring that customers continue to receive safe, reliable and high-quality drinking water throughout the year.

World.title: Ilocos farmers among P187-M insurance beneficiaries
World.content:
Rice fields in Pangasinan were submerged following heavy rains, damaging crops and raising concerns among farmers over potential production losses. — Photo courtesy of DA Ilocos Region

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Farmers in the Ilocos Region are among nearly 25,000 beneficiaries of P187 million in insurance payments set aside by the Philippine Crop Insurance Corp. (PCIC) for losses caused by flooding and other damage from three typhoons and the enhanced southwest monsoon.

The payments cover losses reported from Aug. 1 to 26 in eight regions, mostly in Luzon. Central Luzon had the largest number of beneficiaries at 9,636, followed by the Ilocos Region with 3,874.

In a report on Tuesday, Sept. 8, PCIC President Jovy Bernabe said rice farmers accounted for the biggest share of insurance claims at P132.9 million. Claims from corn farmers reached P9.3 million, while those for high-value crops totaled P42.1 million.

Article continues after this 

READ: PCIC allots P36m in payouts for farmers affected by flooding

“We have issued strict instructions to our regional staff to continue extending their assistance to the affected farmers and speed up the processing of their damage claims,” Bernabe said in a report to Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr.

The payouts come as the Department of Agriculture (DA) assesses the broader impact of the weather disturbances on farm production and food supply.

The DA’s Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Operations Center, in its Sept. 6 report, estimated agricultural damage at P4.13 billion. The weather disturbances affected 97,589 farmers and fisherfolk and 81,383 hectares of agricultural land, with production losses estimated at 100,602 metric tons.

Rice suffered the heaviest damage, with 73,307 hectares affected and production losses of 65,106 metric tons valued at P2.04 billion.

Despite the losses, the damaged rice accounts for less than 1 percent of the 20.3 million metric tons of production projected for the year, limiting its likely impact on overall supply. — Kenneth P. Tabin/Contributor /das

World.title: Balisacan: Falling fertility rate chance to improve living standards
World.content:
Department of Economy, Planning and Development (DEPDev) Secretary Arsenio Balisacan during the INQUIRER roundtable discussion on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. INQUIRER photo by Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — Department of Economy, Planning, and Development Secretary Arsenio Balisacan on Friday described the country’s rapidly declining fertility rate as a “good opportunity” to improve living standards.

The country’s fertility rate fell to 1.7 children per woman in 2025 from 1.9 in 2022 and has been on a continuous decline since 1993, based on the latest data from the National Demographic and Health Survey conducted by the Philippine Statistics Authority.

READ: CPD says falling fertility rate opens doors to better workforce

Article continues after this 

“It is one thing that I’ve been wanting for so many…It’s an opportunity for now; it’s a good opportunity because that means we are going into a demographic stage where the working-age population is growing faster than our dependency population of our overall population,” Balisacan said during a roundtable discussion with INQUIRER reporters and editors.

However, this demographic shift also comes with a downside, particularly for the working-age population, whose taxes help fund pensions and other forms of assistance for the elderly.

“Of course, with the fertility rate continuing to come down, two decades from now or so, we will get into the aging of the population,” he said.

He said the government should use the current demographic window to address multidimensional poverty by investing in decent housing, accessible health services and quality education, particularly in rural areas.

If the government is able to invest in education and health, those who graduate will be equipped with the skills and competencies needed to secure better-paying jobs and earn higher incomes.

Article continues after this 

The country could also reap a demographic dividend, or the potential for economic growth that occurs when the working-age population grows faster than the number of young and elderly dependents.

Balisacan said the government should also create programs for the poor that are well-researched and proven to produce positive results.

Article continues after this 

For him, the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program is one such initiative that can provide long-term solutions to poverty.

“It’s one of these few projects, ayuda, na tlagang nagwowork in terms of achieving its objective. Kasi ang objective niyan to prevent the transmission of poverty to the next generation,” he said.

World.title: Albay under state of calamity as dengue cases hit 1,785
World.content:
Composite image by INQUIRER.net / Daniella Marie Agacer

LEGAZPI CITY — Albay was placed under a state of calamity on Thursday, Sept. 10, after dengue cases reached 1,785, with 14 deaths recorded from Jan. 1 to Sept. 8.

The Sangguniang Panlalawigan (provincial board) approved the declaration following a recommendation from the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (PDRRMC).

Legazpi City recorded the most cases at 378, followed by Bacacay with 254 and Daraga with 188.

Article continues after this 

The 14 deaths included five in Legazpi City; two each in Daraga, Manito and Sto. Domingo; and one each in Malilipot, Camalig and Tiwi.

The resolution, filed by Ex-Officio Board Member Milagros Bal, authorizes the provincial government to mobilize funds and emergency resources for the dengue response.

It also directs provincial offices to coordinate with local governments, barangays, national agencies and the private sector on disease surveillance, vector control, cleanup operations, emergency procurement and information campaigns.

The state of calamity will remain in effect until the Sangguniang Panlalawigan lifts it based on assessments by the PDRRMC and the Department of Health. /mcm

World.title: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Economic Transformation, AIFC and Rybakina’s Rise to World No. 1
World.content:
ASTANA — The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights the country’s economic and financial development, sovereign wealth strategy and global ambitions, alongside Elena Rybakina’s historic rise to world No. 1.

Elena Rybakina becomes world No. 1 for first time after U.S. Open win over Zheng Qinwen

Women’s tennis has a new world No. 1. Elena Rybakina took the top spot from Aryna Sabalenka on Wednesday at the U.S. Open with a quarterfinal win over China’s Zheng Qinwen, 3-6, 6-1, 6-4. It is her first time at the summit of women’s tennis, reported The New York Times on Sept. 9.

“It’s a great achievement, and I feel like you will appreciate and think about it even more when you finish your career,” Rybakina said in a news conference, when asked about the milestone.

Kazakhstan’s AIFC says other countries are seeking to replicate its model

Kazakhstan’s financial hub says its model is attracting interest abroad as competition between financial centres intensifies, while limited market liquidity remains a key challenge, reported Euronews on Sept. 9.

For two days, Astana Finance Days 2026 brought together representatives of global financial institutions that collectively manage more than $26 trillion in assets, as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position in the global competition for capital.

How Kazakhstan’s economic reforms have turned the tenge into the best-performing currency in Europe and Asia

EU Reporter published an article on Sept. 7 examining the tenge’s strong performance in 2026 and highlights Kazakhstan’s accelerating economic transformation, driven by foreign investment, diversification, digitalization, infrastructure development, and the expansion of its financial and technology sectors.

“The Kazakhstani tenge has become the best-performing currency in Asia and Europe in 2026, according to the Financial Times. Since the beginning of the year, it has appreciated by nearly 10% against the US dollar, outperforming all other currencies worldwide except for several currencies of Latin American and African countries. This performance has been underpinned by economic growth driven by the transformation of Kazakhstan’s economic model. The country is rapidly evolving from a commodity-based economy into a financial and technology hub for Central Asia, amid growing inflows of foreign capital,” reads the article.

Erlan Karin’s appointment links reform and national identity

The Times of Central Asia published an article on Sept. 1 about Erlan Karin’s appointment as Vice President of Kazakhstan.

“When President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev put forward Erlan Karin for vice president on Aug. 31, he called him ‘a genuine patriot’ with long experience in government. He also stressed Karin’s part in implementing major reforms, his grasp of long-term state strategy and his understanding of Kazakhstan’s prospects for socioeconomic development.

Karin has spent seven years in senior posts under Tokayev. He also has a sustained interest in a question that runs through the president’s agenda — how Kazakhstan can modernize while remaining connected to its own history and national identity,” reads the article.

From oil reserves to infrastructure: How Kazakhstan invests in future generations

EU Reporter released an article on Sept. 8 examining how Kazakhstan can transform part of its sovereign wealth from financial savings into long-term national capital by investing in infrastructure, healthcare, education, and other assets that can generate lasting economic and social benefits for future generations.

“Savings from the National Fund are already being utilized directly in the interests of future generations. Since 2024, Kazakhstan has operated the National Fund for Children program: every young citizen of Kazakhstan is annually allocated a portion of the fund’s investment income, and upon reaching 18 years of age, the accumulated funds can be used for education or housing improvement. This program has already entered the phase of practical asset utilization. Between February 2024 and Aug. 1, payouts were received by more than 338,000 young Kazakhstanis, totaling approximately $67.8 million. Meanwhile, the funds belonging to minors remain within the National Fund’s assets and continue to be invested until they reach adulthood,” reads the article.

Almaty and Astana set to retain Central Asia’s economic lead

Almaty and Astana are likely to retain their position as Central Asia’s leading economic centers, even as Tashkent and Bishkek record rapid growth and invest heavily in their future expansion. Kazakhstan’s two largest cities benefit from an economic scale, financial infrastructure and established business ecosystems that have been built up over decades, reported the Times of Central Asia on Sept. 7.

“Almaty and Astana benefit from an economic scale unmatched elsewhere in Central Asia. Kazakhstan alone accounts for more than half of the region’s GDP and roughly two-thirds of its inward FDI stock, according to TCA’s Central Asia Balance Sheet. That scale helps generate the fiscal resources needed to build and maintain the municipal infrastructure that supports business activity,” reads the article.

World.title: Kazakhstan Looks to New Players and Products to Drive Next Phase of Digital Finance, NBK Governor Says
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has built the core digital infrastructure for its financial sector and is now entering a new stage focused on developing new products, attracting new market participants and creating innovative business models, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at the Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 in Almaty on Sept. 11.

Speaking at the opening of the third annual summit, Suleimenov said Kazakhstan’s financial sector has already reached a high level of digitalization, with more than 90% of payments made without cash and most basic banking and government services available through digital platforms.

The summit, held on Sept. 11, brings together regulators, financial institutions, technology companies and experts to discuss the future of financial markets, digital currencies, artificial intelligence, digital assets, cybersecurity and other areas of fintech.

Suleimenov said the National Bank’s approach has evolved from simply digitizing its own operations to actively encouraging innovation across the financial market.

“We decided to change the approach altogether – instead of being the one who is pushed, to become the one who pushes the market,” he said, describing the regulator’s role as creating a “push” for the market and encouraging participants to move faster.

Kazakhstan builds digital financial infrastructure

Kazakhstan has established a national digital financial infrastructure. It includes biometric identification, interbank payments, the digital tenge and mechanisms designed to protect citizens and businesses from financial fraud.

The infrastructure has been expanded through successive stages, with the digital tenge entering industrial use in 2023, the National Anti-Fraud Center launched in 2024 and new interbank and QR payment infrastructure introduced subsequently.

The digital tenge is gradually being integrated into government financial processes, including public procurement, budget planning and the management of state funds. Suleimenov said the National Bank, together with the government, intends to increase the volume of digital-tenge operations to 2 trillion tenge (US$4.4 billion) over the next 12 months.

Suleimenov pointed to the interbank mobile payment system launched this year as one of the latest developments. The system includes transfers by phone number and a unified QR code. Since its launch on July 19, it has processed more than 20 million transactions worth around 400 billion tenge (US$888 million), according to the National Bank.

He described the high level of digitalization as a major achievement, noting that in many countries reaching 50–60% of non-cash turnover remains a challenge.

From infrastructure to products

The next challenge, Suleimenov said, is no longer primarily about building the technological “rails” of the financial system but about using them to create products that meet the needs of businesses and consumers.

During the opening plenary, moderator Vitaliy Volyanyuk, co-founder and CEO of Digital Business, asked Suleimenov to assess what the measures introduced by the NBK and other regulators had actually delivered and how Kazakhstan’s financial sector looks today.

Suleimenov described the sector as bank-centered but increasingly diverse, with the domestic financial system, the Astana International Financial Center and emerging digital-finance initiatives creating complementary opportunities.

“Briefly, the system is strong, highly capitalized and digitalized, and it has a huge future,” he said.

But Suleimenov stressed that infrastructure alone would not be enough.

“The second step is, of course, financial infrastructure, on which these solutions have to run. We are also creating that. But now, probably, the main step is creating products,” he said.

“We cannot and will not create the products ourselves,” he added, calling on banks, traditional financial institutions and new financial companies to work both together and in competition to develop new products and business models. The objective, he said, is to make access to financing, payments and cross-border transactions easier for both businesses and individuals.

Digital maturity remains uneven

The transformation, however, is not taking place at the same pace across the entire financial sector, Chair of the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market Madina Abylkassymova said during the summit.

Volyanyuk also asked about the readiness of smaller banks, insurance companies and other financial institutions for digital and AI transformation, rather than focusing only on the largest banks with significant technological and financial resources.

Abylkassymova said the agency had assessed the digital readiness of 94 financial organizations this year, examining process digitalization, data quality, infrastructure, cybersecurity, AI use and employee competencies.

“Banks remain the leaders, with almost 75% already using artificial intelligence. However, a gap remains between banks and other parts of the financial sector, particularly insurance and microfinance,” she said, stressing that digital transformation is not simply about introducing technology.

“It is also about the competencies of employees,” Abylkassymova added, arguing that digital and AI tools need to be embedded into the actual processes of financial organizations.

According to her, the agency is now developing a strategy for large-scale digitalization and further AI adoption across the financial sector. It has identified 1,200 specific measures and prepared individual development plans for the 94 organizations assessed.

Kazakhstan looks to export financial services

Suleimenov identified exporting Kazakhstan’s financial industry as another strategic priority. This includes helping domestic financial companies enter foreign markets and attracting international players that can serve global customers through Kazakhstan’s jurisdiction and financial infrastructure.

He said the country has a strong domestic financial jurisdiction alongside the Astana International Financial Center, which he described as an additional driver of competition and investment.

The next stage, however, will depend on whether market participants can turn the established infrastructure and regulatory framework into products that can compete both domestically and internationally.

“We have a strong foundation, but now we need the market to become more active – with new products, partnerships and business models that will allow us to fully use these opportunities,” Suleimenov said.

The Central Asia Fintech Summit 2026 brings together more than 120 speakers and experts. It focuses on the development of digital finance, including payments, digital assets, AI, cybersecurity, tokenization and anti-fraud technologies.

World.title: Kazakhstan Highlights Middle Corridor Growth and Digitalization at Batumi Forum
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan highlighted the rapid growth of the Middle Corridor and the need to accelerate its digitalization at the Georgian International Maritime Forum in Batumi on Sept. 7-8.

Kazakhstan Deputy Minister of Transport Zhanibek Taizhanov said freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) rose 22% in January-August, while East-West transit increased 55%.

Digitalization drives seamless transit

Speaking at the panel session From Seas to Corridors: The New Geography of Global Trade, Taizhanov stressed the importance of integrating maritime, rail and port infrastructure to make international supply chains more efficient and resilient, the ministry’s press service reported.

He also presented President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to develop a digital map of transport routes, providing an integrated view of transport infrastructure, logistics chains and cargo flows along international corridors.

The Middle Corridor currently has a capacity of 6 million tons, including 182,000 TEUs. Measures to streamline logistics have reduced cargo delivery times from 38 days to 13-17 days, with a target of 10-12 days from China to ports in Georgia and Türkiye.

Kazakhstan is also advancing the Digital Trade Corridor, which enables online cargo tracking and single-window contracting. Its Tez Customs module has reduced transit customs processing from eight hours to 30 minutes, the ministry told The Astana Times.

Infrastructure expansion

The forum brought together government officials, maritime administrations, international organizations, port operators, logistics companies and industry experts.

Discussions covered port infrastructure, maritime cooperation, digital transformation, navigation and shipping safety, and applying the single-window principle in the maritime sector.

Discussions on the Middle Corridor also highlighted the need for further infrastructure investment. Speaking at the 5th International Forum on Freight Transport in the Black and Caspian Regions 2026 in Baku, World Bank Senior Transport and Logistics Specialist Luis Blancas said a new comprehensive report on the Middle Corridor is scheduled for publication on Sept. 27, Trend reported.

The report covers all nine participating countries and identifies 16 critical investment priorities worth around US$25 billion. More than three-quarters of the required investment is already underway, Blancas said.

The report is expected to provide a broader assessment of infrastructure needs as cargo flows between Asia and Europe continue to grow.
