World.title: Türkiye aims to fully utilize BTC pipeline capacity – Bayraktar (Interview)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. Türkiye plans to make greater use of the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline’s transportation capacity and attract oil resources from Central Asia and other Turkic states to the infrastructure, Türkiye’s Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Alparslan Bayraktar said in an exclusive interview with Trend as part of the 5th Azerbaijan-Türkiye Energy Forum.

The minister said the BTC pipeline plays an important role in ensuring energy supply security for the region and Europe.

According to him, around 500,000-600,000 barrels of crude oil are transported daily through BTC from the Ceyhan terminal to global markets. Noting that the pipeline’s transportation capacity is higher, Bayraktar emphasized the importance of bringing oil resources from Central Asia and other Turkic states into the infrastructure.

“Our goal is to bring the oil of Central Asia and the Turkic world into this line as well and fully utilize the existing infrastructure,” he said.

The minister said the energy partnership between Azerbaijan and Türkiye, which began in the 1990s, has expanded from oil and natural gas production to transportation.

He noted that the TANAP and TAP projects play an important role in delivering Azerbaijani natural gas to Türkiye and Europe via Türkiye.

“The total volume of Azerbaijani gas transported through TANAP has already exceeded 100 billion cubic meters,” Bayraktar said.

The BTC oil pipeline has a total length of 1,768 kilometers.

The pipeline was built to ensure the safe transportation of crude oil produced in the Caspian region to the Mediterranean coast.

The project contributes to strengthening economic and political ties between Azerbaijan, Georgia, Türkiye and Western countries, while also generating significant revenues for the transit countries.

Since the pipeline became operational, thousands of social initiatives have been implemented along its route, benefiting more than 750,000 people in over 550 settlements.

BTC has a transportation capacity of 1 million barrels of oil per day. The pipeline uses pipes with diameters of 46, 42 and 34 inches and has eight pumping stations and 98 block valve stations. Along its route, the pipeline crosses several mountain ranges, more than 3,000 roads, railway and communication lines, as well as more than 1,500 bodies of water, including the Ceyhan River, which is up to 500 meters wide.

Considered one of the largest and most complex engineering projects of its time, construction of BTC took four years, from project approval in July 2002 to completion in May 2006. At the peak of construction, 22,000 people worked on the project, around 80 percent of whom were local specialists.

The first batch of oil was loaded onto the British Hawthorn tanker at the Ceyhan terminal on June 4, 2006.

World.title: CIS grants Uzbekistan’s UNICON.UZ status of basic organization for digital development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. Uzbekistan’s UNICON.UZ has received the status of a CIS basic organization for digital development, supporting cooperation in information and communication technologies.

This was reflected in a statement published by the CIS Executive Committee on September 11.

According to the publication, the decision was made by The Commonwealth of Independent States’ (CIS) Economic Council at its 111th meeting in Ashgabat. UNICON.UZ will provide methodological and organizational-technical support for work in the field of digital development across the Commonwealth.

The meeting also addressed financial and other issues, including the development of archival services in CIS member states.

UNICON.UZ is a Uzbekistan-based organization operating within the system of the country's Ministry of Digital Technologies. Its activities cover several areas of the information and communication technology sector, including research, development of national standards, certification and testing of telecommunications equipment, software solutions and digital infrastructure. The organization also provides electronic digital signature services and operates a data center and cloud infrastructure.

UNICON.UZ has also been involved in technical regulation and conformity assessment in Uzbekistan's ICT sector. The country's Ministry of Digital Technologies lists the organization among entities providing services related to telecommunications equipment certification, software assessment and the issuance of electronic digital signature certificates. The ministry has also reported that UNICON.UZ's certification and testing facilities received accreditation for their work with telecommunications equipment.

World.title: Azerbaijan to establish research center on competition
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. A research center in the field of competition will be established in Azerbaijan.

This was reflected in the "National Action Plan on the Development of Competition and the Prevention of Monopolistic Activities for 2027–2029," approved by a decree of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev.

According to the decree, efforts to stimulate scientific research in the field of competition and expand opportunities for applying its findings will be intensified.

The decree noted that from 2027 through 2029, international best practices and existing needs regarding the organization of research in the competition sector and the application of its results will be assessed; a project concerning the organizational model, operational scope, and establishment of a research center will be prepared; and the research center will be formally established and begin operations.

The primary implementing agency for this process is the State Agency for Antimonopoly and Consumer Market Control under the President of Azerbaijan.

Other implementing bodies include the Ministry of Science and Education and relevant state agencies (institutions).

World.title: CIS reviews barriers to mutual trade at Economic Council meeting in Ashgabat
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. The Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) Economic Council reviewed barriers to mutual trade and recommendations for their removal at its meeting in Ashgabat.

This was reflected in a press release published by the CIS Executive Committee on September 11.

According to the publication, the information was prepared using data from CIS member states on trade restrictions, including safeguard, anti-dumping and countervailing measures, temporary bans, licensing and quota requirements, according to the CIS Executive Committee.

The review also covered restrictions imposed by other parties that hinder or slow the development of mutual trade among CIS countries, the press release noted.

The information incorporated the results of meetings of a high-level working group tasked with analyzing claims concerning barriers to mutual trade within the Commonwealth.

The review is intended to support efforts to identify and address restrictions affecting trade between CIS member states.

For reference, the development of trade and economic cooperation is one of the key priorities of Turkmenistan's 2026 CIS chairmanship. Ashgabat's chairmanship concept identifies the expansion of economic cooperation and the removal of barriers to trade among member states among its priorities. Against this background, the review of obstacles to mutual trade in Ashgabat directly corresponds to the agenda of Turkmenistan's chairmanship.

World.title: Kazakhstan proposes ECO network to combat online fraud
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 11. Kazakhstan has proposed creating a network of contact points among the central authorities of Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) member states to speed up the response to online fraud and financial crime, the Kazakh Prosecutor General’s Office said.

The proposal was made during the seventh meeting of prosecutors general of ECO member states, held in Turkestan under the chairmanship of Kazakhstan’s Prosecutor General Berik Assylov.

“Kazakhstan proposed moving from predominantly formalized procedures for international legal assistance to more operational cooperation,” the Prosecutor General’s Office said.

The proposed network would operate under the ECO Secretariat and facilitate the rapid exchange of information on criminals, response to suspicious transactions and, where necessary, the formation of joint investigative and operational groups.

The meeting focused on practical measures to combat online fraud, digital and financial crime by combining resources, information and modern technologies. Prosecutors and representatives from Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, Türkiye and Pakistan participated in the meeting, along with the ECO Secretary General and a representative of the Coordinating Council of Prosecutors General of CIS member states.

Kazakhstan also presented its multi-level system for protecting citizens against online fraud, including biometric identification for online loans, a cooling-off period, voluntary refusal to obtain loans, anti-fraud systems operated by telecom providers and the National Anti-Fraud Center.

These measures helped prevent the issuance of more than 700 fraudulent loans worth over $850,000, while more than 600 money mules were held accountable. Kazakh courts also upheld claims to recover unjust enrichment worth more than $12 million, according to the Prosecutor General’s Office.

A Unified Analytical Platform for Monitoring Online Fraud operates at the Crime Threat Forecasting Center. It combines data from legal statistics, the banking sector, telecom operators, law enforcement and government agencies.

The use of artificial intelligence enables authorities to identify common digital and financial infrastructure used by criminals and predict new fraud schemes, the office said.

The proposed mechanisms received support from the participants. The sides agreed to continue exchanging experience in combating online fraud and financial crime, digital forensics, and the use of artificial intelligence and analytical technologies.

World.title: Nepal estimates reconstruction after deadly floods to cost nearly $7 billion
World.content:
The reconstruction bill after the deadly floods that hit Nepal last month will amount to $US4.78 billion ($6.67 billion), its foreign ministry says.

Spokesman Lok Bahadur Chhetri said that $US57.67 million ($80.43 million) was needed for short-term reconstruction and recovery over the next six months.

Approximately $US4.71 billion ($6.57 billion) was required for long-term reconstruction adapting to a rapidly changing mountain environment, he added.

"Given the scale and extent of the damage, the government is also undertaking a comprehensive post-disaster needs assessment to determine the full extent of loss and damage and the requirement for recovery, rebuilding and reconstruction," Mr Chhetri told reporters on Friday.

A drone view of the aftermath of flash flooding along the Trishuli river in Nepal. (AP: Rajesh Kumar Singh)

At least 12 hydropower projects have been engulfed in mud and debris, and whole villages wiped off the map, after a glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border caused a tsunami-like surge of water, mud and debris to submerge parts of the country on August 26.

The devastation in the valleys below the glacier includes cross-border trade routes, roads, bridges, houses and other infrastructure which was swept away.

Rescuers in Nepal have retrieved 1,385 bodies, while around 5,130 people remain missing, the country's disaster agency said on Friday. In Tibet, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to Chinese state media.

The combined toll is 1,428 people dead and more than 5,649 missing, including around 800 foreigners, among them tourists and pilgrims.

Eight Australians who were originally declared missing in the flood have been found, with 35 still unaccounted-for.

If you want to help support the thousands affected by the crisis, the ABC is supporting the Emergency Action Alliance member charities and their local partners. You can find more information here.

UN estimates $220 million in building damage alone

Nepal's leaders are asking wealthier countries and global agencies for financial help in the wake of the floods, arguing the reconstruction costs show how climate change hits poor countries which do little to cause it.

The Nepal government is finalising a report detailing the extent of the damage, losses and funding requirements for temporary shelters, schools and essential infrastructure, officials said.

A man stands on a mud-covered street, alongside damaged houses, following deadly flash floods and a mudslide in Nepal (Reuters: Tyrone Siu)

A UN preliminary assessment estimated building damage from Nepal's floods at $US158 million ($220 million) alone, warning that total losses — including damage to roads and bridges, agricultural land and humanitarian costs — would be far higher.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah said earlier that Nepal must "strongly raise" with the international community the disasters it has experienced as a result of climate change.

He is expected to take his first foreign trip as leader to address the UN General Assembly on the issue this month.

Nepal's disaster management chief Dharam Raj Uprety told Reuters the estimated cost will be shared with the World Bank and Asian Development Bank, along with the embassies of countries and blocs including the United States, Britain, India, China, Japan and the European Union.

"It's not only a disaster induced by flood, it's massive. A disaster induced by climate change," he said.

Locals seek compensation for lost livelihoods

Nanimaya Senchuri lost her farm in the flood. (Supplied: ActionAid)

Nanimaya Senchuri was one of many in Nepal who lost their farmlands in the floods, buried under mud and debris.

She was inside her house, which she shares with her daughter, when the Trishuli River came crashing down nearby.

"In all my life, I had never seen a flood like this," she said.

As a result, she lost two large plots of farmland, her paddy crop and her banana plantation almost ready for harvest.

The farm not only provided food for Ms Senchuri and her family, but was also her source of income.

She was not sure whether she, and everyone else affected by the natural disaster, would receive compensation needed to rebuild farms and livelihood.

Flood reconstruction costs 'a shared responsibility'

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, contributes a fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions compared to industrialised nations.

While the exact cause of the glacial collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide — increasing the risk of such disasters.

Scientists say glaciers in the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are melting faster as global temperatures rise.

Houses damaged by recent flash floods stand amid thick layers of sludge, mud and debris in Nepal's Nuwakot district.

Nepalese officials have publicly framed the disaster as an example of the disproportionate impact of climate change on poor countries.

Nepal expects global agencies and other partners to "recognise this kind of event and take accountability on that" — though it is not for the country to dictate who should contribute how much — Prakash Pokhrel, a geologist for the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said.

"We need not say what is causing climate change because you already know why climate change is happening and who is contributing the most to it," Mr Pokhrel said.

" Countries like Nepal don't contribute significantly to climate change, but they are facing this level of disaster. So why should it not be a shared responsibility among the global community? "

Houses damaged by recent flash floods stand amid thick layers of sludge, mud and debris in Nepal's Nuwakot district. (AP: Dar Yasin)

China accounts for roughly a third of global emissions, with the United States and Nepal's other neighbour India also among the world's biggest emitters.

China is willing to provide assistance within its capacity for Nepal's post-disaster reconstruction, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Thursday.

Mr Guo said Beijing had immediately extended assistance to Nepal, while rescue and relief work was ongoing back home on its side of the border.

"We believe that under the leadership of the Nepalese government, the Nepalese people will be able to overcome the disaster and rebuild their homes at an early date," he said at a regular news briefing.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Norway's Princess Astrid dies aged 94 two days after King's funeral
World.content:
Norway's Princess Astrid, an older sister of the late king Harald, has died at the age of 94, the royal palace said in a statement, two days after the King's funeral.

Her brother Harald died last month, aged 89, after more than 35 years on the throne, and the princess made her last public appearance at his funeral on Wednesday.

"Throughout her long life, Princess Astrid represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner," King Haakon VIII said in the statement.

"His Majesty the King has received with great sadness the news of the passing of Princess Astrid," the Palace said in a statement.

"The Princess fell asleep today, Friday 11 September, at the age of 94."

The death of the King

King Harald V of Norway died in late August, announced by the European country's royal court.

"King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, 28 August," the royal palace said on its website.

The King was laid to rest after a state funeral and ceremony on September 9.

Royal dignitaries seen at the funeral included Britain's Prince William, Japan's Crown Prince, the kings of Denmark, the Netherlands, Sweden and Spain.

Spain's Queen Sofia, Britain's Princess Anne, and Britain's Prince William leave the Oslo Cathedral after a funeral service for Norway's King Harald V in Oslo. (AP: Markus Schreiber)

Also paying their respects were European heads of state, the presidents of Germany and Finland, France's prime minister, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Representing the United States was Allison Hooker, Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, the Norwegian government said.

King Harald, who was Europe's oldest living monarch, was taken to hospital on August 17.

The palace said he was treated for a bacterial infection in his blood.

"A whole nation is in mourning, and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway," the country's Prime Minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said in a statement following the King's death.

The new King of Norway

His 53-year-old son who succeeded the throne, is now King Haakon VIII.

King Haakon adopted the motto, "All for Norway," a cry that dates back to his great-grandfather.

His wife became Queen Mette-Marit, while his oldest child became Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and the heir to the throne.

King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit wave to the crowd from the balcony of the royal palace, on the day of the funeral of Norway's King Harald V. (Reuters: Claudia Greco )

In recent years Haakon has stepped in as his aging father's health began to fail.

He ascends the throne faced by the task of stabilising the nations monarchy and boosting the royal family's popularity after his wife's past contacts with deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his stepson's rape conviction.

Queen Mette-Marit, 53, the King's commoner wife is recovering from a lung transplant she underwent in June.

Last week, the Queen had to cancel plans to attend her husband's oath ceremony in parliament due to complications after her operation.

World.title: 'Landmark' NT novel wins best fiction at Prime Minister's Literary Awards
World.content:
A novel based on the oral history of Yolŋu people from north-east Arnhem Land has been named as this year's fiction pick at the Prime Minister's Literary Awards.

Darwin-born author Leonie Norrington and co-authors Djawundil Maymuru, Merrikiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs and Djawa Burarrwanga have won the $80,000 fiction prize for their book A Piece of Red Cloth.

Told from the perspective of Yolŋu people, the book tells the story of a grandmother's quest to protect her granddaughter from Macassan trepang fishermen during the 1600s, while they learn to interact with foreigners.

Leonie Norrington says winning the award is a "recognition of history". (ABC News)

The Prime Minister's Literary Awards judges labelled the novel as a "landmark achievement in fiction", writing it "is also an urgent example of intercultural work, setting a high benchmark for collaboration between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal writers".

"It is a profound work of remembrance and re-imagination, fusing oral history, novelistic technique and deep cultural knowledge," the judges said.

Having grown up in the Barunga community, Dr Norrington said her Aboriginal mother Clare Bush inspired her to write A Piece of Red Cloth before she died.

Dr Norrington said her Aboriginal mother wanted the Yolŋu people's story told to help people in other parts of the country to understand the country was "alive" and we are "one with the earth".

"If we only have what she called 'Captain Cook history', then we're always going to have a frontier mentality about our country," she said.

"We can exploit the country because we're not from the country.

Prime Minister's Literary Awards announced Kate Wild's book about the fatal shooting of Kumanjayi Walker and the ensuing murder trial, The Red House, is one of six PMLA winners.

"We could belong to the country and then have more respect for the country and for the first peoples of the country, not just as the first people who lived here, but the people who emerged at the same time as the country."

Speaking to Radio National in 2025, local custodian Merrikiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs said the book explores cultural traditions that are still apparent in modern communities while re-telling the story of how Yolŋu people had been trading with countries overseas for centuries.

Merrkiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs accepted the award in Canberra on Thursday. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"All I can is that we still live like this, like what's happening in the book today," she told the program.

"Even if we are modern people, we still go out bush, we till dig for that yams, for those roots get it up oysters, still live it, still eat it."

Dr Norrington said winning the award was a "recognition of history" and hoped her book could be a driving force for action.

"Our history has been read by the Prime Minister of Australia and now things can change," she said.

Leonie Norrington and Merrikiyawuy Ganambarr-Stubbs were part of the group that collaborated to write A Piece of Red Cloth. (Supplied)

"I think if I was going to have a message to the prime minister, I think it would be that Australia is a terribly, terribly dry and very fragile country and we need to look after it.

"The future generations of Australia really rely on us making good decisions about what we do with this very fragile land."

A Piece of Red Cloth wasn't the only NT winner at the prestigious awards — Kate Wild's book The Red House, about the fatal shooting of Kumanjayi Walker in Yuendumu and the murder trial of police officer Zachary Rolfe, won the non-fiction category.

World.title: Putin and Iranian president arrive in India for summit focusing on war
World.content:
Vladimir Putin has arrived in India for talks ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit dominated by economic challenges and conflict in the Middle East and Ukraine, with the leaders of China and Iran set to attend.

War, global trade turbulence and oil are expected on the agenda at the two-day annual summit which opens on Saturday, when Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to arrive.

It will be Mr Xi's first visit to India since 2019, marking the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours.

The visit comes six years after a deadly military clash between China and India along their disputed Himalayan border.

Xi Jinping is making his first visit to India since 2019. (Reuters: Maxim Shemetov)

Ties between both nuclear-armed China and India have warmed in recent months, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.

But deep mistrust remains within their contested frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating the relationship.

"One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous," Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said in a post on social media on Friday, welcome arriving leaders.

Modi calls for end to Ukraine war India's PM Narendra Modi tells Putin the war in Ukraine needs to end.

Mr Modi is due to hold talks later on Friday with Mr Putin, who last visited India in December 2025. Moscow is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.

India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the Iran war in part by turning to Russia, one of its most important relationships and most controversial fuel supplier in recent years, as the war in Ukraine drags on.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is also expected on Friday, and is also set to hold talks with Mr Modi.

Posters of leaders in attendance of the BRICS summit line the streets of New Delhi. (Reuters: Francis Mascarenhas)

Gulf conflict is the 'fault line'

The BRICS summit was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions typically dominated by Western powers.

It has since expanded to include Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, three countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.

"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V Pant, a professor of international relations and vice president of India's Observer Research Foundation.

" What was seen until last year as an achievement, the expansion of BRICS, today looks like a big constraint on BRICS. "

It will be Mr Pezeshkian's first visit to India as Iranian president, and will put the Middle East conflict firmly in conversations.

Econimist Shilan Shah said the war in Iran would provide a stern test of the expanded group's cohesion.

Mr Shah noted the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.

United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi are all expected to be in attendance.

India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar visited Kyiv this month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was "grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war".

World.title: Freo surge home to claim semifinal classic against Cats
World.content:
The Flagmantle dream is still alive for 2026 after ruckman Luke Jackson produced a Herculean display to lead Fremantle to a pulsating 14-point semi-final win over Geelong in Perth.

In front of 59,725 fans at Perth Stadium on Friday night, Fremantle skipped out to a 38-7 lead before Geelong hit the front in the third quarter on the back of three quick goals to Oliver Henry.

(Getty Images)

Staring down the barrel of a straight-sets finals exit, Fremantle lifted when it mattered most, with Jackson the biggest hero of them all.

Jackson kicked two late goals in the third quarter and set up another for Patrick Voss to give Fremantle back the lead.

In a pressure-filled final term, Geelong cut a 24-point deficit back to eight points with 75 seconds remaining.

But Wharfie Time — played for just the second time this year — sent the crowd into a frenzy, with Voss kicking his fourth goal from the ensuing centre clearance as Fremantle sealed the 18.12 (120) to 16.10 (106) victory.

The win set up a preliminary final against the Swans in Sydney next week.

Henry kicked a career-high five goals for Geelong, while Shannon Neale chipped in with three.

Geelong had made eight preliminary finals in the past 10 seasons, but having to travel to Perth for this year's semi-final proved a bridge too far.

Bailey Smith racked up 29 disposals and 751m gained, while Patrick Dangerfield followed up his five-goal haul against Carlton with two majors and two goal assists.

Jackson (25 disposals, 35 hitouts, eight clearances, two goals) was a clear best-on-ground, while Voss's four goals were also crucial.

Shai Bolton made up for his quiet display in last week's 32-point loss to Hawthorn with two goals from 26 disposals.

AAP

World.title: Bennett bemoans Bunker as Knights stun Souths in elimination final
World.content:
Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett has called out the Bunker as not being good for the game after a controversial no-try call in his side's elimination final defeat to Newcastle on Friday night.

The Knights tore out of the blocks and overwhelmed South Sydney 20-10 in a fiery and dramatic finals clash at the Sydney Football Stadium.

But Bennett was left deeply frustrated at full time, pointedly asking "who is refereeing the game" after Jayden Sullivan had a try taken off him with the Rabbitohs trailing by just 10-6.

Following some neat interplay with Latrell Mitchell on the left, Alex Johnston dropped the ball under pressure from Jermaine McEwen as he ran down the line, before kicking on to allow Sullivan to dot down.

Ashley Klein awarding the try on field for a strip tackle however, Bunker official Chris Butler overruled Klein and said it was in fact a loose carry and that McEwen had slapped the arm of Johnston, not the ball.

Around 10 minutes later, Dom Young came perilously close to putting his foot on the line as he scored to extend the Knights' lead with the Bunker agreeing with the on field official's call, provoking Bennett's ire.

"I think anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock on," Bennett said of the Johnston incident in his press conference.

"The ball got knocked out of his hands.

"The referee awards the try, the Bunker flies in and says no try.

"Then 10 minutes later, Dom Young goes down the sideline, I'm not sure whether he put his foot on the line or not, but the bottom line is the bunker says we go with the referee's call.

"I want to know who's refereeing the game, that's the first thing I want to know. Is it the referee? Or the Bunker?"

The Knights and Souths went toe-to-toe in a thrilling contest. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Bennett, a long-time critic of the Bunker, said the entire process was not good for rugby league.

"It's just not what the game needs," he said.

"I've been in it [the game] a long time, seen a lot of things, and I don't think the Bunker enhances our game.

"I'm happy to live with the referee's call. Always have been, always will be.

"The ref I know is doing his job properly, he'll make a mistake, I'll live with that. My players will make mistakes, I'll live with that.

"What I can't live with is this thing called the Bunker that's supposed to be 100 per cent perfect, but it's not perfect.

"One's a try because the referee says it's a try, the other one is no try because the Bunker says it's no try.

"I wanna know who's running the game."

Knights refuse to be bullied in tense tussle

Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai tore into each other in the opening minutes. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Despite the controversial calls, Newcastle appeared well worth their win, the Knights coming out adamant they wouldn't be bullied by the star-studded Souths squad.

Dane Gagai and Latrell Mitchell set the tone early, their ferocious scuffle in the corner seeing Mitchell throw a punch that mercifully for both men missed its target.

Incredibly, neither man was sent to the bin and, in a throwback to games of yesteryear, from the restart Gagai ran the ball straight back at a crazy-eyed Mitchell, winning the battle and, eventually, the entire war against his former teammate.

Unfortunately for Souths, that missed right hook was as close as Mitchell came to making any impact in the game, the star centre strangely quiet with just seven touches in the first half.

Souths lost talismanic veteran Cody Walker to a calf injury before half time and missed the veteran's poise and creativity.

The Rabbitohs did rally, Campbell Graham scoring not long after, and David Fifita was held up as Souths rallied behind their stricken five-eighth, who retreated to the sheds in tears.

When Sullivan's try was taken away from the Rabbitohs by the Bunker, the home support must have known it was not their day.

Having the try taken off them was doubly disappointing because it was the only time in the game that Mitchell and Johnston linked up in the way Souths needed them to if they wanted to progress.

Newcastle scored not long after, with Johnston then leaving the field with a groin injury, and that was all she wrote.

The Knights will play the loser of the game between the Dolphins and the Warriors as the fairytale season for last year's wooden spooners continues for at least another week.

Look back at how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Being a renter, Jenny missed out on solar boon but that is about to change
World.content:
Australia could soon follow in the footsteps of Germany and the United Kingdom as it prepares to lift a ban on plug-in solar and batteries, unlocking access to the technology for millions of apartment dwellers and renters for the first time.

The move was discussed during a meeting of the country's energy ministers, where they agreed to explore pathways to support the "safe deployment" of plug-in solar across the country.

'Crazy' battery charging fires gas power Australia is leading the world in the adoption of batteries. But in one state, storage is fuelling some perverse and pricey outcomes.

The systems, which are also commonly referred to as 'balcony solar', were legalised in the United Kingdom last month and New Zealand has flagged plans to do the same within 12 months.

Germany is a world-leader in plug-in solar, with an estimated one in 10 households having a system installed.

It can technically be sold in Australia but not legally plugged in and used.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said a third of Australians have solar on their roof, making the technology "more popular than the backyard pool".

"Now we're taking the next step, by looking at how even more Australians can take advantage of free, abundant sunshine to cut their energy bills — even if they don't have a roof.

"All state and territory ministers are on board and will work with the Commonwealth to look at how plug-in solar and batteries can work in Australia to give apartment dwellers more control over their energy bills."

Chris Bowen says a third of Australians have solar on their roof. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Heidi Lee Douglas is the CEO of Solar Citizens, a community organisation that's been campaigning for plug-in solar to be legalised, and welcomed that Australia was now a step closer to that reality.

"This commitment to make plug-in solar and plug-in batteries legal in Australia is great news for more than a third of Australians who rent or live in apartments, and also for low-income households so they can access some of the bill-busting benefits that cheap clean solar home owners enjoy," she said.

"We want to see a firm timeline and deadline by December at the next energy ministers meeting for when plug-in solar and batteries will be available for use in every state and territory.

" Australians are looking for every opportunity to bring down their power bills. "

Heidi Lee Douglas is the CEO of Solar Citizens and says plug-in systems would finally bring more social equity for the technology. (Supplied: Solar Citizens)

What are plug-in solar and batteries?

Plug-in solar systems and batteries can be plugged into regular power points and do not require installation by an electrician.

The power generated by the panels is fed into the home network via an inverter and a standard plug and helps offset electricity used by appliances.

Overseas, they are commonly attached to apartment balconies or installed in backyards and produce between 600-800 watts of power, typically at a cost of up to $1,300.

They are a popular choice for people who live in an apartment and cannot mount rooftop solar as well as renters, many of whom have never considered the possibility of accessing renewable energy.

More than 30 per cent of Australians are renting, which equates to almost 3 million households.

Maiya Irving-Mackinnon is a renter from the Sydney suburb of Marrickville who estimates her electricity bills have increased by about 15 per cent, or $200, over the past 12 months.

Maiya Irving-Mackinnon, a renter from the Sydney suburb of Marrickville, is keen to reduce her power bills by having a plug-in solar panel. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

"Solar has never really been something that we can consider as a renter because we can't install anything on the roof or on a ground floor apartment," she said.

"I would really like to have the option to install solar panels and for that to be subsidised but it's not really something that's been available for a renter before.

" During the day, if we were able to run our electronics at a reduced cost, if not for free, then I think that would make a really big difference to our energy bill. "

Experts have suggested the payback period for plug-in solar systems ranges from four to ten years.

Ms Lee Douglas expects some households will save up to $1,000 a year on electricity bills.

"The average plug-in solar panel will allow you to save about $300-$400 a year, and plug-in batteries will easily double that," she said.

Importantly, renters would be able to take the panels and batteries with them when they moved.

Barriers to overcome

Plug-in solar systems don't need installation; they are as easy to plug in as a kettle or toaster. (Supplied: Holger's Pictures)

The federal government will now work with the states and territories to "identify measures that enable the safe use" of plug-in solar and report back on next steps by the end of the year.

The federal government is yet to indicate whether it is considering offering subsidies or rebates for the technology.

Solar Citizens is calling on plug-in solar and batteries to become legal in Australia by July next year.

But there are still barriers to overcome ahead of then, including ensuring safety standards are up to scratch for when products begin to enter the market.

Executive director of the German Plug-In Solar Association Craig Morris said Australia could look to the safety standards that Germany has developed as a starting point.

"The risk of too many companies coming in and some of them not being serious has gone down," he said.

"If you go back just five years, I think we had a number of companies that you didn't really know too much about them and maybe they were just trying a quick buck.

" But I think in the meantime, the big boys have taken over and pushed out some of the smaller firms. "

Benchmark power price drops Surging levels of renewable energy and better reliability from coal-fired generators are set to give consumers a break, with benchmark power prices to fall up to 10 per cent for consumers and more for small businesses.

Bringing landlords and body corporates on board to allow plug-in solar to be hung on balconies or stationed in backyards is another challenge that would need to be addressed in Australia before the technology is legalised and rolled out.

In Germany, tenants need to get permission to install plug-in solar but landlords need a good reason, such as planned facade renovations, to reject the request.

Mr Morris said ultimately, adoption of plug-in batteries would be crucial in allowing the full benefits of plug-in solar to be fully realised.

"What we're ultimately offering, which is plug-in solar with batteries, or maybe even plug-in batteries without solar, offering flexibility from households," he said.

"The batteries would charge and discharge not in order to optimise our consumption of the solar power we generate, but to optimise operation of the local grid.

"And this can save money across the board, across the country for everyone, even if you don't have a system, because we're going to optimise the usage of these public power lines."

World.title: Former Liberal candidate cautioned over LGBTQIA+ comments
World.content:
An Albany councillor and former Liberal candidate has been cautioned by the State Administrative Tribunal over his comments falsely linking the LGBTQIA+ community with paedophiles.

Thomas Brough, who is an emergency doctor at the Albany Health Campus, was referred to the SAT last year by the Medical Board of Australia after complaints to the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency.

In a settlement proceeding on Thursday, both parties agreed Dr Brough's comments constituted unprofessional conduct.

It comes two months after the tribunal dropped an order from the Local Government Standards Panel for Dr Brough to complete inclusivity training, finding the required course did not exist.

Thomas Brough is an emergency department doctor at the Albany Health Campus. (ABC Great Southern: Kyle Pauletto)

Unprofessional conduct

The decisions put an end to a long-running saga that began with a discussion of the city's pride festival at a council meeting in 2024.

"Within the coalition of the LGBTQIA+, I just want to hone in on the plus," Dr Brough said.

"That includes a group of people who identify as minor attracted persons."

He later doubled down on his comments while speaking to local media, sparking outrage from Albany Pride organisers, who made official complaints.

During his campaign for the WA state election a few months later, he issued a statement apologising for "any hurt that has been caused".

Albany Pride is a major LGBTQIA+ organisation in the Great Southern region. (ABC Great Southern: Jamie Thannoo)

Inclusivity training

The City of Albany engaged an independent assessor in response to complaints around the matter, who found Dr Brough's comments to be in breach of the local government code of conduct.

Under a directive from the Local Government Standards Panel, Dr Brough was asked to apologise and undertake inclusivity training provided by the Australian Human Rights Commission.

Thomas Brough has been a city councillor since 2021. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Dr Brough successfully appealed that decision on the basis the required training did not exist, with SAT member Naomi Eeagling setting aside that part of the order on July 31.

Controversial figure

In 2025, WA Liberal leader Libby Mettam distanced herself from Dr Brough after he made anti-abortion comments during a press conference on hospital funding.

When asked if WA's abortion laws should be reviewed, Dr Brough replied "yes" before saying: "Babies born alive should not be left to die."

Thomas Brough ran as the Liberal candidate for Albany at the 2025 state election. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

In a statement sent to media after the press conference, Ms Mettam said a review of the state's abortion laws was not on the party's agenda.

Dr Brough's comments sparked robust debate in parliament, with Premier Roger Cook declaring there was "something sinister and rotten going on" in the Liberal Party.

Dr Brough ran for the Liberal Party for the seat of Albany at the 2025 state election, but lost to the Nationals' Scott Leary, trailing narrowly on first preferences.

Dr Brough declined to comment.

The ABC understands a link to the State Administrative Tribunal's decision will appear on Dr Brough's entry in the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency's register of practitioners.

World.title: Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night Christian Nicolussi September 12, 2026 — 12:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Wayne Bennett blasted the NRL bunker after Alex Johnston was ruled to have knocked on at a vital stage during the Rabbitohs’ 20-10 loss to Newcastle, and declared: “The quicker they get rid of the bunker, the happier I’ll be.” South Sydney lost Cody Walker to a calf injury, then lost to an impressive Knights who now march on to week two of the finals for a showdown against the loser of Saturday’s Warriors-Dolphins clash. Loading Approaching the hour mark at Allianz Stadium on Friday night, Latrell Mitchell squeezed a pass for Johnston who appeared to have the ball stripped from him by Knights backrower Jermaine McEwen. Play was allowed to continue, Johnston kneed the ball forward, then Jayden Sullivan kicked it further ahead before scoring.



Referee Ashley Klein awarded a try, but bunker official Chris Butler had other ideas, claiming McEwen was trying to make a tackle, and Johnston simply lost the ball. Rather than potentially go ahead 12-10, Souths were on the back foot, and 10 minutes later conceded a try to Dominic Young, who appeared to put his right foot on the touchline. Did Jeremaine McEwen strip the ball from Alex Johnston? Nine Bennett complimented Newcastle on playing a “tremendous game”, and was mindful to not deflect from the result, but he was also clearly frustrated with the bunker, which was meant to eliminate every contentious call. “Anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock-on,” Bennett said.



“The ball was knocked out of his [Johnston’s] hands. “The referee awards a try, then the bunker buys in and says it’s no try. “Ten minutes later, Newcastle winger Dom Young goes down the sideline, I’m not sure if he put his foot on the sideline, but the bottom line is the bunker comes back and says, ‘we’re going with the referee’s call’. “I want to know who is refereeing the game, that’s the first thing I want to know. “Is it the bunker or is it the referee?



“In the case of Alex Johnston ... you can look at that 50 times, everyone can come up with a different opinion. It’s just too technical. It’s not what the game needs. Cody Walker hobbles off with a calf injury. NRL “I’ve been in the game a long time, I’ve seen a lot of things, and I don’t think the bunker enhances our game to the [level] we believe it does.” Bennett said he was happy to live with referees’ making poor calls, just as he was prepared to cope with mistakes made by his own players. “But the bunker was meant to be 100 per cent bulletproof, and it’s not,” he said.



“It won’t stop here tonight. There will be more instances through the play-offs, I can promise you.” Related Video Video icon 1:05 Joey pleads with Rabbitohs to extend Walker Bennett was also confused by a call in the first half to penalise Mitchell when he appeared to be struck first by Knights centre Dane Gagai. The Mitchell-Gagai duel was one of the great match-ups of the evening. Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook thought “common sense prevailed” with the decision to strip Souths of the Johnston and Sullivan try, while Cameron Smith said during the live commentary it did not deserve to be a try.



The Knights looked like a team that was fresh from the bye the previous week, and looked in more sync in attack. Souths were not helped by Walker breaking down on the half hour, with the playmaker immediately signalling to the sideline for help. He would have been unlikely to play on next weekend had Souths progressed, but Bennett confirmed the club was keen for him to play on in 2027, even though a deal was yet to be formally struck. Aside from Walker, then Johnston failing to finish the game with a groin complaint, Souths had enjoyed a good run with injuries at this time of year. World.title: AFL LIVE: Dockers avoid a violet crumble, advance to a prelim final after Chris Scott left fuming from no-goal call
World.content:
Dockers coach Justin Longmuir says he has breathed a sigh of relief. His side was facing a straight-sets exit after finishing the season on top of the ladder.

They jumped out of the blocks at Perth Stadium with a six-goal opening term, but had to withstand a Geelong fightback during the third term - at one stage, Geelong held an eight-point lead.

But a four-goal burst to close out the third term set up their 14-point victory - 18.12 (120) to 16.10 (106). It was a huge improvement from last week’s shock loss to Hawthorn.

“I thought we played a clearly much better brand of footy (than last week),” Longmuir told Channel 7.

“We played the win tonight, and you know, it got a bit hairy in the third quarter, and we clearly didn’t start the third quarter well. But I’m so proud of the way the players fought back at the back end of that third quarter.

“Clearly, it was an important part of the game. We lacked a bit of composure at times in the last quarter, but yeah, really proud of the week we had, and really proud of the effort.”

Longmuir will now begin preparing for next week’s preliminary final clash against Sydney in Sydney.

World.title: Fremantle v Geelong player ratings: While Dockers stood up under pressure, these Cats guns will rue one that got away
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Fremantle v Geelong player ratings: While Dockers stood up under pressure, these Cats guns will rue one that got away

Loading

All the pressure was on the Dockers as they desperately tried to avoid being the second top-of-the-ladder side in as many seasons (after the Crows last year) to bow out in straight sets. And in the Cats, they faced a proven finals foe that was never going to give in. That’s exactly what makes the Dockers’ 14-point win so impressive. Steve Barrett (Fremantle) and Marc McGowan (Geelong) run their eye over every player in from this semi-final. Josh Treacy lifted after his performance against the Hawks. AFL Photos



Fremantle (3) Caleb Serong: Predictably had Oisin Mullin for company, and eventually quelled the tag in a fine – and anticipated – return to form after he was below his usual standard against Hawthorn. His magnificent 55-metre goal in the fourth quarter all but sealed a preliminary final berth. 7.5/10 (5) Heath Chapman: Struggled to contain Ollie Henry, especially in the third term when the Cats were gathering steam, and his decision-making was shaky at times. He did salvage his night with a strong finish. 5.5/10 (6) Jordan Clark: One of Fremantle’s few bright spots in their qualifying final meltdown was industrious against the Cats, his old side. He generated tremendous run out of defence, racking up 621 metres gained and wasting almost none of his 25 touches. 7/10



(8) Andrew Brayshaw: One of the Dockers’ prime movers through the middle, his performance won’t create headlines, but he was as consistent as ever across four quarters and used the ball smartly. 7/10 Luke “the Unicorn” Jackson was nothing short of brilliant for the Dockers. AFL Photos (9) Luke Jackson: When Fremantle needed something special, their “Unicorn” delivered. After running amok in ruck in the opening term, he was becalmed in the second, before unleashing a match-winning third quarter for the ages. The big fella booted two goals for the term and contributed to three others. Titanic. 9/10 (10) Shai Bolton: The Dockers needed a bright start, but they couldn’t have dreamt of a better one than what their exciting No.10 crafted, twice bursting away from Bailey Smith in the middle and booting two goals in the opening 80 seconds. He continued to give Geelong fits, even when the disciplined Mark O’Connor ran with him. 8.5/10 View post on X



(13) Luke Ryan: Had his hands full with Patrick Dangerfield at times, but still managed to consistently provide plenty of drive and run out of the back half for Fremantle. 6/10 (16) Murphy Reid: When he’s at his best, this young gun’s poise and creativity are off the charts. His playmaking was elite, especially in the first half, fashioning a fine bounceback from an under-par showing against the Hawks. 7.5/10 (17) Judd McVee: Called up to replace the injured Brandon Walker, he didn’t have much of an impact aside from a few glimpses in the second stanza. 4.5/10 (18) Mason Cox: He crashed packs, booted a goal, got in faces and provided occasional ruck relief for the rampant Jackson. He did his bit. 4/10 (20) Patrick Voss: What a return to form following his qualifying final shocker against Hawthorn. He booted four majors, exerted himself on the contest and ensured Tom Stewart’s hands were kept full. His goal right on three-quarter-time was massive. 8/10



View post on X (21) Oscar McDonald: He covered plenty of territory and his intercepting was important in the first half. He went to Ollie Henry in the fourth quarter, but generally had less impact as the evening wore on. Still, this was a better night for him than the rough one he had a week earlier against Jack Gunston. 5/10 (23) Karl Worner: He provided defensive pressure at the contest with calmness when exiting the backline was in his hands. His disposal efficiency was 100 per cent - you can’t ask much more than that from your half-backs. 7/10 (24) Jye Amiss: Thrashed by Tom Barrass a week ago, he was unsighted for long stretches against Geelong. He slotted an important goal in the second stanza and had a real crack. He was kept under wraps for most of the game by Jack Henry, but still managed 2.1 from his three kicks. 4.5/10 (25) Alex Pearce: His intercepting and decision-making on the last line was sound, as was his attack on the contest. His direct opponent Shannon Neale probably just took the honours, though. 5.5/10



(26) Hayden Young: That long goal he kicked out of the centre ball-up was one for the ages – as was his whole second quarter when he helped the Dockers get on top at stoppage. He had a game-high nine inside-50s to go with 556m gained. One of Fremantle’s real game-breakers. 8/10 View post on X (28) Neil Erasmus: He was solid on his wing, where he often found himself matched up with Jeremy Cameron. His ball use was sound and he played his role. 6/10 (32) Michael Frederick: He nailed a nice goal on the run during the Dockers’ sizzling opening-quarter surge, then another huge one in the fourth. In-between he was often unsighted, whether on a wing or at half-forward. 5/10 (34) Corey Wagner: The recalled utility was strong at the contest, mixing time on the wing with stints forward of centre. His tackling was immense but his ball use iffy. He made some amends with a magnificent long kick into attack for a strong Amiss mark and goal against the grain in the third quarter. 6/10



(35) Josh Treacy: Following his stinker against Hawthorn, the spearhead was much better against Geelong. He booted an important goal in the third term to restore Fremantle’s lead, while his powerful contested marking was a feature. 7/10 (39) Sam Switkowski: He provided his customary forward pressure and was involved in a number of the Dockers’ scoring chains. 5/10 (43) Isaiah Dudley: The little goalsneak bobbed up with two goals in a second-quarter cameo, but his disposal was rushed and imprecise at other times. 5/10 (44) Matthew Johnson: Bravely overcame a massive knee to the back from Dangerfield to have an impact after half-time. He spent some time in the centre-square as Fremantle tried something different during the Cats’ flurry. He followed a huge one-on-one win against Ollie Dempsey with a calm kick to Frederick for a crucial late goal. 6/10 Chris Scott could barely believe his eyes after a shot on goal from Ollie Dempsey was ruled a behind due to “inconclusive evidence” to overturn the umpire’s call. Seven



Geelong (2) Jay Polkinghorne: Dished the handball that led to Shaun Mannagh’s second-quarter goal, but had a quiet night overall. 1/10 (3) Bailey Smith: He was part of a beaten midfield early, but worked tirelessly and made his mark with his tackling before setting up consecutive goals to give the Cats their first lead in the third term. Won plenty of the Sherrin. 8.5/10 Patrick Voss and Bailey Smith aren’t exactly shrinking violets. AFL Photos



(4) Tanner Bruhn: Had a challenging night following Dudley around in defence, but fought back to have a better second half. 5/10 (5) Jeremy Cameron: Cameron’s night summed up his season. He still kicked two goals, but he has struggled to impact games like he did last year. 5/10 (7) Shaun Mannagh: Played a key role in keeping Geelong in the contest in the first half when few other Cats were firing. He generated several opportunities for himself and others, and even won four first-half clearances. 7/10 (9) Max Holmes: Looked poised to have a big second half after a strong finish to the second quarter, but his second game back from his ankle setback was largely muted by his standards. 6/10 Mitchell Edwards (pictured here competing with Voss) didn’t have his best night for the Cats. AFL Photos



(11) Mitch Edwards: Welcome to the finals cauldron. He hurt his pinky finger in the first quarter, but the flogging he received from Jackson would have been most painful of all. 3/10 (14) Connor O’Sullivan: He grabbed nine marks, and generally held his own in defence, even when the Cats were under siege early. 6.5/10 (17) Lawson Humphries: Like many Cats, Humphries had a slow start, but he warmed to the task and ended up being one of his team’s top contributors, using the ball neatly and repeatedly cutting off Docker forays. 7/10 (21) Ollie Wiltshire: Found space inside 50 to mark and goal in the first quarter, but was unable to have much of an impact. 3/10 (28) Ollie Dempsey: The All-Australian Cat couldn’t break loose for his typical game-breaking moments, but never stopped trying. 5/10



View post on X (30) Tom Atkins: A night to forget for the rugged Atkins, including conceding the last free kick and goal to Voss that sealed Fremantle’s victory. 2/10 (32) Gryan Miers: Miers’ work-rate spike in the third-quarter comeback, but where was he in the first half? Geelong needed more from him. 3/10 (33) Shannon Neale: Took a strong grab in the opening quarter and bobbed up for a pair of goals in the second term, including his 50th of the season, but was largely unsighted after half-time until a late goal. 5.5/10 (34) Oisin Mullin: The Irishman has become a very reliable AFL footballer who can be trusted in the biggest of matches. As always, he was strong defensively, but also won his share of the ball. 7/10



Patrick Dangerfield stood strong in the finals yet again. AFL Photos (35) Patrick Dangerfield: The champion Cat might not have been his match-winning self from a week ago, but still had some terrific moments, including an early 50-metre strike. “Danger” remains a force. 7.5/10 (36) Ollie Henry: The Cats’ best forward, and possibly best player, with a career-high five goals, including to keep them alive in the final term. He never stopped presenting and mostly finished his work. 8.5/10 (38) Jack Henry: Had a series of shaky first-half moments, including slipping to concede an easy goal to Cox. Improved in the second half and had EIGHT intercepts, but it wasn’t his best performance. 4/10 (39) Zach Guthrie: Guthrie was caught out of position a few times in the first half, but that wasn’t always his fault. Intercepted well and was very good in the third-quarter fightback, including two touches in one passage that led to an Ollie Henry goal. 7/10



(42) Mark O’Connor: Was used through the middle on occasion when the tide was against Geelong, and was solid without playing a major role. 5/10 (44) Tom Stewart: A rare finals downer for Stewart, who conceded two goals to direct opponent Voss in the opening quarter and was later outmarked by Treacy. He had nothing like his usual impact. 4/10 (45) Brad Close: He had two direct goal assists, including a clever pass to Shannon Neale, but went missing for large chunks of the game. 5/10 (46) Mark Blicavs: Another veteran Cat who struggled. Chris Scott used his star utility in his usual bevy of roles to try to get him going, including in the ruck against Jackson, but Blicavs didn’t fire a shot. 4/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSeptember 11 attacks ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on Maria Tsvetkova , Idrees Ali and Joseph Ax September 11, 2026 — 11:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day. In New York, family members of the victims joined Vice President JD Vance and four former US presidents at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s North Tower. New York City Fire Department (FDNY) members visit the memorial ahead of the ceremony. Bloomberg The site of the World Trade Centre attacks on Friday, now the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that will last for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.



Other moments of silence, marking when the other three airplanes crashed and the two towers collapsed, will follow. For the first time, a seventh silence will be observed to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward. A woman and child pause at the memorial on Friday morning. Spencer Platt/Pool Getty Images North America via AP People walk in the Oculus near the memorial on the 25th anniversary of the attacks. AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis Gregory Carafello came to the ceremony to honour the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm that lost more than 650 employees in the attacks. Carafello himself was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate. “Everyone should realise that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.”



US Vice President JD Vance speaks with former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg as former President George W. Bush arrives for the ceremony. AP Photo/Adam Gray Former President Bill Clinton, former First Lady Michelle Obama and former President Barack Obama listen to speakers at the memorial in New York. Olga Fedorova/POOL EPA via AP In Arlington, Virginia, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain early on Friday to watch the unfurling of an American flag at the west side of the Pentagon where American Airlines Flight 77 hit, killing 184 people in all. President Donald Trump is expected to speak at a ceremony there. Mourners will also hold a ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein



An American flag is unfurled at the Pentagon early on Friday morning. Bloomberg US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth watched the flag unfurling ceremony as rain fell at the Pentagon. Bloomberg The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security. But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families, first responders and rescue workers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter-century ago and the heartbreak that followed. Loading



Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower. Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him her father’s grave last week and was attending a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday. Related Article September 11 attacks Australians remember lost loved ones 25 years on from September 11 attacks “This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather. “We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added.



A generation of Americans has grown up since 2001 who are too young to remember the attacks but whose lives were fundamentally altered by them. Related Article September 11 attacks The day that changed America and shaped the world we know today The attacks initiated the “war on terror,” which led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements – a promise being tested by the current Iran war. At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks. At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, has faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected.



Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Rudy Giuliani, former mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony. Bloomberg Related Article September 11 attacks John Howard witnessed the 9/11 attacks as PM. It changed his leadership forever Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died. Patrick Whalen’s father, also named Patrick, was a New York City firefighter who responded to the attacks and continued working at Ground Zero for months amid the dust and rubble. In 2020, he was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer linked to exposure to toxic carcinogens, and died in 2021.



“The government told him it was safe to breathe, and, obviously, it was not true,” the younger Whalen said after a New York City Fire Department memorial service this week. A woman mourns at the September 11 memorial plaza in Lower Manhattan. Dave Sanders/Pool The New York Times via AP The names of all 2977 victims were read aloud over several hours. Bloomberg Information that the air at Ground Zero was safe to breathe came from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Its former administrator, Christine Todd Whitman, apologised in a 2016 interview with The Guardian, saying the agency did its best with the knowledge it had. The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show. Twenty-six have died this year alone.

World.title: Police conduct welfare checks after dozens of Triple Zero calls fail due to Optus outage
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaEmergency services Police conduct welfare checks after dozens of Triple Zero calls fail due to Optus outage James Costa Updated September 11, 2026 — 10:32pm ,first published 9:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of Triple Zero calls struggled to connect to the Telstra national emergency line because of an Optus outage on Friday, Triple Zero Victoria says. Victoria Police said it was completing welfare checks on impacted callers following the outage on Friday afternoon. “Just before 7pm, Optus has provided details of 39 calls that experienced difficulty connecting to the Telstra national Triple Zero (000) Emergency Call Person,” Triple Zero Victoria chief operations officer Paul Santamaria said. Optus confirmed an outage on Friday afternoon. Getty Images Earlier on Friday, Optus confirmed it became aware of an outage at “approximately 1.30pm AEST and immediately mobilised technical teams and restored services as quickly as possible”.



Optus confirmed later in the evening that the outage lasted for one hour and 16 minutes, affecting some customers in Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, and the Northern Territory. The telco said that a network issue resulted in intermittent call dropouts, adding that it referred around 40 calls to Victoria Police for welfare checks. “We are still determining whether calls were able to connect to a different network and this will be established in coming days,” an Optus spokesperson said. The Tasmanian Department of Police, Fire and Emergency Management said Optus had advised it of an outage that affected three Triple Zero calls in Tasmania. “Police subsequently contacted the callers, and it was determined they did not require immediate police or emergency services,” the department said.



Some Optus customers took to social media earlier in the day, stating they had lost service or were unable to make or receive calls. Optus sent a text message to customers saying that in Victoria, South Australia, the Northern Territory and Tasmania “Optus has loss of coverage due to this outage”. Related Article Updated

Telecommunications Optus sued over Triple Zero outage linked to two deaths “Emergency service calls can be accessed where other mobile provider coverage is available or are able to call via Wi-Fi.” In July, Australia’s communications regulator sued Optus over last year’s Triple Zero outage, alleging the telco failed to connect emergency calls on 1005 occasions and exposing it to penalties of more than $500 million.



The Australian Communications and Media Authority filed civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court against Optus Mobile over the September 18 outage, when a bungled firewall upgrade blocked calls to Triple Zero across South Australia, Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Far West NSW for about 13 hours. The outage was linked to two deaths. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Wayne Bennett has never liked the bunker. He wants it gone after Friday night Christian Nicolussi September 12, 2026 — 12:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Wayne Bennett blasted the NRL bunker after Alex Johnston was ruled to have knocked on at a vital stage during the Rabbitohs’ 20-10 loss to Newcastle, and declared: “The quicker they get rid of the bunker, the happier I’ll be.” South Sydney lost Cody Walker to a calf injury, then lost to an impressive Knights who now march on to week two of the finals for a showdown against the loser of Saturday’s Warriors-Dolphins clash. Loading Approaching the hour mark at Allianz Stadium on Friday night, Latrell Mitchell squeezed a pass for Johnston who appeared to have the ball stripped from him by Knights backrower Jermaine McEwen. Play was allowed to continue, Johnston kneed the ball forward, then Jayden Sullivan kicked it further ahead before scoring.



Referee Ashley Klein awarded a try, but bunker official Chris Butler had other ideas, claiming McEwen was trying to make a tackle, and Johnston simply lost the ball. Rather than potentially go ahead 12-10, Souths were on the back foot, and 10 minutes later conceded a try to Dominic Young, who appeared to put his right foot on the touchline. Did Jeremaine McEwen strip the ball from Alex Johnston? Nine Bennett complimented Newcastle on playing a “tremendous game”, and was mindful to not deflect from the result, but he was also clearly frustrated with the bunker, which was meant to eliminate every contentious call. “Anyone who plays rugby league or knows rugby league knows that was a knock-on,” Bennett said.



“The ball was knocked out of his [Johnston’s] hands. “The referee awards a try, then the bunker buys in and says it’s no try. “Ten minutes later, Newcastle winger Dom Young goes down the sideline, I’m not sure if he put his foot on the sideline, but the bottom line is the bunker comes back and says, ‘we’re going with the referee’s call’. “I want to know who is refereeing the game, that’s the first thing I want to know. “Is it the bunker or is it the referee?



“In the case of Alex Johnston ... you can look at that 50 times, everyone can come up with a different opinion. It’s just too technical. It’s not what the game needs. Cody Walker hobbles off with a calf injury. NRL “I’ve been in the game a long time, I’ve seen a lot of things, and I don’t think the bunker enhances our game to the [level] we believe it does.” Bennett said he was happy to live with referees’ making poor calls, just as he was prepared to cope with mistakes made by his own players. “But the bunker was meant to be 100 per cent bulletproof, and it’s not,” he said.



“It won’t stop here tonight. There will be more instances through the play-offs, I can promise you.” Related Video Video icon 1:05 Joey pleads with Rabbitohs to extend Walker Bennett was also confused by a call in the first half to penalise Mitchell when he appeared to be struck first by Knights centre Dane Gagai. The Mitchell-Gagai duel was one of the great match-ups of the evening. Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook thought “common sense prevailed” with the decision to strip Souths of the Johnston and Sullivan try, while Cameron Smith said during the live commentary it did not deserve to be a try.



The Knights looked like a team that was fresh from the bye the previous week, and looked in more sync in attack. Souths were not helped by Walker breaking down on the half hour, with the playmaker immediately signalling to the sideline for help. He would have been unlikely to play on next weekend had Souths progressed, but Bennett confirmed the club was keen for him to play on in 2027, even though a deal was yet to be formally struck. Aside from Walker, then Johnston failing to finish the game with a groin complaint, Souths had enjoyed a good run with injuries at this time of year. World.title: AFL LIVE: Dockers avoid a violet crumble, advance to a prelim final after Chris Scott left fuming from no-goal call
World.content:
Dockers coach Justin Longmuir says he has breathed a sigh of relief. His side was facing a straight-sets exit after finishing the season on top of the ladder.

They jumped out of the blocks at Perth Stadium with a six-goal opening term, but had to withstand a Geelong fightback during the third term - at one stage, Geelong held an eight-point lead.

But a four-goal burst to close out the third term set up their 14-point victory - 18.12 (120) to 16.10 (106). It was a huge improvement from last week’s shock loss to Hawthorn.

“I thought we played a clearly much better brand of footy (than last week),” Longmuir told Channel 7.

“We played the win tonight, and you know, it got a bit hairy in the third quarter, and we clearly didn’t start the third quarter well. But I’m so proud of the way the players fought back at the back end of that third quarter.

“Clearly, it was an important part of the game. We lacked a bit of composure at times in the last quarter, but yeah, really proud of the week we had, and really proud of the effort.”

Longmuir will now begin preparing for next week’s preliminary final clash against Sydney in Sydney.
