He hurt his pinky finger in the first quarter, but the flogging he received from Jackson would have been most painful of all. 3/10 (14) Connor O’Sullivan: He grabbed nine marks, and generally held his own in defence, even when the Cats were under siege early. 6.5/10 (17) Lawson Humphries: Like many Cats, Humphries had a slow start, but he warmed to the task and ended up being one of his team’s top contributors, using the ball neatly and repeatedly cutting off Docker forays. 7/10 (21) Ollie Wiltshire: Found space inside 50 to mark and goal in the first quarter, but was unable to have much of an impact. 3/10 (28) Ollie Dempsey: The All-Australian Cat couldn’t break loose for his typical game-breaking moments, but never stopped trying. 5/10



View post on X (30) Tom Atkins: A night to forget for the rugged Atkins, including conceding the last free kick and goal to Voss that sealed Fremantle’s victory. 2/10 (32) Gryan Miers: Miers’ work-rate spike in the third-quarter comeback, but where was he in the first half? Geelong needed more from him. 3/10 (33) Shannon Neale: Took a strong grab in the opening quarter and bobbed up for a pair of goals in the second term, including his 50th of the season, but was largely unsighted after half-time until a late goal. 5.5/10 (34) Oisin Mullin: The Irishman has become a very reliable AFL footballer who can be trusted in the biggest of matches. As always, he was strong defensively, but also won his share of the ball. 7/10



Patrick Dangerfield stood strong in the finals yet again. AFL Photos (35) Patrick Dangerfield: The champion Cat might not have been his match-winning self from a week ago, but still had some terrific moments, including an early 50-metre strike. “Danger” remains a force. 7.5/10 (36) Ollie Henry: The Cats’ best forward, and possibly best player, with a career-high five goals, including to keep them alive in the final term. He never stopped presenting and mostly finished his work. 8.5/10 (38) Jack Henry: Had a series of shaky first-half moments, including slipping to concede an easy goal to Cox. Improved in the second half and had EIGHT intercepts, but it wasn’t his best performance. 4/10 (39) Zach Guthrie: Guthrie was caught out of position a few times in the first half, but that wasn’t always his fault. Intercepted well and was very good in the third-quarter fightback, including two touches in one passage that led to an Ollie Henry goal. 7/10



(42) Mark O’Connor: Was used through the middle on occasion when the tide was against Geelong, and was solid without playing a major role. 5/10 (44) Tom Stewart: A rare finals downer for Stewart, who conceded two goals to direct opponent Voss in the opening quarter and was later outmarked by Treacy. He had nothing like his usual impact. 4/10 (45) Brad Close: He had two direct goal assists, including a clever pass to Shannon Neale, but went missing for large chunks of the game. 5/10 (46) Mark Blicavs: Another veteran Cat who struggled. Chris Scott used his star utility in his usual bevy of roles to try to get him going, including in the ruck against Jackson, but Blicavs didn’t fire a shot. 4/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSeptember 11 attacks ‘These were people like you and me going to work’: America remembers 9/11 victims 25 years on Maria Tsvetkova , Idrees Ali and Joseph Ax September 11, 2026 — 11:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday to commemorate the nearly 3000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Centre, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania – and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day. In New York, family members of the victims joined Vice President JD Vance and four former US presidents at Ground Zero in Lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8.46am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Centre’s North Tower. New York City Fire Department (FDNY) members visit the memorial ahead of the ceremony. Bloomberg The site of the World Trade Centre attacks on Friday, now the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, a sombre recitation that will last for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.



Other moments of silence, marking when the other three airplanes crashed and the two towers collapsed, will follow. For the first time, a seventh silence will be observed to honour the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward. A woman and child pause at the memorial on Friday morning. Spencer Platt/Pool Getty Images North America via AP People walk in the Oculus near the memorial on the 25th anniversary of the attacks. AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis Gregory Carafello came to the ceremony to honour the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm that lost more than 650 employees in the attacks. Carafello himself was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate. “Everyone should realise that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.”



US Vice President JD Vance speaks with former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg as former President George W. Bush arrives for the ceremony. AP Photo/Adam Gray Former President Bill Clinton, former First Lady Michelle Obama and former President Barack Obama listen to speakers at the memorial in New York. Olga Fedorova/POOL EPA via AP In Arlington, Virginia, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain early on Friday to watch the unfurling of an American flag at the west side of the Pentagon where American Airlines Flight 77 hit, killing 184 people in all. President Donald Trump is expected to speak at a ceremony there. Mourners will also hold a ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington. President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump at a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein



An American flag is unfurled at the Pentagon early on Friday morning. Bloomberg US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth watched the flag unfurling ceremony as rain fell at the Pentagon. Bloomberg The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security. But for many whom the attacks directly affected – the victims’ families, first responders and rescue workers – the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter-century ago and the heartbreak that followed. Loading



Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower. Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him her father’s grave last week and was attending a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday. Related Article September 11 attacks Australians remember lost loved ones 25 years on from September 11 attacks “This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather. “We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added.



A generation of Americans has grown up since 2001 who are too young to remember the attacks but whose lives were fundamentally altered by them. Related Article September 11 attacks The day that changed America and shaped the world we know today The attacks initiated the “war on terror,” which led to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security and the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements – a promise being tested by the current Iran war. At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks. At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colours Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, has faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected.



Zohran Mamdani, mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Bloomberg Rudy Giuliani, former mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony. Bloomberg Related Article September 11 attacks John Howard witnessed the 9/11 attacks as PM. It changed his leadership forever Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died. Patrick Whalen’s father, also named Patrick, was a New York City firefighter who responded to the attacks and continued working at Ground Zero for months amid the dust and rubble. In 2020, he was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer linked to exposure to toxic carcinogens, and died in 2021.



“The government told him it was safe to breathe, and, obviously, it was not true,” the younger Whalen said after a New York City Fire Department memorial service this week. A woman mourns at the September 11 memorial plaza in Lower Manhattan. Dave Sanders/Pool The New York Times via AP The names of all 2977 victims were read aloud over several hours. Bloomberg Information that the air at Ground Zero was safe to breathe came from the US Environmental Protection Agency. Its former administrator, Christine Todd Whitman, apologised in a 2016 interview with The Guardian, saying the agency did its best with the knowledge it had. The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show. Twenty-six have died this year alone.

World.title: Police conduct welfare checks after dozens of Triple Zero calls fail due to Optus outage
World.content:
Updated NationalVictoriaEmergency services Police conduct welfare checks after dozens of Triple Zero calls fail due to Optus outage James Costa Updated September 11, 2026 — 10:32pm ,first published 9:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dozens of Triple Zero calls struggled to connect to the Telstra national emergency line because of an Optus outage on Friday, Triple Zero Victoria says. Victoria Police said it was completing welfare checks on impacted callers following the outage on Friday afternoon. “Just before 7pm, Optus has provided details of 39 calls that experienced difficulty connecting to the Telstra national Triple Zero (000) Emergency Call Person,” Triple Zero Victoria chief operations officer Paul Santamaria said. Optus confirmed an outage on Friday afternoon. Getty Images Earlier on Friday, Optus confirmed it became aware of an outage at “approximately 1.30pm AEST and immediately mobilised technical teams and restored services as quickly as possible”.



Optus confirmed later in the evening that the outage lasted for one hour and 16 minutes, affecting some customers in Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, and the Northern Territory. The telco said that a network issue resulted in intermittent call dropouts, adding that it referred around 40 calls to Victoria Police for welfare checks. “We are still determining whether calls were able to connect to a different network and this will be established in coming days,” an Optus spokesperson said. The Tasmanian Department of Police, Fire and Emergency Management said Optus had advised it of an outage that affected three Triple Zero calls in Tasmania. “Police subsequently contacted the callers, and it was determined they did not require immediate police or emergency services,” the department said.



Some Optus customers took to social media earlier in the day, stating they had lost service or were unable to make or receive calls. Optus sent a text message to customers saying that in Victoria, South Australia, the Northern Territory and Tasmania “Optus has loss of coverage due to this outage”. Related Article Updated

Telecommunications Optus sued over Triple Zero outage linked to two deaths “Emergency service calls can be accessed where other mobile provider coverage is available or are able to call via Wi-Fi.” In July, Australia’s communications regulator sued Optus over last year’s Triple Zero outage, alleging the telco failed to connect emergency calls on 1005 occasions and exposing it to penalties of more than $500 million.



The Australian Communications and Media Authority filed civil penalty proceedings in the Federal Court against Optus Mobile over the September 18 outage, when a bungled firewall upgrade blocked calls to Triple Zero across South Australia, Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Far West NSW for about 13 hours. The outage was linked to two deaths. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Close libraries for a day or kill animals - Christchurch councillor says over Orana Park financial woes
World.content:
A Christchurch city councillor is calling on his colleagues to fill the $4 million hole in Orana Wildlife Park's budget.

The park's leaders admitted on Friday it was in financial crisis and cash reserves were set to run out early next year.

The zoo had developed a financial sustainability and recovery plan to deal with the crisis, two years after raising concerns about "inevitable financial demise" if Christchurch City Council did not provide annual long-term funding.

The council ultimately agreed to provide $500,000 per year for three years.

Orana Wildlife Park in need of $4 million to stay open Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Orana Wildlife Park Trust co-chair Dr Ken Hughey said the future was challenging.

"We believe the support is out there," he said.

"We're already working with key partners in that space and we're incredibly positive that we'll get to the immediate shortfall of just around $4 million. We hope to have a big announcement to make within about three weeks."

Spokespeople for the ministers of Finance, Conservation and Culture and Heritage confirmed their offices had not yet been approached by the zoo.

Orana Wildlife Park Trust co-chair Dr Ken Hughey. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka announced in August $30,000 for Orana Wildlife Park for a breeding programme for the critically endangered white-bellied skink.

Ash Murphy, a manager in the Department of Conservation's terrestrial biodiversity unit, said that funding was on hold - alongside $145,000 to be shared with Auckland Zoo for a breeding programme for Hamilton's frogs - while Orana Wildlife Park showed DOC the work could be completed.

"Orana Park has been a DOC partner in conservation for many years and they've have been doing great work managing breeding programmes for some of DOC's most threatened species like the kākāriki karaka/orange-fronted parakeet," Murphy said.

"DOC staff will meet with Orana Park next week to talk about the 27 native species held at the park, including those in the captive breeding programmes.

"DOC is confident in Orana Park's ability to provide good care for the birds and other native wildlife they have."

Christchurch mayor Phil Mauger said, in a statement, the council was aware of the zoo's financial plight and council staff were preparing a report to be considered by councillors at an upcoming meeting.

Christchurch mayor Phil Mauger. RNZ/Nathan Mckinnon

But Harewood ward councillor Aaron Keown said he would sign a cheque for $4 million right now if it was up to him.

"You're talking numbers like that $4.1 million, those sort of numbers can be found across multiple places," he said.

"You could literally close every library for one day a week and you'd have that much money spare. If you were to ask the people of Christchurch would they rather have all the libraries open just six days a week and we can have Orana Park flourishing or we keep all the libraries open but we execute all the animals at Orana Park and don't be part of an international breeding programme and a national breeding programme?

"There's so many places councils could save money and then put it into breeding programmes so we don't have to put down those animals and close up the park because that's your alternative to not funding it properly.

"That's your alternative to not funding it properly - I'll call a spade a spade - those animals will have to have a long sleep."

Councillor Aaron Keown said he would be extremely disappointed if other councillors did not get behind Orana Wildlife Park. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

He had suggested introducing a regional targeted rate for Christchurch city and the Waimakariri and Selwyn districts to provide ongoing support for Orana Wildlife Park.

"It should be a regional targeted rate, exactly the same as the museum," Keown said.

"Now the museum collects 20-odd million dollars a year. We only need one-fifth of that for Orana Park. You do it on a regional [basis], but then we have a schools programme where because regionally you've been paying rates to fund the park all schools then have access to do a schools programme each year which is funded by that rate. So then schools only pay the transport to and from.

"Now you suddenly get value for that spend and so that's the type of way that I would look at funding that park and picking up the shortfall. And a lot more kids would learn a lot more about animals and animal welfare and international conservation by doing visits there."

He would be extremely disappointed if other councillors did not get behind Orana Wildlife Park.

SAFE says the priority now is the welfare of the animals. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

But animal rights group SAFE said Orana Wildlife Park's dire financial situation demonstrated zoos were no longer affordable and New Zealand needed to work towards ending them.

SAFE chief executive Debra Ashton said traditional zoos no longer worked commercially and the public expected greater animal welfare.

"It's a pretty dire situation for them to be under but obviously the priority now is the welfare of these animals," Ashton said.

"These institutions are increasingly outdated and fail to meet the physical, psychological and welfare needs of animals anyway.

"If zoos were genuinely prioritising conservation and animal welfare they would focus on creating expansive natural habitats and supporting wildlife in their natural environments.

"It's pretty clear that this is a very expensive undertaking which is why we need to stop doing this."

The government should support genuine conservation, help zoos transition away from animals as entertainment, Ashton said.

Friday's revelation of Orana Wildlife Park's financial dire straits follows a difficult two years of scrutiny for the zoo.

A sign at the park in 2024. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

In 2024 a 1News investigation revealed a string of animal deaths and injuries at the zoo.

The park's leaders responded by defending its track record and saying allegations of poor animal welfare were "taken out of context".

Orana Wildlife Park chief executive Lynn Anderson resigned in November 2024 and was replaced by Rachel Haydon in February 2025.

The zoo also paused taking new animals for six months in December 2024.

World.title: Political aftershock of 9/11 still being felt 25 years later - Helen Clark
World.content:
Twenty-five years later, former NZ Prime Minister Helen Clark is lamenting the unlearnt lessons from political mistakes made in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks on New York's World Trade Center.

Clark was at the helm of the nation and en route to Europe, when terrorists flew planes into the 'Twin Towers', triggering a US response that reverberated around the world and forced other countries to choose sides in the Middle East.

"What I remember is being in the lounge at Hong Kong Airport and seeing these images coming through on the TV screen, no sound, of what appeared to be smoke coming out of skyscrapers," she told John Campbell on RNZ Morning Report.

"We had no idea what was going on - where was this, what was happening - and got on the next flight.

Helen Clark discusses being PM during 9/11 attacks Morning Report Download MP3 8m

"Jim Anderton was deputy prime minister and had taken command of issuing statements for the government.

"I landed in Rome and quickly made the decision that I would have to go back, because - for those who weren't around at the time or don't have a clear recollection of it - it was just such an incredibly dramatic and tragic event.

"No one quite knew if this was the start of a series of more attacks or what we were heading into. There was considerable confusion at home and abroad about what was happening."

Clark's passage home ran into further obstacles, when she encountered an Ansett airline strike in Melbourne, which saw her complete the journey on an NZ Air Force Lockheed P3 Orion.

al Qaeda operatives flew planes into New York's World Trade Center. AFP/SETH MCALLISTER

Over the months that followed, New Zealand had to decide what part to play in the American quest for revenge against al Qaeda, who were hiding in the White Mountains of Afghanistan.

When the ruling Taliban refused to co-operate with the US, it also became a target.

"In late 2001, when this shocking attack happened, the world was with the US," Clark recalled. "Whatever people around the world may have thought of the US, they were deeply shocked to see, in the American heartland, there were innocent people being killed from terrorist bombs.

"Here we start to unpick what went wrong.

"Firstly, I think the Taliban were so isolated, they didn't see the seriousness of the American resolve to go after the al Qaeda headquarters, so when they didn't co-operate, the US went after them.

"That was always an issue in terms of international legality, because there were those that argued the Taliban gave al Qaeda sanctuary, so they had a responsibility, and there were others that said this is al Qaeda operating out of caves, what could the Taliban have done about that anyway.

"There was that kind of debate going on."

Under Clark, New Zealand opted to support the Afghanistan invasion, but not the subsequent extension of that campaign into Iraq, which was accused of building 'weapons of mass destruction'.

"In the end, there was quite a large international response in Afghanistan, which led to quite a long presence or us and for others," she said. "Where things spun out was the US, having taken out the Taliban at the end of 2001, then thought why not move onto Iraq, and that was where they went many steps too far and that became a terrible tragedy for Iraq.

Saddam Hussein's downfall left a power vacuum in Iraq. AFP / FILE

"No one particularly mourned the going of Saddam Hussein, but that war was said to have killed, in rough figures, from 500,000-700,000 people, and who knows how many died because of the poverty, marginalisation and hunger that came from that."

Clark saw alarming similarities between the Iraq war and the action against neighbouring Iran in recent months.

"A lot has happened in the last 25 years and, with the benefit of hindsight, we can see the points at which things went badly wrong.

"I think more the similarity is the spurious reasons for going to war. There was never any evidence of weapons of mass destruction.

"I myself went to see the United Nations inspector in charge off getting rid of the Iraqi nuclear weapons towards the end of 2002 in New York and he assured me they could find absolutely nothing.

"Fast forward to February this year and the attacks on Iran on the basis they were on the imminent point of developing a nuclear weapon. This was never true and it takes me back to the allegations of the Vietnamese using 'Yellow Rain' or whatever - that was never true either.

"Before countries go to war, citizens should be demanding what is this proof. I think we had our eyes open in 2003 and knew there was no proof.

World.title: Student killed at Auckland train station named
World.content:
The student hit and killed by a train earlier this week has been named as Vintonia Luka Viqasi.

Mount Albert Grammar School on Thursday confirmed the deceased was one of its students, killed at Baldwin Avenue Train Station on Wednesday.

Police were called at 3.28pm on Wednesday to reports a pedestrian was struck at the rail crossing.

The student's name was revealed in a verified Givealittle page set up to support the family with funeral and other costs. Police were yet to confirm his name to RNZ.

"Our family is heartbroken to share the devastating loss of little Vinnie Jr, also known as Buka who was tragically taken from us far too soon," the page, his aunt Angelica Lall wrote.

"Vinnie Jr was a much-loved son, grandson, nephew, cousin and friend. His life was precious, and his loss has left a space in our family that can never be filled."

She said any money donated would go "directly to (mother) Jahna Fiu, and their three daughters, Jorjia Fiu, Eden and Eva, to help with the unexpected costs that come with losing a child, including funeral and bereavement expenses and loss of income while they are unable to work".

"It will also give them some breathing room to take the time they need to grieve and begin navigating life without little Vinnie."

As of 6.45pm on Friday, more than $10,000 had been donated by nearly 200 people.

In an email to parents earlier this week, Mount Albert Grammar School headmaster Patrick Drumm said their thoughts were with the family of the boy and they were actively being supported.

World.title: Members of public gave CPR to dying Auckland man, allege medical centre refused use of defibrillator
World.content:
A woman who gave a man dying on an Auckland footpath CPR says she is reluctantly speaking out after she claims a medical centre refused to help the man or let members of the public use their defibrillator.

Police confirmed they were called to a sudden death on New North Rd in Mt Albert at 4.25pm on Thursday and said the death had been referred to the coroner.

Leoni Mcinroe, a former anaesthetic technician, was at her shop on New North Rd when she saw a commotion outside, by the Mt Albert Medical Centre.

"I saw someone on the ground and ran down there. I asked if an ambulance was called and a lady told me yes, and I asked if anyone had been into the medical centre to ask for help and a young couple told me they had and the receptionist told them he wasn't their patient so they couldn't help."

The practice manager of the Mt Albert Medical Centre, Monali Barot, said they were "deeply saddened by the tragedy" and were cooperating fully with authorities.

Mcinroe said she stepped in and began performing CPR for about 15 minutes until emergency services arrived.

She said it was a man in his late 60s or early 70s lying on the busy road, just next to the bus stop.

She said the young couple told her the man had a fainty pulse and unusual breathing when they arrived.

"When we were administering CPR, his head was bashing on the concrete. And because it was uneven, there was nothing, we all looked around for something to go under his head to prevent that impact, I asked that young woman again, please go and ask for something for under his head, we have to have something under his head."

But again, she said the medical centre refused, so they took a pillow anyway.

As the public gathered there was talk of finding a defibrillator, Mcinroe said, which she was told the medical centre also refused.

Eventually, one was brought over from a nearby gym.

"I didn't fully understand the resistance that was coming from the medical centre because I kept saying, where are they? Why haven't they come down?

"You'd expect better from a medical centre, wouldn't you? Oh, it's just mind-blowing."

She said she was "sickened" by how the centre treated the public.

"Their lack of humanity… I'm just sickened. Doctors are under oath to assist. It's beyond a belief.

"I'm utterly disgusted."

Mcinroe said she told police about the refusal from the medical centre who told her to lay a complaint with the Medical Council - which she said she has.

World.title: Auckland businesses on CRL opening
World.content:
The road cones are gone, the sculptures unveiled and 23 new trains are set to start carrying commuters on Auckland's very own City Rail Link.

Although it won't be open to the public until Sunday, the CRL was officially opened by the Prime Minister and Auckland Mayor at a ribbon cutting ceremony on Friday morning.

But as dignitaries congratulate one another on completion of New Zealand's biggest-ever infrastructure project, Auckland businesses continue to suffer due to years of disruption caused by the project.

Minister for Rail Winston Peters serenaded the crowd with a rendition of Johnny Cash's Folsome Prison Blues ahead of the ribbon cutting ceremony at what will become New Zealand's busiest train station, Te Waihorotiu.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon hailed the occasion as a major achievement.

"Every business that can access a larger workforce, every customer who can reach a shop or event more easily will contribute to a stronger economy and that will be great for all of us.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown said it was a great day to be an Aucklander, heaping praise on those involved, including his predecessor Len Brown who initiated the project. But the mayor couldn't resist having a crack about the problems that have plagued the CRL.

"Many people have told me to be positive today and I'm very positive - positive about how CRL is a game changer for the city. But the fact remains that this took too long and cost to much and it is disappointing."

RNZ/Calvin Samuel

The cast of high-powered dignitaries who spoke paid tribute to the CBD businesses who've done it very tough as a result of the disruption caused by the project, wishing them prosperity now that it's complete.

But fifteen metres above the glitzy Te Waihorotiu Station on Victoria St West, Shobhana Ranchhodji Roma Blooms is not popping the champagne just yet.

RNZ/Calvin Samuel

"Words are just not enough to say what we went through. It was hard.

"Everything was shut down, you could not get into any part of Albert St, Victoria St, all the way up to mayoral drive. You could not come into this area."

While hugely relieved the disruption was over, she would only believe the benefits promised by the CRL when they happened.

"I am prepared for those 50,000 people that they say are going to catch that frikkin' train.

"I am ready for what they are telling me. Every business is listening and I am fingers crossed that is the truth."

Shobhana Ranchhdoji from Roma Blooms on Victoria St West. RNZ/Matthew Theunissen

Next door at Accord Barbers, owner Rafat is giving CBD resident Adrian a very snazzy fade cut.

"It's been too hard. Covid before that and now we have this construction stuff so we are looking forward to fixing this stuff.

"We need to see the people come back to the city."

Adrian feels like the city has been in poor shape for about six years.

"You know, Covid recovery really set the city back and then the CRL's had a massive impact on the surrounding businesses.

"The most exciting part that I'm looking forward to is seeing all the construction gone and people back into the city."

PJ Singh has been running Coffee Club franchise for nearly four years, the past two and a half of which, he said he had been left with no money after paying wages and bills.

"In 2023 they said there's a delay in the project and the date extended to 2025 then 2026.

"We're really hoping the amount of loss we took in the last couple of years will be worth working for the city rail link."

RNZ/Calvin Samuel

Up at Auckland's bohemian capital, Karangahape Rd, Emily and Melody-Jazz were on shift at the much-loved People Being People op shop.

"I'd say Karangahape Rd used to be a very safe space for Queer people and recently it's kind of gone down hill with the rising homelessness issues and so there's reputation of it being unsafe and so people don't want to come here anymore," Emily said.

Melody-Jazz couldn't wait.

"I've been waiting for such a long time for this to open. It will be so good, because I live out west as well.

"I think it cuts down to 40 minutes and it used to take like an hour and half."

World.title: Dunedin councillor Benedict Ong trespassed from the University of Otago
World.content:
Controversial Dunedin councillor Benedict Ong has been trespassed from the University of Otago grounds and premises following student complaints about inappropriate and unwanted behaviour.

The Otago University Students' Association confirmed plans to trespass Ong from its premises on 2 September and urged the university to ban him from the campus.

Ong claimed that student concerns were false and malicious attacks in a social media post that included a photo of him on campus with tape over his mouth.

The university confirmed Ong has been served a notice of trespass on 11 September after it considered complaints from students and has discussions with them.

Ong was no stranger to controversy, after being asked to resign by his colleagues for breaching the council's code of conduct in March and a suspension from all committees and subcommittees for nine months following another conduct complaint in May.

On 10 September Ong shared text messages he said were from university proctor Dave Scott, with the first saying Scott had been tasked with serving Ong documents on behalf of the university and the association.

According to the shared messages, Scott wanted to hand the documents to Ong discreetly and asked where they could meet before the councillor requested a public statement, saying he believed it was a "wrongful ban".

The third message said Scott preferred not to present the documents at his workplace or ask police to serve them.

In the post, Ong asked them to be served outside the Dunedin Public Art Gallery before an extraordinary council meeting on 11 September.

Speaking to media outside the gallery, he confirmed he had not been served yet, but expected to be.

He refused to take responsibility, saying his actions did not provoke the trespass and claimed complaints about his behaviour at a campus protest were politically motivated.

He called for video footage from the protest to be released - which the university said, in a letter Ong posted on social media, validated reports that two students asked him to move and appeared uncomfortable when he refused to do so.

On 3 September, the university invited Ong to respond to the proposed trespass notice and gave him until 3pm 7 September to respond, in the letter.

In response, Ong said he believed a deadline was inappropriate because he was elected by the Dunedin community "which has generationally subsidised our oldest University".

In the letter, university registrar Dr David Clark told Ong the association had reported two incidents at a campus protest alleging that his physical proximity or contact was unwanted and he had refused to move when asked by two students.

Clark also noted that Ong had taken photos at student flat parties and posted on social media about being near the St David Street building at 3am and at Ubar late at night.

"Your behaviour towards students on campus within these contexts has led to them reporting that they feel uncomfortable and unsafe," he said.

The association said the complaints had come from a variety of students this year and there were concerns he was interacting with students who were vulnerable because they had been drinking, Clark said.

Possible options raised included a trespass notice covering all university grounds and premises or limiting access to specific premises, dates, times or purposes.

Ong has continued to claim the allegations were false, his visits to Ubar were well documented on his social media accounts and "student supporters" had asked to take photos with him.

The university confirmed it did not intend to make any further statements to help protect the privacy of students.

World.title: Resold tickets for Warriors v Dolphins could be cancelled, Ticketmaster warns
World.content:
Warriors fans furious as tickets being re-sold for hundreds more Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Warriors fans who snapped up tickets to Saturday's NRL finals qualifier match through unofficial resale sites could find their tickets cancelled, Ticketmaster has warned.

Tickets for the clash with the Dolphins at Mount Smart Stadium sold out within minutes of going on sale to the general public on Tuesday.

Not long afterwards, listings began appearing on TradeMe and other online marketplaces, with some sellers asking hundreds of dollars more than what they paid.

One listing offered four tickets in the Eastern Stand for a buy-now price of $1200, describing them as "arguably the best seats in the house. Right where the Warriors walk out".

The seller did not offer an explanation for why they were selling the tickets.

Another seller was asking $500 for two tickets in the uncovered South Stand - seats which ordinarily cost $25 for an adult during the regular season, although the price for the play-off was increased to around $45.

For some fans, the practice crossed a line. The question-and-answer sections of some listings became impromptu battlegrounds, with frustrated supporters accusing sellers of cashing in on the huge demand for one of the biggest Warriors games in years.

"You're a dog for selling these tickets to make money and actual fans can't even go to see it live," one person wrote.

"You are an actual scumbag," another posted.

Others questioned whether the practice of on-selling the tickets at large mark-up breached the terms and conditions set by Ticketmaster, the official ticketing agent for the game.

In a statement to RNZ, a Ticketmaster spokesperson recommended fans only purchase tickets through authorised ticket sellers.

"Ticketmaster does not guarantee the authenticity of tickets purchased from unauthorised third-party resellers or resale sites.

"While only a relatively small number of tickets appear to have been listed for resale, the NRL's ticket terms restrict unauthorised resale for the Warriors game.

"Tickets identified as sold or transferred in breach of those terms may be cancelled."

'Pretty crap'

Fans are calling it gutting, gross, a kick in the teeth and against the culture of the Wahs.

Super-fan Woody Materoa said it was gutting. He jumped online for tickets but didn't make it on to the site in time.

"We're quite big fans of the Warriors and to sort of see people getting tickets that are not even going to attend the game is pretty crap."

They were planning to fly up from Blenheim to watch the game.

"There's always going to be somewhere that's going to take advantage of that sort of stuff but yes you know, they're trying to make money, whereas we just want to watch the game."

Materoa said something should be done to stop this from happening again.

"It's supposed to be a game that's enjoyed by all Kiwis, you know, especially called 'New Zealand Warriors'. So I think they do need to take action," fellow fan Paul Natac said.

He's been a Wahs fan since 1995, when he was just 13 years old.

"They really made it accessible for people who are vulnerable, you know, where a little bit of joy of watching rugby league helps them. The Warriors have done a really good job at $10 tickets sometimes over the season, and then all of a sudden originally $44 tickets are being sold over a hundred bucks, 200, 300 even. Some of them are $500 per ticket."

Natac missed out on securing tickets in both the pre-sale and general release and had considered buying marked-up tickets.

"I can afford it, so shall I just buy it? And at the end of the day I just kind of calmed down and went, at the end of the day, I'll just be promoting this behaviour for the next game."

Sports commentator Sam Ackerman said scalping wasn't in the spirit of the Wahs culture.

"The members who appear to be doing it, that's a kick in the teeth because they are part of that experience and they know exactly what that investment emotionally means."

He said it's hard to digest.

"People have bought more than they want for the purpose of on-selling, not just on-selling for a bit, on-selling for ridiculous profits as well. And it means that there's been conversations of having to tell kids who idolise these players, who go along to all the games, being part of that journey, that they can't go."

He also believed something needed to change.

"This is a club and a sport that has been embraced by all socioeconomic communities. This is a sport, a competition, a team for the people. And some people have decided to take that out of their hands."

Consumer spokesperson Jessica Walker. Supplied / Consumer NZ

Consumer spokesperson Jessica Walker said there's no law that prevents people from purchasing tickets and reselling them at a higher price.

"Which is obviously really disappointing for people who are looking for tickets to any major event and find that they can't because they have been snapped up by people looking to make a profit on them."

The one exception to the rule was events covered by the Major Events Management Act 2007, which applied to major events that were deemed to provide a substantial benefit to the country.

The Warriors game did not qualify.

"We really urge people to be aware that if you are buying a resold ticket, you need to look out for terms and conditions from the official seller that if they know a ticket has been resold, then they don't have to honour it.

"Another thing to be aware of is if you buy a resold ticket and then the event is cancelled. The official ticket agent is likely to refund the original purchaser. So then it would be on you as the person that bought the resold tickets to chase the person who originally purchased the ticket to get a refund."

She said while best practice was to stick to official ticket sellers or to buy off people you know, if you're going to buy a resold ticket - at least use your card.

"Because if things go wrong, you can approach your bank to try and ask for something called a charge back."

Walker said it's something Consumer thought the Government needed to clamp down on.

"It is not fair that people are priced out of being able to go and see things that they want to see, but a sporting event, a gig, a concert, festival, it should be equitable and we need to have better protection. So they were not at the mercy of people who do buy them all up and then inflate the cost significantly."

World.title: NZ government agencies leaving door open to hackers, cyber security company warns
World.content:
Government agencies risk leaving door open to hackers Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Government agencies that haven't beefed up email security could be leaving the door open to hackers, according to an international cyber security company.

It follows revelations data may have been stolen form Dunedin-based company ZenTech and published online.

International Cyber Security company, Proofpoint claims 50 percent of New Zealand government agencies are exposed when it comes to email security.

Senior director of Asia Pacific and Japan, Steve Moros told Checkpoint many of New Zealand's government agencies did not have high enough email security.

"50 percent are at [a high level of email security] at the moment."

He said there had been some progress as last year only 26 percent of New Zealand's government agencies had the highest level of email security.

DMARC reject, an email security setting that blocks messages that fail authentication checks, was becoming a requirement for agencies, Moros said.

He said the nearly $310,000 scam targeting Whanganui District Council proved the importance of email security.

The Whanganui District Council identified in January 2023 that an international payment made the previous December had been sent to a fraudulent bank account.

Moros said artificial intelligence was also making it much easier for hackers to target companies.

"That's why we need to make sure we get real progress getting all government agencies to the right level of enforcement, we've got to close the gap."

He said there was "no real excuse" for agencies without high level email security but acknowledged it was a complicated process.

"This is all around protecting people to stop them from being lured into losing their hard earned money.

"Or potentially exposing records to these hackers who will then use it to go make money through exploitation, essentially ransom so 'if you don't pay we will publish the information'."

General manager for the government digital delivery agency, Richard Ashworth, said the goal of the Secure Government Email (SGE) Framework is to provide technical settings for email security that meet industry standards.

The settings will provide:

transmission security through encryption

message integrity through digital signing

protection against domain spoofing

World.title: How two premierships in one year was the making of Isaiya Katoa
World.content:
In the four years since the remarkable season that forged Isaiya Katoa's first legend the Dolphins playmaker has proven time and again why he is the sort of player whose ascension was not expected but awaited.

On Saturday, Katoa will play in his first ever NRL semifinal when the Phins travel to Auckland to face the Warriors in the pick of the week one match-ups.

Katoa heads to New Zealand as the game's prince of playmakers amid a transformation from star of the future to star of the present.

It will be his first finals match of any kind since 2022, the season before his NRL debut and the year the limitless possibilities of his future revealed themselves.

Katoa has established himself as one of the top young halfbacks in the game. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

It began in the February, when Katoa signed with the Dolphins on his 18th birthday he already carried a mighty reputation among the league types who know about these things.

The hype around Katoa was enormous right from the jump, which doesn't feel like much of a burden now he's lived up to it but has crushed many a promising halfback before they could even get going.

With the Dolphins missing out on a host of big names for their inaugural season, they made a big bet that Katoa could become the star they need.

Given the lack of junior football over the past two seasons due to the pandemic that was no sure thing but Katoa showed his quality in that year's SG Ball competition, as he steered Penrith to the Under 19s grand final.

The Panthers were hardly a one-man band with future Parramatta hooker Ryley Smith and Warriors five-eighth Luke Hanson joining Katoa in the side, as did current Panthers dummy half Billy Scott.

The Windsor Wolves rake knew Katoa well by that point, having played against him growing up and with him at Patrician Brothers Blacktown.

"You could tell from a young age that he'd play NRL," said Scott.

"He was so mature, so calm and ahead of the game."

All of Katoa's poise didn't help in the early running as a Sydney Roosters containing Ethan Strange, Robert Toia, Solesi Foekti and Siua Wong ran out 20-0 leaders inside the first 25 minutes.

But Katoa laid on one try and helped create two more to claim man of the match honours as Penrith fought their way back to win 22-20 courtesy of a sideline conversion in the final seconds.

In the weeks that followed, the simmering tension between the Panthers and Dolphins over the latter landing Katoa came to a head.

He was excluded from the club's Jersey Flegg side for much of the season in a decision Penrith stressed was not personal, a claim which would eventually ring true.

After playing rugby, where he led Barker College to a Combined Associated Schools premiership win and occasional games back home for Glenmore Park Brumbies, Katoa was recalled by the Panthers, not for the Under 21s but straight into a reserve grade semifinal.

With Penrith's NRL side resting their entire starting side for the final round of the season, the reggies got the call up to the firsts and the kids had to step up to the seconds for the major preliminary final against North Sydney.

Alongside Isaiah Iongi and the Puru twins, in one of his first games against battle-hardened men, Katoa scored a try and set up two more amid a 22-14 win.

Then came another semifinal, a grand final qualifier in Jersey Flegg where the Roosters waited yet again.

NRL's unlikeliest blockbuster In a season bereft of quality, the Dolphins and the Warriors will meet in a marquee clash that doubles as the NRL's most unusual big game showdown.

In his first game with the side for the season, Katoa set up a try and kicked a field goal in a 27-22 victory.

Newcastle awaited in the grand final, as did an epic. The Knights were more than handy — Fletcher Sharpe lined up at fullback and Kurt Donoghoe a future partner-in-crime of Katoa's at the Phins, was at five-eighth.

Even though Katoa had been away from junior representative footy all season every Newcastle player knew what was in store.

"He was always one of the guns. You'd do a whole week of video pretty much just on him — which is still the same now," said Sharpe.

"He can be tricky to get a read on because he's got so many parts to his game."

Thomas Cant captained the Newcastle side at second row and despite having appeared in 38 NRL matches since he still calls this decider one of the hardest games he's ever played.

In the end it went to double extra time after the sides were locked at 18-all. Golden point beckoned and the two teams would play until there was a winner.

If you think that winner came from anyone but Katoa you haven't been paying attention.

"Honestly, my main memory is how good winning felt. We just stayed present and stayed in it. You get what you deserve, and if you put in the work it'll work out," said Scott, who again played alongside Katoa.

"He missed a few field goals in that game but even that's a credit to him — he stayed calm and when he needed to he nailed it."

All told, Katoa played six finals matches for Penrith that season across three different grades and won them all.

Just for good measure, he capped the season with a World Cup campaign with Tonga and his Test debut. He completed his HSC via correspondence during the tour and on return began life as a Dolphin.

Progress over the next three years was steady and over the last 18 months Katoa has fully blossomed.

The moment of Katoa's glory has seemingly arrived. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Unlike other young halves, who rely on their running game, all of Katoa's brilliance comes from between his ears and in his hands.

He is not a jack rabbit, but a craftsman with an artisanal touch and it was all there in those days with Penrith, clear as day through the grainy footage.

He holds the ball out in front, showing it this way and that. He delays his pass until the exact right moment when one defender has passed the point of no return and space must exist somewhere on his outside.

His poise, execution and inexplicable ability to make defenders sit on their heels and play with a desperate uncertainty because they don't know what's next is unmissable once you know what you're looking at.

Those talents have held up at every level since, becoming more finely honed until now when they will be battle-tested by a Warriors team who take no prisoners in front of more than 25,000 Kiwi screamers.

It will be a pressure unlike any Katoa has ever known and win or lose, there will be other days like this to come.

That has felt like his fate since Katoa's year of winning dangerously, which had an air of promise at the time but can now be retro-fitted into prologue, a mere taste of what was to come.

Before, Katoa was the son of a golden tomorrow and those days have now arrived and all those wins four years ago remain proof that while many are called, few are chosen.

World.title: Quick hits: NFL goes AFL, Jonas Brothers rock, and 100k fans see rare sight
World.content:
The NFL's first match in Australia lived up to the hype, with more than 100,000 fans packing the MCG to watch the San Francisco 49ers defeat the LA Rams.

There was more than just football on the field, with the Jonah Brothers rocking out at half-time and belting out one of the great Aussie anthems.

The NFL brought American flair to the MCG, but the game had a little AFL flavour.

Here are the quick hits from the historic season opener.

1. An anthem so nice he sang it twice

With the NFL playing its first ever match in Australia, it also meant that our national anthem was sung before an NFL game for the first time.

The honour of singing Advance Australia Fair was given to singer, and Commonwealth Games swimmer, Cody Simpson, and our man did us proud.

Simpson even gave the anthem a little twist at the end, this was a special occasion after all.

After completing the anthem, Simpson then sang the final two lines again, as planes flew overhead at the G.

2. A little AFL flavour at the 'G

Melbourne was getting a taste of America with the NFL.

The pageantry of pre-game, tailgates outside the MCG, and plenty of NFL fan fare.

But the NFL made sure to add some Australian flavour to its game as well.

Loading Instagram content

The first points of the match belonged to San Francisco 49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro, who kicked a 20-yard field goal in the first quarter.

Officials raise their arms in their air to signify a successful kick, but for this field goal, the action was a little different.

The officials extended their arms and made the same gesture for a goal in Aussie rules, a fitting touch for any game of footy played at the MCG.

3. 100,021 fans witness a rare sighting in the NFL

The NFL came to Australia with the intention of drawing a huge crowd, and putting on a spectacle.

That was achieved, and then some, with an official crowd of 100,021 packing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground. The official capacity of the MCG is 100,024, meaning the NFL was just three shy of claiming that every seat was filled on Friday.

And those 100,021 fans got to see something that most Americans never will: the centre catching a pass.

The centre is the player who snaps the ball between his legs to the quarterback at the start of the play.

The centre has two jobs:

Get the ball to the quarterback

Protect the quarterback or running back

But on a historic day in Melbourne, 49ers centre Jake Brendel became the hero of big men everywhere.

Midway through the second quarter, Brendel snapped the ball to quarterback Brock Purdy, and then protected his QB by blocking Rams defensive lineman Kobie Turner.

When Purdy threw his pass down the middle, Turner was able to jump in the air and get his hand to the ball.

As the ball hung in the air, threatening to be intercepted by the Rams, Brendel quickly reacted and caught the pass for a two-yard gain.

Frankly, it was a pity the MCG crowd did not get to see Brendel cut loose for a big run, but seeing him claim the first reception of his career was a moment that would not have been on any NFL bingo cards.

4. Jonas Brothers tribute to John Farnham

The superstars at the MCG on Friday were not restricted to footballers.

American pop rock band Jonas Brothers were the headline act at half-time.

The performance, albeit short, had all the the style and chorography of the half-time show at the Super Bowl.

And there was a nice touch to an Australian legend during the performance.

The American stars sang one of the great Aussie anthems, You're The Voice by John Farnham.

The capacity crowd at the MCG was in full voice for the famous song, a great nod to one of Australia's greatest artists.

5. Kittle wants a shoey, and to go home

There are few better personalities in the NFL than star San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle.

His interviews are always a highlight, especially after a 49ers win over their rivals in LA.

Following his side's impressive 27-7 win over the Rams at the MCG, Kittle gave a trademark interview with American broadcaster ESPN.

He was asked about the Australian tradition of a shoey, which the American star claimed he wanted to try.

"Are you trying to set me up to get in trouble?" he asked the reporter when quizzed on whether he would want to try a shoey.

"Wherever I can do one, I'm gonna try to find one in the stands."

Kittle finished off his interview in similarly entertaining style.

He said how much he was excited to leave Melbourne and head home, before appearing to make sure his comment did not come across like he, and his teammates, did not enjoy their week down under.

"We embraced going to Australia — 15-hour flight, we were here the whole week — it was a grind but we did it," he said.

"We'll see you guys back in America, I can't wait to go home. I did love Australia though, this place is awesome."

We loved having you George, bar the Rams fans here who have gone through a painful defeat.

World.title: Gliders return to world stage after missing last Paralympics
World.content:
Australia's women's wheelchair basketball team has returned to the world stage, two years on from missing qualification for the Paris Paralympics.

It has been a lean decade for the Gliders, once considered amongst the world's best, failing to qualify for the 2016 Paralympic Games as well.

But a new dawn appears to be breaking for the team, which, anchored by an experienced core and energised by an exciting group of tournament debutants, has begun its tilt at World Championship glory in Canada.

The Gliders have not competed in a major international tournament since the World Championships in 2023. (Supplied: Basketball Australia)

The tournament serves as an important stepping stone for the Gliders, with the side having already set the goal of a podium finish at the Brisbane 2032 Paralympics.

Meanwhile, Australia's men's side, the Rollers, are gunning for a third World Championship title, after missing the medals in Paris.

Taking the long way around

While the Gliders have been plotting their return to the top of the international game, China has emerged as a true powerhouse of women's wheelchair basketball, having medalled at the 2021 and 2024 Paralympics, as well as the 2022 World Championships.

So, a first-round tussle with the Asian powerhouse was always going to be a tough task for the Australians, and something of a baptism by fire for their three tournament debutants.

The Gliders went down by 11 points in their opener on Wednesday night, but it was a game of real promise for the Australians, according to emerging star Katelin Gunn.

"We haven't played as well as we have against China in quite a few years," Gunn told ABC Sport from camp in Ottawa.

The meet is Gunn's first major international tournament, but she has been in and around the Gliders' set-up since making her international debut in 2022.

Loading Instagram content

She was a member of the side that qualified for the tournament by the skin of its teeth late last year, triumphing in a gruelling repechage in Madrid after missing direct passage to the competition.

Head coach Jeremy Symot, who was appointed Gliders boss last year after a highly successful stint in the Australian domestic league, named the same 12-player squad for both the repechage and the World Championships.

The roster includes team legends Shelley Matheson and Sarah Vinci, who boast 40 years of international experience between them, as well as superstar centre Georgia Munro-Cook, fresh from her 3x3 bronze medal at the Commonwealth Games.

Gunn believes the squad is as strong as she has ever seen it, and that the shared experience of last November's repechage has pushed it to a new level.

"We took a lot of learnings from Spain and we will build more and more on them," Gunn said.

"In the few training sessions we've had together as a group, we have just connected more than ever."

Destination Brisbane

Munro-Cook captained the Gliders in their last Paralympic campaign in 2021. (supplied: Griffith University)

A 73-30 loss to Canada in their second game on Friday morning means that the Gliders now face an uphill battle to progress from Group A, with the Australians likely requiring handsome victories in their remaining pool matches.

But regardless of whether a knockout-round berth does prove elusive for the side in Ottawa, the tournament is a vital next step on the road to Brisbane 2032.

Gunn, who will be in her late 20s by the time of a potentially career-defining home Games, is aware it will take time for her team to reach its potential.

"It's all about building each game, each benchmark event, getting closer to where we want to be," she said.

"It's a slow process, but hopefully we'll be closer to where we want to be by the end of this competition."

World.title: 49ers ransack 'Rams House' in epic Melbourne NFL show
World.content:
The Melbourne Cricket Ground is bathed in sunshine on a September's day as thousands of fans stream in from all corners.

Fans of one team in red jerseys and the other in blue and gold take your mind back to the Sydney-West Coast AFL grand finals from two decades ago.

Atmospheres such as this is usually only reserved for the likes of the AFL grand final or the Boxing Day Test, but it is very quickly apparent that this is bigger than both.

49ers cap Aussie week with win The San Francisco 49ers have claimed a commanding win at the MCG, beating the LA Rams 27-7 in the NFL's historic first match in Australia.

It is a Friday morning, and despite it being a sunny September day, the AFL is nowhere to be seen because the National Football League is in town.

If NFL commissioner Roger Goodell had any fears about how the league would be able to fill a 100,000-seat stadium on a Friday morning, scenes from hours before the game would have had him resting easy.

Hours before the game begins, the fact that it was early in the morning did not stop hundreds of fans from getting stuck into drinks at the Pullman Hotel across the road from the MCG, with the positive vibes no doubt welcomed by the same venue recently in the news for all the wrong reasons.

On the drive to the MCG, NFL merchandise stuck out like a sore thumb before the historic venue was even within eyesight.

Melburnians are proud of their city's reputation as a sporting hub and they were not going to miss this opportunity to show up and show out.

Melbourne's sports-crazy fans did not waste the opportunity to showcase what a sports-mad town they live in. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

If you were not familiar with the history of the LA Rams and the San Francisco 49ers, this is no ho-hum game of football. These two teams do not like each other.

After making their way through the organised security booths in the Yarra Park precinct, a set-up which meant there were no lengthy queues you'd usually associate with an event of this magnitude, fans wasted little time before slinging barbs between each other.

A group of four Rams fans from Los Angeles described their visit to Australia for the game as "a trip of a lifetime" as they proudly proclaimed the MCG to be "Rams House" for the day.

With these two teams bitter rivals it is unusual to see fans from the different sides fraternising, but that is exactly what one couple travelling from the US has done. The husband, Jamie, is a 49ers fan and the wife, Carmen, is a Rams fan.

Quick hits: NFL goes AFL, Jonas Brothers rock, and 100k fans see rare sight The NFL's first match in Australia lived up to the hype, with 100,000 people packing the MCG to watch the San Francisco 49ers defeat the LA Rams. Here are the quick hits from the historic season opener.

"Typically, hanging out is forbidden in those places, so we thought if we come here it would be okay," Jamie said pre-game.

However, the fandom wasn't solely Americans making sojourns Down Under either, with the chance to watch a NFL game in real life a rich reward to Aussie fans who usually toil through all hours of the night just to catch a glimpse of their favourite teams in action.

One such fan, Zac, got into American football through his father who had spent some time in Buffalo, and therefore became a tortured Bills fan.

Zac did not follow in his father's footsteps and instead followed the Philadelphia Eagles. He was overjoyed at getting a fist pump from Eagles icon Nick Foles who was in Melbourne covering the game for Netflix.

"It's so weird watching a game at 3am and your team scores and you can't make any noise in your living room because your entire family is asleep," he said.

"So it's just you and your cat watching the TV going, 'F**k yeah.'"

Fans were given masks to form the flags in the stands. (ABC Sport: Chris De Silva)

He described the experience of watching a regular season NFL game in Melbourne as "surreal".

"You're absolutely jazzed and your adrenaline is high, and then half an hour later you've got to get up for work on a Monday morning," Zac said of the usual experience of watching an NFL game played in the US.

As the pre-game festivities got underway there was a real juxtaposition of Australian and American culture.

Indigenous dancers performed a Welcome to Country dance with American breakdancers doing their thing in close proximity.

The juxtaposition of the two cultures was never more evident than when the Shane Warne Stand sign being flanked by LED advertising boards showing the Stars and Stripes from the American flag during Infinity Song's rendition of The Star Spangled Banner.

There was a real sense of an Australian and American juxtaposition as the Shane Warne Stand sign was surrounded by the US stars and stripes. (ABC Sport: Chris De Silva)

There was just one thing the fans from the two nations agreed upon: booing former Collingwood president Eddie McGuire as he ran out for the coin toss alongside Australian artist G-Flip.

Despite the clash being nominally a Rams home game there was no secret as to who dominated the stands as Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, the 2025 league MVP, was roundly booed as he ran out with his team amid blue and yellow smoke.

With all the festivities going on it was easy to forget that there was an actual football game to be played. And with the smell of the smoke still in the air, we finally got things underway.

The Rams, who were roundly criticised for not flying to Australia earlier ahead of the game, sleepwalked their way through much of the first quarter until Stafford linked up with star receiver Puka Nacua, who tip-toed his way along the sideline for some solid yardage.

The Los Angeles Rams players ran onto the MCG through a blaze of smoke and received raucous boos from the 49ers-heavy crowd in attendance. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Nacua's run meant that teammate Kyren Williams was able to run into the end zone in the opening moments of the second quarter for the historic first-ever NFL touchdown on Australian soil.

Williams's name will be mentioned in trivia competitions in pubs all around Australia for decades to come.

Despite this being a game between two California-based teams, NFL fans from all corners evidently found their way to the MCG, with just about all of the NFL's 32 franchises represented in some form in the stands.

As the Rams mariachi band came out during the quarter-time break, three fans wearing a Sam Darnold jersey, a Dak Prescott jersey and a Joe Montana jersey broke out into a salsa.

San Francisco's Brock Purdy (right) comfortably won the battle of quarterbacks, with his highlight of the day a 39-yard touchdown pass that put the 49ers ahead. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

While much is made of American sport's half-time shows, the entertainment began well before the Jonas Brothers took centre stage.

Along with the mariachi band there was a separate band with a small stage set up near the usual AFL interchange benches, breaking into varying covers of classic hits such as Bryan Adams's Summer of 69.

With NFL games taking over three hours of actual time there is an emphasis on keeping the fans engaged throughout, especially during stoppages.

Fans were asked to vote for which song they wanted to sing in unison and unpredictably picked Daryl Braithwaite's Horses, which might as well be Australia's other national anthem at this point.

NFL MVP Matthew Stafford had his work cut out for him at the MCG. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

As 100,021 fans later broke out into a passionate rendition of Horses there was something indescribably magical about it.

With the big show in town, Australia's footy stars that usually aren't able to get a moment of breathing room in Melbourne were able to slip into relative obscurity.

A current and former St Kilda cohort of Rowan Marshall, Jack Steele and Luke Dunstan were packed in among fans sitting in the fourth tier of the MCG, all decked out in Rams gear.

Despite proclamations of the MCG being Rams House, the home side gradually found themselves in trouble after Williams's opening touchdown.

Fred Warner (pictured) and the 49ers had the last laugh after making the most of their Melbourne trip. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

An incredible goal-line stop from the 49ers defence denied a Stafford tush-push at the very end of the third quarter.

It was the kind of stop you would expect from the Rams's star-studded defence of Myles Garrett and the recently unretired Aaron Donald, and it became very obvious that this would not be the day the Rams would remember fondly.

A touchdown from Deebo Samuel sent the 49ers into raptures once again and the underdogs had claimed a dream start to their season, downing their more-favoured rivals 27-7 despite a 12,640-kilometre road trip.

The 49ers had arrived and well and truly ransacked Rams House and run away with the chocolates.

The NFL came, it saw, and it well and truly conquered Melbourne.

World.title: Sydney Roosters claim NRLW minor premiership after another perfect season
World.content:
The Bulldogs have flirted with the biggest upset in NRLW history before the undefeated Roosters charged home in the final 20 minutes for a 42-12 win at the Sydney Football Stadium.

Entering last night's game in Sydney with just three wins all year and having conceded 178 points in four consecutive losses, the Bulldogs led until the 52nd minute, only to run out of steam with strike centre Monica Tagoai in the sin bin.

While they were far from their best, it was a 26th consecutive regular-season win for master coach John Strange's Roosters side, who remain on track to reclaim the premiership they lost to the Broncos last year, with their only loss in round five of 2024.

The Roosters will now enjoy the bye afforded to the top two teams in week one of the six-team finals format.

Despite being huge underdogs, the visitors had the early ascendancy, and it took almost 12 minutes before Otesa Pule crossed for the Roosters to get the scoreboard ticking.

It did not take long after that for Corban Baxter to slip a gem of a pass to Jessica Sergis, who ran 40 metres to score her competition-leading 15th try of the season.

Just when it looked like the floodgates would open, the Bulldogs worked their way back down the field, and Tagoai powered her way over to bring her side within four points with 10 minutes left in the half.

Seven minutes later, the Dogs' five-eighth Andie Robinson flew high over Baxter to pluck a pinpoint Tayla Preston bomb from the air and touch down.

With Preston's conversion, they were surprise 12-10 leaders at the break, leaving the shortest-priced favourites in NRLW history shell-shocked.

To make matters worse for the Roosters, Baxter left the field at half-time for a head injury assessment and failed to return after the interval.

The Bulldogs stayed on top for the opening 13 minutes of the second stanza, before Tagoai was sin-binned by referee Karra-Lee Nolan for a hip-drop.

Five minutes later, Isabelle Kelly, starting in her 50th game as captain of the Roosters, tore through the middle of the Dogs' defence and found prop Millie Elliott in support for the competition leaders to reclaim the lead.

Taina Naividi was next over the stripe and Canterbury's dream was over.

More tries followed to Pule, Mia Woods, Sergis and Jocelyn Kelleher for a final score that somewhat flattered the minor premiers.

Despite the loss, it was a brave effort from the Bulldogs and coach Brayden Wiliame, in his final game at the helm before Mark O'Meley takes the reins in 2027.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: The innovative and lucrative athletics format sidelining some of its stars
World.content:
World Athletics is set for its latest attempt at a slimmed-down, cashed-up event, with the so-called Ultimate Championship starting Saturday morning (AEST) in Budapest.

The event starts less than a week after the conclusion of the Diamond League season, with all the bells and whistles expected from a track and field meet trying to cut through on a global stage.

Winners will receive US$150,000 ($209,530) and even the eighth-placed athletes picking up a six-figure pay cheque as part of an overall US$10 million ($14 million) purse.

Held over three straight night sessions, the track at Hungary's Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre will illuminate to highlight the event happening in that moment.

Rather than a lengthy program including qualifying runs, there will be just one final for many events and semis in the 100m, 200m, 400m and hurdles races.

Loading Instagram content

In a year without an Olympics or world championships, World Athletics president Sebastian Coe said the event will answer a simple but important question.

"Who's the best?" he said.

"Nobody goes into the sport to figure out who's second best, they go in wanting to know who the best is. And I think at the end of these championships we will have gone a long way to identifying that."

To confirm that, there will be no podiums, only weighty prize purses and bragging rights between the 381 fierce competitors.

Patterson claims Diamond League final title Eleanor Patterson continues her outstanding season by winning the women's high jump at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Most of the traditional track events will be contested (although 3,000m steeplechase, 10,000m and race walking are out) with only Olympic gold medallists, world champions and the current top-ranked athletes invited.

That includes Australian sprint stars Lachlan Kennedy in the 100m and Torrie Lewis in the 200m; Sarah Billings in the 800m; Abbey Caldwell, Jessica Hull and Cameron Myers in the 1,500m; and Ky Robinson, Rose Davies and Hull in the 5,000m.

Diamond League winner Eleanor Patterson and world champion Nicola Olyslagers will compete in the women's high jump, while Commonwealth Games gold medallists Kurtis Marchall (pole vault) and Mackenzie Little (javelin) are also competing.

As part of the hype around the meet, World Athletics held a catwalk fashion event before a televised lane draft for the 200m, allowing athletes to choose which heat and lane they will run in.

Torrie Lewis will race in a stacked semifinal heat. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot/World Athletics)

The draft order was based on world rankings, with American Olympic champion Gabby Thomas picking first and placing herself in lane seven of the first semifinal heat.

World 100m and 200m champion Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, made the next selection and placed herself right inside her US teammate, kicking off the mind games early.

Lewis, choosing 10th, selected the outside lane in that first race and immediately going up against the best of the best.

"It is the confidence for me," 2008 Olympic 100m hurdles gold medallist Dawn Harper-Nelson said as she hosted the event.

"This is what the lane draft is about."

Coe said the innovations on display would show what the sport can be in the future, but that may sound some alarm bells for those athletes and disciplines without an invitation to Budapest.

Discus did not make the cut for the Ultimate Championship. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The field program is very restrictive, with men's and women's events for high jump, javelin, long jump and pole vault, while only men's hammer throw and women's triple jump made the cut.

That left many on the outside looking in, including Australian discus star Matt Denny, who said the Ultimate Championship highlighted "a bigger issue in our sport".

The payday and spotlight could be life changing for track and field athletes who travel the world to compete without many opportunities for the sort of prize money afforded to other sports stars.

"I support the concept of the Ultimate Championships," Denny wrote on Instagram.

"Athletics needs innovation. We need to improve the broadcast product, attract new audiences and find better ways to grow the sport.

"But innovation should not come at the expense of opportunity."

Loading Instagram content

The main argument for the disciplines that were included boiled down to a lack of audience interest in those that missed out, but Denny said that was an unfair metric when it is not athletes who make broadcasting decisions.

"When events are minimally shown on broadcasts for the last 20 years, you lose the reasoning to say people don't want to watch," he wrote.

"You cannot control what gets shown, what gets promoted, whose stories are told and which events receive the greatest exposure, then simply point to the result numbers as proof that people do not care about everything else.

"If an event is struggling for attention, before deciding the event is the problem, we should be asking whether we have genuinely given it the opportunity to succeed."

The post received praise from fellow omitted athletes like Australian hammer throw national champion Steph Ratcliffe, race walker Rhydian Cowley and American shot put great Chase Jackson.

But even invited athletes like Dutch 400m star Lieke Klaver and European javelin champion Julian Weber backed Denny's sentiments, with Weber praising the post as "so true".
