World.title: Rams coach refuses to blame late arrival for thumping NFL loss at MCG
World.content:
LA Rams coach Sean McVay says his team's decision to arrive in Melbourne the day before the NFL's historic first match in Australia was not the reason his side was comprehensively beaten 27-7 by the San Francisco 49ers in front of 100,021 fans at the MCG.

The 49ers arrived a week ago, while the Rams raised eyebrows by touching down in Melbourne 28 hours before kick-off.

Despite scoring the first touchdown of the game, the Rams were outplayed by their rivals in the NFC West division.

49ers ransack 'Rams House' in epic Melbourne NFL show Much was made of the Melbourne Cricket Ground being 'Rams House' for the week, but after arriving earlier than their fancied rivals the San Francisco 49ers ran away with the chocolates as the NFL put on a show for the ages.

Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, the reigning NFL MVP, had a tough day in the Melbourne sunshine, completing 15 passes from 25 attempts for 155 yards and one interception.

Stafford did not finish the game, missing the Rams' final drive of the match with his side down by 20 points.

In contrast, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy shrugged off an early interception to control the game for his side. He completed 25 passes from 34 attempts for 205 yards, with three touchdowns and one interception.

Asked post-match if arriving in Australia the day before kick-off led to his side's sluggish performance, McVay said he did not believe that was why they were heading home with a 20-point defeat.

"They outplayed us in every facet. I didn't do nearly a good enough job. This is a humbling day for us," he said.

"I don't believe [the late arrival] is why we didn't play well enough, I really don't.

"It's easy in hindsight to be able to say it was a miss but those are responsibilities that I'll take, and then you try to be able to look at it."

Sean McVay says the Rams did not play well enough to win in Melbourne, and were not hampered by their late arrival. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Just three points were scored in a tight opening quarter, with 49ers kicker Eddy Pineiro nailing a chip shot from 20 metres.

The Rams scored the opening touchdown of the game on the opening play of the second quarter, with running back Kyren Williams converting up the middle from five yards.

Purdy lost two potential throwing targets in the second quarter, with rookie wide receiver De'Zhaun Stribling and tight end Jake Tonges limping off.

The 49ers took a three-point lead into half-time, thanks to a 39-yard deep pass to Demarcus Robinson.

San Francisco received the ball to start the second half and produced a perfect drive down the field, finished with a short pass from Purdy to Mike Evans, playing his first match for the team after a decade with Tampa Bay.

Leading 17-7, it was the 49ers defence that made the defining play of the game, stopping the Rams on the goal line.

On 4th and goal, Stafford tried to sneak over the goal line but was stopped short, after wide Rams receiver Puka Nacua was tackled just centimetres short on the previous play.

The 49ers came onto the field and Purdy orchestrated a clinical 12-play, 99-metre drive that ended with a 15-metre touchdown pass to Deebo Samuel.

Both teams now head back to the United States.

The 49ers host the Miami Dolphins at home on Monday, AEST, while the Rams host the New York Giants in a prime-time match on Tuesday, AEST.

Revisit all the live action of the first season-proper NFL match played in Australia in our live blog below.

World.title: Opals knocked out of World Cup as luckless captain's torn ACL confirmed
World.content:
The Opals have been knocked out in the quarterfinals of the Women's Basketball World Cup in a 23-point loss to Spain just hours after receiving more devastating injury news about captain Ezi Magbegor.

Half an hour before the tip-off in what turned out to be a comprehensive 89-66 loss to Spain, Magbegor's WNBA team, the Seattle Storm, revealed the star forward had torn her ACL.

Magbegor, who only returned to the court in early July after partially tearing her Achilles in March, went down early after taking a knock to her right knee in Australia's qualification final win over Italy.

"It makes me emotional when I see anyone go down," Opals coach Sandy Brondello said after the loss to Spain.

"But Ezi's come back from an injury and it's just another injury. [It's] just really unfortunate. She's a key part of what we want to do. It sucks, but that's sport isn't it?

"She's got to have a great recovery and she'll get back, I don't have a doubt about that. Just disappointed for Ezi that she's going through another rehabilitation."

The inexperienced Opals struggled without some of their biggest stars. (Supplied: FIBA)

Magbegor joined fellow stars Alanna Smith (leg injury) and Jade Melbourne (illness) on the sidelines, while veteran Sami Whitcomb was ruled out before the tournament with injury and Cayla George did not play due to pregnancy.

Smith suffered a lower-leg injury in the opening game of the tournament, while Melbourne played only three minutes against Italy and could not take the floor in the quarterfinal.

The Opals made a great escape after surrendering a 20-point three-quarter-time lead against the Azzurre thanks largely to a 30-point explosion by 21-year-old Izzy Borlase, but the missing players were too much to overcome in the final-eight showdown.

Ally Wilson was Australia's top scorer with 13 points as the team shot just 40 per cent from the field and had 23 turnovers.

Veteran Steph Talbot said she her young team's lack of big-tournament experience was evident in the game, and said it was a strange experience hitting the court with only eight teammates.

"It's very weird. It was very quiet, very unusual. We were all looking around like, 'Is this it?'" she said.

"But a job's a job and we fought hard to the end. I'm really proud of the effort they put in. It's definitely a different experience."

Brondello said the difficult World Cup would be valuable experience for the team, which boasted seven players in their first major international tournament, with the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics looming large on the horizon.

Tech.title: Why Apple’s next computer should be for the smart home
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

John Ternus didn’t mention Apple Home once during his first keynote as Apple CEO. But he did open by describing an “intelligent personal hub” that prioritizes local processing, protects your privacy, and integrates with all your other devices, apps, and services. While Ternus was talking about the iPhone — not a new smart home device — what he spelled out is exactly what I want to see Apple make: an intelligent home hub, a computer for your home.

Rumors suggest Apple’s first smart home hub with a screen is imminent. While that’s long overdue, it’s likely to be more interface than infrastructure, a device that can run your home locally but still uses the cloud. What the smart home needs is a computer to run it — one that controls and processes data from connected devices locally, improving speed, reliability, and privacy while securely storing your digital life, from photos and files to music and movies. Crucially, it would do all this inside your home.

The cloud has worked well for years, but the recent proliferation of AI-powered home features, such as generating text descriptions from security camera footage, makes local computing more compelling. On-device processing can be faster and more private, and it depends less on an internet connection. These features will also evolve quickly to feed more context to our smart homes, bringing more utility but also a greater need for privacy and security.

The category of smart home super hubs emerged at IFA in Berlin this month. This is the Anker Eufy MindBase, a smart home hub that supports dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Zigbee, and is a Matter controller. It runs an on-device, Anker-developed LLM with support for 16 wireless cameras with expandable local storage up to 48 TB. Photo by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

This type of dedicated home computer — or smart home brain — was an emerging category at last week’s IFA consumer tech show. Anker launched its Eufy MindBase home hub, and Ugreen debuted its HomeAgent, both combining network-attached storage, local AI to process and store footage from cameras, with a smart home hub to connect all your devices.

But one piece is still missing: networking.

A hub. AI. A router. Are you getting it? Call it an Apple Home Server.

Most home routers haven’t caught up with today’s smart home. Despite years of talk about smarter routers, manufacturers and ISPs still seem reluctant to take on the complexity. Comcast has had Thread and Matter support in its gateways since 2022, but hasn’t turned them on. Connecting devices to your home network remains one of the most frustrating parts of the smart home, with manufacturers, ISPs, and platforms all pointing fingers when things fail. Ikea’s recent troubles rolling out new Matter-over-Thread devices are just one example.

Here’s where Apple could step in and combine all three — a smart home hub, local storage with AI processing capabilities, and a home router — into one device. A hub. AI. A router. Are you getting it? Call it an Apple Home Server.

There’s no evidence Apple is building such a thing. But the company’s recent contributions to OpenWrt, the open-source software that powers most routers, could be a tentative first step.

One Apple box for your home: Connect it to your modem, and it becomes your Wi-Fi router, Matter Controller, Thread border router, smart home hub, private AI computer, and home server. It stores your files, photos, music, and movies; processes your camera footage locally; runs your automations even when the internet is down; and optionally backs everything up to iCloud. It wouldn’t be another smart home hub; it would be the computer your home needs. Plug it in, sign in with your Apple account, and it just works.

That last part is crucial, and plays directly to Apple’s strength: hardware that is “super easy to use without a big learning curve,” as Ternus put it this week. Apple also has experience combining these pieces. AirPort Express put networking and media streaming on one box; AirPort Extreme and Time Capsule added NAS capabilities; and HomeKit Secure Routers brought Apple’s security into the network itself.

Apple walked away from all these products in 2018, saying at the time it might return to the space if it found a meaningful way to progress routers further. The pieces have never fit together more perfectly than they do now.

Apple’s Airport Express is a much-missed device. Resurrecting it as part of a powerful whole-home computer for today’s smart home setups would be a popular move. Image: Apple

Apple is deeply involved in developing Matter and is spearheading the Thread networking protocol. An Apple Home Server could bring the entire smart home stack together, letting Apple control everything end to end and remove much of the complexity. Matter even has a blueprint for part of this device: the Matter Home Router Access Point device type combines Wi-Fi networking and Thread Border Router functionality, and Apple’s contributions to OpenWrt focus on HRAP implementation.

According to reporting by Matter Alpha, Apple’s code includes production-grade networking infrastructure that could be turned into a consumer product. There’s no evidence that’s what Apple is doing; it could simply be for router manufacturers. But the pieces are falling into place. With Apple bringing Apple Intelligence to its HomeKit Secure Video service in iOS 27, a Home Server device could take that service to the next level with fully local processing.

Local is the key. An Apple Home Server would be a supercharged Apple Home Hub, powering local-first smart home automations, keeping data private and secure at home, and improving responsiveness for devices like smart lights, locks, and security cameras. It could work alongside existing home hubs — the HomePod, Apple TV, and rumored HomePad — for voice and screen interfaces.

Apple loves subscriptions. But it loves its premium hardware even more.

This might go against the grain. Apple loves subscriptions. But it loves its premium hardware even more, and this would undoubtedly be premium hardware. Also, a device like this would give Apple a powerful foundation for everything it does in the home: iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple TVs, HomePods, its existing digital services, and potential future AI-powered ones. And, unlike a typical smart home hub, it could appeal to anyone who wants a reliable, private home router and a way to store their digital life at home.

Smart home infrastructure is broken, and Apple is uniquely positioned to fix it. An Apple Home Server is the hardware backbone Apple Home has always needed. As our digital lives move deeper into the cloud and AI makes the smart home more dependent on data, the case for a computer to run our homes gets stronger, and building one on open standards could limit lock-in.

Apple has all the pieces. The smart home has been waiting for someone to put them together. If Apple finally builds it, the only surprise will be that it took this long.

Tech.title: Samsung says ‘Tim Cook’ bought a Galaxy Fold
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

That isn’t Apple’s former CEO promoting the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in a new Samsung ad — “Tim Cook from Palmerston North” just happens to have the same name and look a lot like him. Released right as Apple announced its iPhone Duo, the ad mimics Apple’s cinematic product launch videos, with “Tim Cook” saying “the future is here.” Samsung also takes a jab at Apple’s Tim Cook with a reference to his recently-updated profile picture.

It’s the latest in Samsung’s long-running history of ads dunking on its biggest rival, like one ad from over a decade ago that makes fun of iPhone fans willing to wait in lengthy lines for Apple’s latest phone. Then there’s the ad for the Galaxy Note 8 that features a viral shot of a diehard Apple fan with a haircut matching the iPhone’s notch. Samsung did a whole series of “Ingenius” ads teasing Apple’s Genius Bar tech support, with customers asking an Apple Store employee if iPhones have various Samsung features, like a headphone jack or an included fast charger.

Not all of the ads take a comedic tone, though. A 2024 Samsung ad responded to controversy around Apple’s “Crush” iPad ad with a scene of a woman playing a damaged guitar on a recreation of Apple’s set, featuring the tagline “Creativity cannot be crushed.”

Samsung and Apple’s rivalry has even inspired spinoff ads from other companies — Microsoft once released an ad suggesting the two camps “kind of like fighting.”

Tech.title: Ikea supersized its cheap Bluetooth speaker and added an optical input
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ikea’s new Badkruka wireless Bluetooth speaker is now available in the US for $59.99. It’s reminiscent of the colorful and tiny $10 Kallsup speaker that Ikea debuted earlier this year at CES 2026, but at almost seven inches tall, the boxy Badkruka isn’t designed with portability in mind as it also lacks a rechargeable battery.

Color options aren’t as expansive as the Kallsup, either. The Badkruka is available with a black plastic finish or a pink one that almost looks like a wood grain texture. Wherever you end up using it will need a power source within reach, but audio sources can be connected over Bluetooth and, similar to the Kallsup, you can wirelessly connect the Badkruka to several other speakers that support multi-speaker mode to better fill your home or a larger space with sound.

Image: Ikea

You can also connect a pair of Badkruka’s for stereo sound, the speaker supports Spotify Tap, and it comes with three different EQ modes tailored to several music genres. If you don’t want to go wireless, the Badkruka can also be connected to home theater gear, your TV, or a PC’s TOSLINK port using an included optical cable.

Tech.title: Arizona’s lifeline for chip manufacturing is drying up
Tech.content:
Arizona, an epicenter for the bipartisan push to revive American chip manufacturing, is about to lose more than a quarter of the water it typically pulls each year from the Colorado River.

The 1,400-mile waterway is a crucial lifeline for the region and other western states. A recent federal decision on how to manage its dwindling flow hits Arizona, and its already drought-prone desert communities, particularly hard. The river provides more than a third of the Grand Canyon State’s water. Arizona has been a manufacturing hub since the start of the semiconductor industry, and now it’s where TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to make advanced chips for AI — a water-intensive effort.

City planners and industry leaders have already taken precautions to conserve water and find alternative sources. It’s a resource that is likely to become more expensive for manufacturers and residents alike as they learn to rely less on the Colorado River. That’s already raising tensions over who shoulders the costs for new infrastructure needed to adapt, as well as what constitutes a good use of water. The challenges that come with managing a limited water supply are only going to grow as AI demands a larger share.

TSMC and Intel are expanding massive factories to make advanced chips for AI — a water intensive effort

“Our economy is changing, and that’s really painful,” says Kathryn Sorensen, research director at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University. “When there’s a water scarcity issue you have to start looking at what the uses of that water are that bring the most value to the community.”

Agriculture has been a major part of Arizona’s economy since it became a state, and still gobbles up more than 70 percent of the state’s water. Industrial uses, including the chip manufacturing that’s had a foothold in the state since the 1940s, account for just 6 percent.

While the amount of water that semiconductor factories, or fabs, use is still quite small compared to agriculture, the chip industry is growing fast. Fabs use “ultra-pure” water to clean surfaces and etch sensitive chips. It takes more municipal water to create a smaller amount of ultra-pure water through deionization and reverse osmosis. A typical facility might use 10 million gallons of ultra-pure water a day, which could require up to 16 million gallons of municipal water.

New chip factories are sprouting up in Arizona’s desert with the help of federal funding. President Joe Biden signed the ​​CHIPS and Science Act into law in 2022, setting aside $52.7 billion to expand domestic chip manufacturing. Armed with a $7.86 billion grant from the government, Intel is planning to spend $32 billion on two new factories and an expansion of an existing facility in Arizona. In 2025, the company’s facilities in Chandler, Arizona withdrew more than 2.7 billion gallons of freshwater, according to its latest corporate responsibility report.

TSMC, the world’s largest chipmaker, received up to $6.6 billion in CHIPS Act funding and decided to build at least six new semiconductor fabs in Phoenix. TSMC’s first fab in Arizona uses roughly 4.75 million gallons of water a day, the company told The Verge last year. It’s approximately equivalent to the water usage of more than 14,000 homes a day, or 2 percent of Phoenix’s housing. That amount grows with each new fab the company builds, and with the more advanced manufacturing processes TSMC is developing. The company recycles 65 percent of the water it uses in Arizona, TSMC says, a figure that’s supposed to grow to at least 90 percent when it finishes building a water reclamation plant.

“There’s not enough water for everything we want to do with it.”

The Colorado River is the state’s biggest renewable source of water. But the Colorado River Basin has faced “unprecedented” drought for more than a quarter century, according to the US Bureau of Reclamation. Climate change, unfortunately, is also making the region more dry as growing water demand adds to decades of overuse.

“There’s not enough water for everything we want to do with it,” Sorensen, who previously worked as the director of Phoenix Water Services, says. “So what do we have enough water for? What are the uses we most value? Is it cotton or is it microchips?”

With 40 million Americans from Denver to Los Angeles relying on water from the Colorado River, states have been tussling over how to allocate the remaining water for years. Guidelines for how to manage that water, collectively known as the “Law of the River,” expire this year. After states failed to reach an agreement on their own, the US Department of the Interior finalized its own plan in August for how to move forward. It outlines steep cuts for downriver states: Arizona, Nevada, and California. Arizona stands to lose the most, at least 760,000 acre-feet of water a year starting in 2027. An acre-foot represents how much water it would take to cover an acre with a foot of water, and is enough to supply about three homes with water for a year in the Phoenix area. The City of Phoenix uses about 300,000 acre feet of water in a year.

Maricopa County, home to Intel and TSMC’s chip fabs, isn’t as reliant on water from the Colorado River as other counties. Its primary resource is groundwater, but surface water flowing from the Colorado and Salt rivers still make up close to 40 percent of the county’s supply.

Local leaders insist that Phoenix and other cities in the region are prepared for water cuts, citing plans to make up for the shortfall with underground water stores and other surface water sources. “For the most part, they’ve planned accordingly and can fall back onto water that was previously stored underground,” Sorensen says.

But even without sudden tap water shortages, Sorensen expects utility bills to climb over time. The transition to alternative water resources will entail new infrastructure, like new wells and pipes. That’s likely to be the most significant driver of higher tap water prices, Sorensen explains.

Meanwhile, the city of Phoenix is pushing back, with Mayor Kate Gallego arguing that the federal government’s decision to cut the state’s intake “does not provide the fair, basin-wide leadership the Colorado River crisis demands.” That said, “Phoenix is prepared for this moment because of decades of planning and conservation, we will push for new federal support to mitigate the rising cost of water that will result from this federal decision,” Gallego added in an August press release. A spokesperson for the city declined to comment further in an interview.

TSMC in particular, located in Phoenix, will be subject to the same price hikes as its neighbors. Phoenix is unique in that it sets the same water rates for companies as it does for residential customers. Cities often charge industrial customers less if they want to attract certain businesses.

“The cost of water will increase for TSMC,” Sorensen says. “Everyone pays the same rate for water in the city of Phoenix, whether you’re a mom-and-pop store, a family of eight, or TSMC.”

TSMC and Intel declined interviews with The Verge for this story. Both have made public commitments, however, to minimize the amount of fresh water they consume.

“A stable supply of water is critical to chip production,” TSMC deputy spokesperson Nina Kao said in an emailed statement. “One of the reasons the city of Phoenix was selected for our US expansion is because of their long-term water plan, which includes varied water supply sources, as well as steps taken in preparation for reduced water supplies over the course of decades.”

Apprehensions are still mounting over the impact that AI and the tech industry as a whole have on the region. AI has spawned a new generation of semiconductor factories, chip packaging plants, and data centers across Arizona.

“A stable supply of water is critical to chip production.”

“It’s almost happening at a level that’s difficult to wrap your head around,” says Jennifer Martin-McLeod, a program manager for the Grand Canyon chapter of Sierra Club. “To try to say ‘Everybody take a breath and think through what we’re doing’ is difficult when you have that steamroller of money coming at your state to try to make it all happen overnight.”

She has broader concerns about the health of the Colorado River and wildlife that depends on it. Over the long term, Sorensen points out that a shortage of water from the Colorado River will result in the depletion of groundwater in Central Arizona, as most cities cope by increasing how much water they draw from local aquifers. “It’s something they can sustain, but it is only sustained at a cost to future generations,” she adds.

The impact of water cuts next year will be felt most by typical residents, Martin-McLeod says. “For me, that’s going to mean serious lifestyle changes. … But to an enormous chip manufacturer, that’s maybe just part of the cost of doing business, you know?”

Tech.title: Insta360 launches a single-lens Osmo Pocket rival you can actually buy in the US
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Insta360’s first compact steadycam, the Luna Ultra, made a splash this year by beating DJI to launch with two lenses. Now it’s followed the Ultra with a slightly stripped back Pro model, which drops to one lens but has a unique advantage: It can shoot vertical video in 4K. Plus, unlike DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4, you can buy it in the US.

At its heart, the Luna Pro is mostly an Ultra with the telephoto lens stripped out. It uses the same 1-inch-type 8K sensor as the Ultra’s main camera, and has a similar design including the detachable 2-inch touchscreen that doubles as a remote, and the same four-hour battery life and NFC tag for quicker file transfers. It’s a bit smaller and lighter thanks to dropping the second lens, but that’s about it.

Insta360 has given the Pro one crucial upgrade though: It can use that 8K sensor to record 4K vertical video at 30fps. The Luna Ultra — like both of DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4 and 4P models — is limited to 3K resolution when you record in portrait, forcing some people to hold the whole gimbal sideways to get the footage they need. It’s a relief to see the Pro fix that omission, and Insta360 told me that it will also be added to the Luna Ultra in a firmware update, currently expected to be released on September 20th.

The Luna Pro’s single camera uses the same sensor as the Ultra. Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge 4K30 vertical recording is the main new feature, a boon for social media creators. Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge The 2-inch OLED is once again detachable, doubling as a remote control for the whole camera. Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge The NFC tag has moved into the camera head, and is used for opening the Insta360 smartphone app for quicker file transfer. Photo: Dominic Preston / The Verge

The Luna Pro is out now in the US for $599.99, compared to $769.99 for the Luna Ultra. In Europe it starts at £469 / €529, just a little more than the £429 / €479 DJI Osmo Pocket 4, which is (officially) unavailable in the US following a ban on the company.

Update, September 11th: Added confirmation that the Luna Ultra will receive a firmware update to add 4K vertical video.

Tech.title: Apple addresses iPhone Duo copycats
Tech.content:
is a deputy editor and Verge co-founder with a passion for human-centric cities, e-bikes, and life as a digital nomad. He’s been a tech journalist for 20 years.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple was far from the first company to announce a passport-shaped folding phone this year, but that doesn’t mean it wasn’t copied. As my colleague Dom Preston already explained, it’s almost impossible to keep product development secret when Apple and its competitors all share the same global suppliers.

Apple’s new CEO John Ternus and head of marketing Greg ‘Joz’ Joswiak addressed the topic during an interview with TechRadar’s Lance Ulanoff and Mark Spoonauer of Tom’s Guide.

“People knew through leaks that we were working on a foldable,” said Joz. “Unfortunately, they got the aspect ratio, and a lot of coincidental instances of people finding that an interesting aspect ratio.” By “people,” Joz means Samsung, Huawei, and Xiaomi who all announced wide foldables ahead of Apple.

What did remain a secret is the folding nano-texture display unique to the iPhone Duo. “What I’m super proud of — we kept it secret,” said Joz. “We put the extra security on it. We didn’t talk about it to anybody.”

The whole interview is worth a watch. Ternus’ boyish enthusiasm is a refreshing change from the more measured Tim Cook, signaling his roots as a hands-on engineer. You can see it when describing his first interaction with a prototype of the display. “Oh this is it, this is what I want,” he said, eagerly grinning.

The new head of Apple, unlike Cook, is clearly a product guy, just like its mercurial founder.

Tech.title: Slack can now vibe-code interactive charts and reports inside chats
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new feature coming to Slack will allow you to build interactive reports, polls, dashboards, presentations, microsites, and other tools directly inside a chat. With Slackforce Surfaces, you can describe to Slackbot what you need, and it will use AI to gather information from relevant conversations and connected apps, like Google Drive or Salesforce, to create it.

Once Slackbot creates a Surface, you can share it with colleagues and pin it to channels, allowing other people to view it, interact with it, and leave comments. In one example shared by Slack, a user asks Slackbot for help creating an arcade-themed visualization of AI token usage. The AI assistant then generates an interactive dashboard showing token usage across different divisions, such as sales, design, and engineering.

“You’re not exporting your data to some other tool to make sense of it, you’re asking Slackbot to build the dashboard, the deck, the report right where the conversation already is, and your whole team can act on it together,” Ryan Gavin, Slack’s chief marketing officer, tells The Verge in an email.

This update comes just months after Slack overhauled Slackbot to make the tool more like an AI assistant, allowing it to summarize information across channels, sort through messages, and find time to schedule meetings. It also added collaborative vibe coding channels last month.

It seems like there are many other ways to use Surfaces, too, like building a live dashboard for a customer support queue that other workers can view, or creating a weather-themed financial forecast that pulls in data from connected apps. Slack notes that the feature will only pull information that you’ve given its AI tools permission to access.

Slackforce Surfaces is available to all customers — including those who use it for free — with Slackbot enabled in their workspace. You’ll be able to use it with live data starting in October.

Tech.title: Schools are catching on to Big Tech’s playbook
Tech.content:
It’s the hot new thing in tech, and it’s where all the jobs are. Students who don’t learn to use it fall behind. And to help them catch up in time, its creators are graciously providing the resources and curriculum for learning it, often pro bono.

That’s the narrative AI companies are pitching schools on right now, but according to New York Times education technology reporter Natasha Singer, it’s also how the tech industry has built its influence in classrooms for the past 15 years.

In a new book, Coding Kids, Singer details how tech companies took a central role in promoting computers and coding skills in education, promising computer science skills were the ticket to high-paying jobs. But by the time many of those students entered the workforce, new technologies had thrown that promise into question. Meanwhile, the companies got schools to help them create a new class of would-be workers, and trained students on using their products and software, making them likely future customers.

“I worry we have collective amnesia”

Now, the AI industry is pitching itself to schools with similar force. “I worry we have collective amnesia,” Singer told me on a recent episode of The Vergecast. “Have we learned any lessons from these past tech cycles in schools that are going to inform the rollout of AI, make sure that it benefits education, and put in the safeguards now — not a decade from now?” Fortunately, in some ways, she believes the answer is yes.

Singer’s book recounts how more than a decade ago, the country’s largest tech companies embedded themselves directly into school curricula through courses for Advanced Placement Computer Science Principles classes. Apple and Microsoft each created their own curricula, featuring their own tools like Apple’s Swift or Microsoft’s Minecraft. “What’s striking about this is you can imagine that parents would not want, say, Pfizer AP Biology, or Northrop Grumman AP Physics, or ExxonMobil Environmental Science AP,” Singer says. She found that those in the medical field would likely understand why — medical students who are trained by a company on how to implant their proprietary device, one expert told her as an example, rarely choose to try another.

Google has also made itself a dominant force in education through its distribution of low-cost laptops called Chromebooks. Singer tracked their ubiquitous adoption across schools through the 2010s, which she says was accelerated even further during the school shutdowns of the covid-19 pandemic. Google also introduced its Classroom app to help teachers communicate things like assignments and grades. By the time generative AI took off, Singer writes, Google was already a key platform provider for many schools, and well-positioned to promote it.

Even when companies weren’t directly involved in education, they backed nonprofit groups like Code.org. Code.org kicked off its viral education campaign with a splashy celebrity-laden video that included tech moguls like Microsoft founder Bill Gates and then-Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, urging kids to learn to code. Code.org founder Hadi Partovi took a startup-style approach to promoting computer science education, and had little planned for how to capitalize on the attention of the video once it took off, Singer writes. He ultimately funneled that attention into a similarly splashy “Hour of Code” campaign across the country, urging schools to engage in entertaining hour-long courses introducing kids to coding building blocks.

At the time, there wasn’t much pushback, Singer found — though there were some attempts at alternatives. One group of academics engaged in a more traditional, methodological approach to testing and rolling out their own computer science curriculum. It had the express goal of diversifying the kinds of students enrolled in such courses, and taught students to think about big questions around the internet and technology, and scrutinize builders’ motivations.

Eventually, backlash arrived. Some recent graduates say they feel let down that they were told to code their whole lives, just to find such entry-level jobs to be diminishing, Singer told me. Some schools are getting rid of ubiquitous Google Chromebooks, and research around the world is finding that adding technology to the classroom often doesn’t have a significant impact on actual learning.

“Most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech”

“I’m not arguing against tech education or tech in schools,” Singer says. “But what I am saying is most parents want more than just getting kids to learn to use tech. They want kids to learn how to be informed citizens in a democracy, and they want kids to figure out what their passions are and who they are and what their beliefs are… And so if we let the tech industry dictate or even heavily influence what happens in schools, then the question we’re asking is, how can we get AI into schools faster? Which is a product question, and not, ‘What are the most important things we want kids to learn?’”

While the AI industry of the 2020s may be pulling from the 2010s playbook, there already appears to be one distinct difference: Parents and school districts are pushing back. Just last week, the nation’s largest school system, New York City, banned elementary and middle schools from letting students use AI in the classroom for the coming school year. A day later, Los Angeles announced an even broader restriction that included high schoolers. And unlike the few-and-far-between critiques Singer documented in the early days of tech’s coding push, there appears to be a vibrant grassroots movement fighting the screen- and AI-ification of the classroom among parents and teachers alike.

“I think schools are beginning to figure it out,” says Singer, who’s “optimistic” that teachers and students are looking for a broader kind of tech education. That curriculum could teach kids “to ask deep questions about how companies are steering us with their technology, how software and AI are designed to affect our choices, and what role students have to use the tools productively. But also to push back if they like, and to not feel like they’re in a world where AI is driving them.”

Tech.title: Scammers target hundreds of thousands of crypto owners after Trezor confirms data breach of email provider
Tech.content:
Hardware crypto wallet maker Trezor is warning customers for the second time in as many months that one of the companies it relies on was hacked, exposing the data of Trezor’s customers to hackers.

In a blog post this week, the hardware wallet maker said a cyberattack on Brevo, a marketing tech company that Trezor uses to send newsletters, allowed hackers to send around 347,000 phishing emails to Trezor customers with a malicious link purporting to come from the wallet maker.

The link, when tapped, downloads an app that asks the victim for their wallet backup password. According to Trezor, one of the email subject lines said: “Critical Security Alert: STM32 Entropy Vulnerability.”

With a stolen wallet password, a hacker can irreversibly steal the person’s funds on the public blockchain.

Brevo said in an incident status post that the hackers were able to access 138 Brevo accounts to send out the mass volume of phishing messages. Brevo said that the hackers abused a flaw that meant the hackers’ access was “not properly scoped.” The company said that the hackers’ access was “wrongly granted” to all organizations that the hackers’ accounts could reach.

The breach highlights a common security incident, where hackers compromise data held by third-party companies that are necessary for fulfilling orders or purchases from customers. Trezor says none of its products, wallets, or account system was affected by the incident.

This is the second breach in recent weeks affecting Trezor, after the company alerted customers in August that one of its shipping partners was compromised in a data breach. The incident at the mailing company ShipMonk exposed the names, phone numbers, email addresses, and postal addresses of at least 81,000 people who bought and received Trezor wallet hardware.

The data breach could put crypto owners and other wealthy individuals at risk of targeted violence and so-called “wrench” attacks, which rely on physical attacks to extract passwords from people.

In the weeks following the breach at ShipMonk, some people have received letters by mail claiming to be from Trezor, featuring a QR code that, when scanned, opens up a fake page that attempts to steal the victim’s crypto wallet password.

Trezor said it was reevaluating its relationships with its vendors and warned customers that their email addresses may be used again for future phishing attacks.

Tech.title: Thrive Capital led VCs into pro sports ownership; Collaborative Fund just upped that play
Tech.content:
Collaborative Fund, the 15-year-old, New York-based generalist venture firm that has roughly $1 billion under management and that made early bets on Lyft, Reddit, Sweetgreen, and Olipop, among others, is taking a stake in the soccer club D.C. United and its stadium, Audi Field.

It’s the latest — and smallest — firm to try something that Thrive Capital opened the door to just months ago: turning venture money into pro sports ownership.

To recap, Joshua Kushner’s Thrive launched a new vehicle, Thrive Eternal, explicitly built to hold “iconic franchises and cultural institutions” for decades, funded by many of the same investors already in Thrive’s venture and growth funds. The firm kicked things off by announcing a stake in the San Francisco Giants. Months later, the same vehicle — with former Disney CEO Bob Iger, a Thrive partner, joining as co-owner — bought the Lakers outright for a record $12.5 billion.

That’s new. Historically, money has poured into pro sports two other ways: individual tech fortunes and private equity. For example, Vinod Khosla and his family agreed this summer to buy the Seattle Seahawks for a record $9.6 billion soon after the Khosla family also took a stake in the San Francisco 49ers alongside OpenAI chairman Bret Taylor. That was a personal-wealth play, the kind we’ve seen over and over.

Private equity firms have also been at this for years, including Sixth Street, which holds stakes in the Boston Celtics, the New England Patriots, and MLB’s San Francisco Giants; Ares, which owns a piece of the Miami Dolphins outright and separately financed Chelsea’s stadium plans through a $500 million preferred-equity deal; RedBird, which owns AC Milan outright and holds a minority stake in Fenway Sports Group, the holding company behind Liverpool and the Red Sox; and Arctos, with minority positions scattered across MLB, the NFL, the NBA, and European soccer. (Apollo, the newest entrant, has mostly stuck to sports financing deals so far rather than ownership stakes.)

Thrive and Collaborative are doing neither of those things. At the same time, the two firms’ approaches to sports ownership look very different. Thrive built a stand-alone, permanent-capital vehicle specifically to hold trophy assets. Collaborative is investing out of the same early-stage fund it uses to write seed and Series A checks, and treating the deal less like something to buy and hold and almost more like infrastructure.

In a memo shared with TechCrunch, Collaborative Fund founder and managing partner Craig Shapiro framed the deal as an extension of what the firm already does. “A franchise is the ultimate consumer product,” he wrote, arguing that D.C. United’s status as one of Major League Soccer’s original clubs gives Collaborative access to an institution with a decades-long fan base to build on.

He pointed to the tailwinds around American soccer specifically (a World Cup just behind the sport, the LA Olympics ahead of it, soaring youth participation numbers in the U.S.), as well as D.C.’s ownership of Audi Field in Washington, D.C., plus a talent-development pipeline through Loudoun County, Virginia, and rights to a future Baltimore expansion team.

Indeed, the thesis Shapiro laid out at a TechCrunch StrictlyVC event Thursday night in New York is less about owning a piece of an appreciating asset — the sports team itself — and more about what the team makes possible. Collaborative wants to turn Audi Field into what he describes as a living showcase for its own portfolio.

As a backer of both fitness band maker Whoop and the beverage brand Olipop, for example, Collaborative Fund is imagining a Whoop wearables activation for fans, or Olipop drinks woven into game-day concessions. He’s thinking about the stadium’s foot traffic — tens of thousands of people showing up on a predictable schedule — as a distribution channel at a time when, because AI is making more of daily life feel synthetic, live experiences are becoming more valuable.

Shapiro doesn’t dwell on this, but it surely helped sell Collaborative’s investors that team valuations have been soaring, so the stake could pay off on its own. Soccer valuations in particular have been on a tear. Inter Miami’s franchise value has roughly doubled in the two years since Lionel Messi arrived, MLS’s average club value is up roughly 134% since 2019, and D.C. United’s own valuation has climbed from $35 million in 2008 to $785 million today, factoring in its ownership of Audi Field and the surrounding real estate.

If Shapiro is right that a franchise is also “the ultimate consumer product,” it could be a pretty good place to park money. Time will tell.

The deal is subject to MLS approval.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang explains why Nvidia will grow an astounding 70% next year
Tech.content:
Founder, CEO, and tireless Nvidia hype man Jensen Huang told attendees at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology conference on Thursday why his company’s AI domination — and revenues — will continue its record-breaking growth streak through the end of next year.

He can see the future.

There’s been endless hand-wringing over whether Nvidia’s party will end as it faces increasing competition for GPUs and AI chips from all directions: the hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, each building their own) and the AI labs (Anthropic and OpenAI, which are building their own), as well as from newly public competitor Cerebras and startups such as Etched.

“Most people think Nvidia builds a chip. I mean, you need airplanes to ship what we build,” Huang said, adding that the company continues to battle a perception from its early days. Nvidia invented the GPU, which back then were largely sold to consumers to improve PC gaming. “One GPU now is not $399. It’s $8.5 million dollars. That’s one GPU, all connected with NVLink, 2 million parts, right? 250,000 kilowatts. That’s a GPU, and we ship thousands of them.”

He added that orders for just one product, a computer system that combines 36 Grace CPUs with 72 Blackwell GPUs, is currently experiencing 27% month-to-month sales growth.

Huang didn’t limit his bullish view to current sales though. He took the opportunity to reiterate Nvidia’s revenue outlook for next year — guidance the company provided last month when it reported yet another record-breaking revenue quarter. That’s when he first said revenue could grow by 70% next year.

“I think we could grow 70% year over year. We’re confident about that,” Huang said again on Thursday. Analysts expect the company to end its current fiscal year at about $400 billion in revenue. So 70% growth would mean around $680 billion next year.

Huang explained why he’s confident: His company is so embedded in every area of AI that he believes he can see the future.

“Nvidia runs every model. Every single lab can use us,” the CEO said, mentioning that this includes models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google, as well as open-weight offerings. “We are a foundational platform of the AI ecosystem, foundational platform of the AI industry.”

Nvidia’s fingers extend all the way from its suppliers, such as memory chip makers, to data center projects and startups.

“We’re tracking every single gigawatt of land, power, shell around the world. Literally everything on the planet,” he said. (“Shell” refers to the shell of a data center building before it is outfitted with computers).

“I mean, just think about all my partners. How many neoclouds are reporting back to us? How many OEMs are reporting back to us? How many clouds are reporting back to us? How many AI-native companies are reporting back to us? We’re working with everybody, and so we kind of know where everything is,” he said.

That comment led to inevitable questions about Nvidia’s so-called circular deals, in which it invests in companies that turn around and buy its wares. Such schemes famously contributed to the downfall of a previous generation of internet build-out suppliers like Lucent Technologies.

Huang had a simple, albeit cheeky, response. “Well, it’s not circular because we put a little bit of money in, and a lot of money comes back.” He went on to joke, “I look at the spreadsheet, we put in $1 and $100 comes back in. Is that circular? If that is, let’s do more of that.”

Quips aside, he insisted that before any of these companies gets an investment, Nvidia makes sure it has real contracts generating revenue from customers. All told, he said he’s seen $100 billion worth of such contracts, “I’m not taking any risks. … I need a sure thing.”

Time will tell whether Nvidia’s stronghold on AI can really persist long term. If there’s one golden rule of the tech industry, it’s that all big things get disrupted. Right now, even Huang admits that much of AI’s growth is coming from AI-native startups that are raising vast sums and spending most of that cash on their own AI use. As the AI industry matures, expect companies to become more efficient in how they use infrastructure and tokens.

But for now, Nvidia has its finger in every pie and sees another year of plenty in its future.

Tech.title: Mark Wahlberg is coming to TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, and he wants to talk about your work, not his
Tech.content:
Let’s just get this out of the way: Mark Wahlberg is as A-list as it gets. He broke out in 1997’s “Boogie Nights,” and in the nearly three decades since, he’s built one of the highest-wattage careers in Hollywood: two Academy Award nominations, a Golden Globe nod for “The Fighter,” multiple Emmy nominations as a producer (HBO’s “Entourage” among them), and a filmography that spans crime dramas, comedies, and action blockbusters. Right now, he’s back on-screen in “By Any Means,” a manhunt thriller set during the 1966 Mississippi civil rights killings.

He’s also signaling where he’s increasingly turning his attention. Wahlberg will sit down with Bruce K. Lee, founder and CEO of Keebeck Wealth Management, on the main stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 to talk about that progression. Grab your ticket here so you don’t miss a moment of this session and Disrupt 2026. Ticket prices increase on September 25.

From Hollywood to business venture

His acting career is really just part of the picture. Over the past two decades, Wahlberg has built a production company, a restaurant chain, apparel and fitness ventures, a slate of angel investments, and the now-25-year-old Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation, which supports inner-city kids and teens. He’s used his Hollywood success to launch big projects well outside the movie business — and in a fireside chat at this year’s Disrupt, he’s going to give us a peek into how.

Building an investing mindset

Wahlberg, who’s leaned almost entirely on entrepreneurial instinct about people, culture, products, and markets, is now someone who’s been building institutional-level investing discipline, with Lee as his guide, and with a growing focus on healthcare and wellness startups. It’s a rare, unvarnished look at how someone with Wahlberg’s cultural intelligence has worked his way into some of the most sophisticated rooms in business and finance.

He also discusses where high-profile entertainers and athletes sometimes get it wrong (Wahlberg is candid about having had to unlearn some of his own old instincts); how he’s used the trust built over a massive career to drive access and deal flow; and which technologies he’s most focused on right now and why.

Go inside Wahlberg’s playbook
